#3430. GTA: Boston Would Go Wicked Hard, Kid

Considering that Grand Theft Auto 6 just launched after a 13-year wait, it’s safe to say that we won’t be getting another one any time soon. That’s fine, because Leonida is so enormous that I know I’ll still be finding secrets in it years from now. And yet, I can’t help myself. I’m already wondering where the series could possibly go next. Allow me to offer one unsolicited idea: Massachusetts.

That’s right suckers, Miami and Los Angeles’ time is over. It’s time to let me drive a sports car down the Freedom Trail as I barrel through Boston blasting Dropkick Murphys. You can chalk this up to a little Thanksgiving homesickness, as I wasn’t able to travel to my home state for the holiday, but I am convinced I am on to something here.

The thing that really makes GTA 6 so special is Leonida. Rockstar’s digital recreation of Florida is a perfect playground for GTA’s sandbox chaos, and it takes advantage of the state’s geographical diversity to do that. You’ve got a bustling Miami to build on for Vice City, but you also have a mix of run-down towns, rural farmlands, beaches, and quiet islands. That wide array of locations makes for a more varied GTA experience, as you bounce between areas with very different speeds.

You know what other state has that feel? Massachusetts, baby! You’ve got Boston at the heart of it all, a historic city that’s unlike any Rockstar has ever recreated. Just outside the city limits, you’ve got a host of quaint suburban towns filled with shopping malls and banks. Go west, and you’ll end up in the deep wilderness, just as you find yourself in when you go north in Leonida. On the east side, you’ve got Cape Cod, a vacation getaway built on a fishing economy. And just off the coast, you’ve got scenic islands like Martha’s Vineyard and Nantucket. Boil all of that down into a tight GTA map, and you’ve got all the same basic ingredients that make Leonida fun to explore, but in a state that looks and feels very different.

Rockstar is no stranger to the region, either. 2006’s Bully was set in a fictional town in New England. Even though that was 20 years ago, Rockstar nailed the feeling of suburban ennui that exists throughout the state. It’s easy to see how the team could recapture that spirit by including its own take on Harvard in a GTA game. Hell, why not just make the town of Bullworth canon to GTA?

There’s more to Leonida than its landmarks, of course. Florida also makes for a great GTA setting because it’s full of the kind of strange Americans Rockstar loves to lampoon. GTA 6 gets to play around with conspiracy theorists, right-wing gun nuts, rich playboys, and more in its wide cultural satire.

Well guess what? Massachusetts is full of ripe comedic targets too! Within Boston alone, you’ve got your pick of loudmouthed bros who always seem eager to get into a bar fight. That’s contrasted with wealthy retirees living in beach bubbles, hustling Italian-Americans in Boston’s North End, artsy communities in towns like Northampton, and so much more. There’s so much to satirize beyond your typical Masshole, even though Rockstar could have a field day poking fun at the accent.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

More than anything, I’m dying to see Boston’s obsessive sports culture make its way into GTA. You get some nods to the real sports world of Miami in GTA 6, but it would most assuredly be the central focus of a Boston-set game full of loudmouthed Red Sox and Patriots fans. Let me go to Gillette Stadium and plow through Patriot Place in a bulldozer, cowards! And considering how much Rockstar enjoys lampooning current cultural trends, there’s even fertile ground to dig into the rise of sports betting and treat it as a criminal enterprise. I mean, Rockstar must be licking its lips at the prospect of making a fake Kalshi, right?

My wishlist of things I’d love to see in Grand Theft Massachusetts is long: Faneuil Hall! Boston Dynamics! Logan Airport! I’m sure that people from just about any other state in America feel the same way about their home. So much of the fun of GTA 6 is getting such a wide view of Florida that really emphasizes how diverse a single state can be. It’s easy to flatten them out, judging them by their cultural urban epicenters or voting demographics, but a good road trip will show you just how vibrant even the smallest pockets of the country can be. Every state deserves to be roasted as bad as Florida.

#3428. The Best Scene In Focker In-Law, According To Director John Hamburg [Exclusive]

This article contains minor spoilers for "Focker In-Law."

Although it's not the only way comedy sequels can be successful, whether or not they stand out often comes down to their jokes. After all, while most of the great comedy sequels earn their status by being just as much or nearly as unique as their predecessors, if the jokes are lacking, then it's all for naught. This is why many comedy sequels are identified not by their character arcs or plot but by their gags and setpieces. "Gremlins 2: The New Batch" will primarily be known for its inclusion of wilder and weirder Gremlins, "Addams Family Values" has a memorable Thanksgiving play sequence, and so on.

So far, the "Meet the Parents" franchise has enjoyed its longevity thanks to adding new stars to the Focker family and beyond. "Meet the Fockers" introduced Barbara Streisand and Dustin Hoffman as the parents of Ben Stiller's Greg Focker, while "Little Fockers" used the occasion of the Fockers having babies to include new faces such as Jessica Alba's Andi. This month's "Focker In-Law" continues the tradition by casting hot young talents Skyler Gisondo and Beanie Feldstein as the Focker children, with Ariana Grande also turning up in a major role as Greg's son's fiancé. However, writer/director John Hamburg cleverly understood that he couldn't solely rely on the cast to make his film stand out. He wanted to conceive a sequence that would match the cringe comedy outrageousness of the original film while using all his stars in a big way. He does so in the moment where Greg sings John Legend's "All of Me" to Jack Byrnes (Robert De Niro), which, according to Hamburg himself, is the best scene in the movie.

One of the things "Focker In-Law" does really well is escalation, in which Greg Focker makes a series of choices which have minor consequences at first but quickly snowball into increasingly more ludicrous events. The apex of this is when Greg (Ben Stiller), who has taken it upon himself to keep Henry (Skyler Gisondo) from proposing to Olivia (Ariana Grande) by hiding the engagement ring, discovers at the last minute that Henry had secretly planned to sing a song at dinner with everyone present. Scrambling, Greg decides to perform the song himself, and dedicate it to his occasional family nemesis, Jack.

When I had the opportunity to speak to Hamburg about the movie, he chose this setpiece as the best scene in the film from a subjective and objective perspective. As he explained:

"I'd say for this movie, it's recency bias, but there's a scene where Greg serenades Jack. And most of the cast is sitting around this table and Owen Wilson's at the piano. And that was just a really epic moment in my career as a filmmaker. To have these amazingly talented people gathered on one set and then have Ben singing and Bob's reactions are so priceless. It was just like everything kind of came together. That's like the dream for a comedy filmmaker, to have that. And then the audience reaction was so great. [...] There's many [great scenes], but of many, I'd say that sequence is one I reflect on. It's like, that was a really fun couple of days of shooting."

Given how well it works both in and out of context, the scene is absolutely a standout moment. And who knows, maybe Stiller will sing again in the next "Focker" film because of it.

#3427. 5 Best Book Series To Read If You Like The Hunger Games

Unless you've been living under a rock for multiple decades, you've probably heard of "The Hunger Games." Written by Suzanne Collins, this hybrid of "Battle Royale" and reality television hit shelves in 2008 and introduced readers around the world to Katniss Everdeen, a young woman trying to support her family with illegal game hunting in the deeply impoverished District 12 of a reformed North America known as Panem. When Katniss' beloved younger sister Primrose is chosen, or "reaped," via a random lottery to participate in the annual Games (where two "tributes" from all 12 districts are forced to compete to the death on live television until one victor emerges), Katniss volunteers as tribute, and her time as a Hunger Games participant begins.

"The Hunger Games" kicked off the property of the same name and was followed by sequels "Catching Fire" and "Mockingjay," released in 2009 and 2010. Naturally, a "Hunger Games" film franchise followed in 2012 and spawned four blockbusters. ("Mockingjay" got split into two parts, something that director Francis Lawrence regrets.) Then, in 2020, Collins released her first literary "Hunger Games" prequel, "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" — which centers on the origin story of future Panem president Coriolanus Snow — and five years later, we got "Sunrise on the Reaping," which explains precisely how Katniss' eventual friend and mentor (and her fellow District 12 victor) Haymitch Abernathy won his Games.

If you've already read all of the "Hunger Games" books and seen all the movies (including the pretty great movie version of "Sunrise on the Reaping," which is now out in theaters), what should you check out next? From dystopian classics to other YA favorites, we've got some ideas.

A lot of dystopian novels are referred to as "speculative fiction," which means that the scenario laid out by the author could conceivably happen in real life ... so, let's hope that Nana Kwame Adjei-Brenyah's novel "Chain-Gang All-Stars" doesn't come to pass. Released in 2023, this novel imagines a world where the incarceration system in the United States is, somehow, even worse than it is in our reality — in that prisoners are allowed to enroll in a program called CAPE, which stands for "Criminal Action Penal Entertainment." Not only are the inmates in CAPE constantly monitored (with their every move broadcast to hungry audiences), they're also sent across the country to constantly participate in gladiator matches against each other that are, you guessed it, televised as well. The book's title comes from the reimagined version of a traditional "chain gang," where the prisoner-gladiators are called "Links" and given two options to leave: either they're High Freed, meaning released, or Low Freed, meaning killed.

Throughout "Chain-Gang All-Stars," we follow the Angola-Hammond Chain in the system and, more specifically, Hamara "Hurricane Staxxx" Stacker and Loretta "Blood Mama" Thurwar, the two female fighters in a secret relationship who open the book. As we move through the unsettling world Adjei-Brenyah concocted in "Chain-Gang All Stars," we follow a wide variety of prisoners participating in this gut-wrenching game ... and it's sort of impossible to not think of the "Hunger Games" franchise as you read it, albeit in a good way. After you wrap up all five "Hunger Games" books, check out "Chain-Gang All-Stars." (Nina Starner)

When it comes to seeing people die horrible deaths in death games televised for the entertainment of an oppressive ruling class, no book does it on a larger scale than Matt Dinniman's "Dungeon Crawler Carl." The book takes place after Earth has been taken over by an alien corporation that seeks to mine the planet for resources. Those who aren't killed during the initial invasion are then forced to compete in an intergalactic reality show program, an RPG-like "dungeon crawl" where they have to navigate various levels of a labyrinthian dungeon, each filled with increasingly dangerous monsters and scenarios.

What makes "Dungeon Crawler Carl" unique is how it blends together ridiculous video game and tabletop RPG logic with an unhealthy dose of pop culture references, the humor of a Douglas Adams book, and the brutality and social commentary about unchecked capitalism and authoritarianism of "The Hunger Games." Indeed, reading Dinniman's book and its follow-ups is like playing a fun RPG session, in that it's chaotic, messy, hilarious, and weird, all while packing a serious emotional punch full of heartbreak and cruel twists and turns. But rather than reveling in their misery, Dinniman's characters rage against the corporate machine in an effort to break it. What you end up with is a story about the necessity of resistance and the importance of community, both of which are themes that will resonate with "Hunger Games" fans. And did I mention it features an endlessly quotable talking cat? (Rafael Motamayor)

I don't think it's possible to have a conversation about young adult dystopian books and films like the "Hunger Games" stories without discussing "The Handmaid's Tale." Margaret Atwood's landmark 1980 book set a standard for dystopian narratives rivaled only by George Orwell's "1984," but Atwood's specificity is what makes her imagined world so terrifying — in that "The Handmaid's Tale" takes place in a world where a religious totalitarian regime oppresses women and queer people. Offred (meaning "of Fred"), our heroine, works as one of the titular handmaids, which means she's prized for her fertility and used as a "vessel" (that's putting it politely) for her Commander, Fred, to impregnate instead of his un-fertile wife. As Offred exists in Gilead (which forbids women from having quite literally any rights and punishes them with death if they even try to stray), we follow her every move in the novel, learning bits and pieces about her life before Gilead as June, a mother and wife with the freedom to live as she pleased.

"The Handmaid's Tale" was adapted into a Hulu series in 2017, and while I do think Elisabeth Moss did an incredible job playing Offred, the show ran through Atwood's book by the end of Season 1 and kept its wheels spinning for, in my opinion, far too long (although it at least gets its final message right.) If you haven't read Atwood's book but are familiar with its well-known red costumes and overall vibe, I couldn't possibly recommend it more. Its prose is beautiful, its subject matter is terrifying, and it's a clear precursor to and inspiration for the stories found in the "Hunger Games" franchise. (Nina Starner)

Though certainly not as dark in tone as "The Hunger Games," the pop culture celebration that is author Ernest Cline's "Ready Player One" is an oddly fitting companion piece for fans of the world Suzanne Collins built. One could even look at it as a bit of a palette cleanser, albeit one that still scratches a similar itch.

For those not familiar, the book takes place in 2044 and focuses on Wade Watts, who spends his days in the virtual utopia known as the OASIS. Wade's devoted his life to studying the puzzles hidden within this world's digital confines, themselves based on their creator's fixation on pop culture — with the promise of massive power and fortune to whoever can unlock them.

"Ready Player One" is jam-packed with pop culture references and is lighthearted in a lot of ways. However, it's also terribly dystopian, as the OASIS is not only people's sole escape from the harsh realities of the outside world, there's very little person-to-person communication anymore outside of the virtual space. Beyond that, the rush to solve the puzzles and nab the fortune results in a deadly game for Wade and many others, which is where the "Hunger Games" of it all comes in.

Steven Spielberg's 2018 movie adaptation left a lot to be desired for many fans and, yes, a "Ready Player Two" movie was in the works in 2021, though it's yet to materialize. Setting the film aside, the novel remains a true gem filled with wonderful world building, fully-realized characters, and just a dash of "kill or be killed" to make the whole thing extra exciting, elevating it beyond the barrage of references it might have otherwise been. (Ryan Scott)

The funny thing about Pierce Brown's "Red Rising" series is that the first book in the still-ongoing saga is very much a "Hunger Games" riff ... until it's not. Set in a distant future where humanity has been rigidly split into various genetically modified castes that determine a person's role in society, the story follows Darrow, a young Martian "red" whose wife is murdered by the ruling "gold" regime, sending him on a quest for revenge that ultimately spans the entire solar system. But before the sweeping space opera can begin, Darrow infiltrates the gold caste and must survive the Institute, a deadly school where young people are violently set against one another in not-so-simulated combat and conquest.

Those who enjoyed the blend of youthful angst, action, sci-fi world-building, and dystopian politics of "The Hunger Games" will take quickly and easily to "Red Rising," which offers a similar flavor with a harsher, more masculine edge. However, starting with the second book "Golden Son" and continuing into later installments, Brown takes things in a wholly new direction, turning his Suzanne Collins riff into the kind of sprawling, detailed, intense, and morally murky epic that would make Frank Herbert and George R.R. Martin proud. This is the perfect stepping stone for "Hunger Games" fans hoping to branch out into a different flavor of science fiction. It's familiar enough, until it is suddenly, and brutally, not. (Jacob Hall)

#3425. Netflix's Near-Perfect 8-Episode Sci-Fi Series Is a Weekend Binge Worth Revisiting

Perhaps one of streaming's greatest tragedies was the shocking cancellation of the pitch-perfect sci-fi dark comedy The Boroughs. While the logistical reasons are certainly understandable, the series' brilliance may have thrown some viewers for a loop. The eight-episode Netflix series, created by Jeffrey Addiss and Will Matthews and executive produced by the Duffer Brothers, follows a grieving widower who relocates to a seemingly picturesque retirement community, only to discover something sinister lurking underneath. With a dynamic mix of cozy mystery elements and daring sci-fi tropes, The Boroughs moves across genre lines to deliver an emotional, character-driven story.

When Sam Cooper (Alfred Molina), a recently widowed retired aerospace engineer, moves into the idealistic New Mexico retirement community known as The Boroughs, he soon realizes that everything is not what it seems. After noticing mysterious deaths and unexplained disappearances that local authorities ignore, he discovers an ominous threat operating behind the scenes. Sam teams up with a misfit group of fellow residents to stop this otherworldly threat that is harvesting their time and life force.

Though the premise is rooted in sci-fi intrigue, what makes The Boroughs unique are the individuals at the center of the story. Like Stranger Things did with teenage sleuths, The Boroughs focuses on a generation often deemed "too old" to play in the sci-fi sandbox. As with stories like The Thursday Murder Club, unsuspecting underdogs make the most fascinating protagonists. They aren't presented as wise mentors who assist younger adventure-seekers but actually take the lead themselves, investigating the supernatural threats lurking beneath their seemingly idyllic community.

Netflix's inability to create sustained hits could result in long-term issues.

However, The Borough's eight episodes don't shy away from the elephant in the room, with the characters' ages playing a major role in the action. By diving deep into the realities of aging, including managing cancer medication, memory care concerns, and grief, the series presents their daring journey as something bigger than simply letting time get the best of them. When the characters do have moments to reflect and grapple with mortality, loneliness, and purpose, these themes are presented as universal realities that viewers of any age can relate to, emphasizing the brilliance of Addiss and Matthews' creation.

The Boroughs is a beautifully crafted series, with practical and technical worldbuilding playing an equally important part in the storytelling. The show was filmed across the great state of New Mexico, and its cul-de-sac was crafted to feel warm and welcoming, creating an immersive setting. Other parts of the community are imbued with nostalgia, giving the characters a reason to reminisce while also doubling as a means of emotional entrapment.

Visuals aside, The Boroughs taps some heavy hitters to play the story's senior-citizen sleuths. The acclaimed ensemble, featuring the likes of Molina, Geena Davis, Alfre Woodard, Bill Pullman, Clarke Peters, and Denis O'Hare, captures the genuine heart of the show. Molina is quite grounded as the standoffish and guarded Sam Cooper, while Davis gets to lean into the cougar trope, clearly having immense fun as Renee. Woodard and Peters earn the most complex and alluring relationship, and their moments of emotional intimacy are welcome amid the wild sci-fi chaos happening around them. O'Hare is at his finest, bringing nuance to an individual who knows the end is near. Perhaps the most heartbreaking performance comes from Ed Begley Jr. as Edward, a man who lives in The Manor, the long-term care wing.

Given the cast's terrific on-screen chemistry, any scene shared by these elite actors feels like a masterclass in acting. They're so strong that the prospect of more to the story was quite exciting until Netflix pulled the plug. Reported production costs of $10 million or more per episode, the high-caliber cast, and an alleged viewership drop-off were cited as factors in Netflix's decision to cancel The Boroughs after one season. Once you finish this near-perfect series, you'll be stunned that the business side of television got in the way of something truly special.

Now, new DLC for survival game Star Trek: Voyager - Across the Unknown​​​​​​​ will revisit the iconic storyline. Players won't just be able to relive "Year of Hell," however, they'll be able to change the course of history.​​​​​​​

Players will start with a fully repaired and fully equipped ship​​​​​​​ before encountering the Krenim. Crew members can also die, leaving the Voyager crew scrambling to stay alive​​​​​​​. Daedalic Entertainment says that the goal of the DLC "isn't to finish with a perfect ship. If players want to follow the plot of the "Year of Hell" episodes, that is absolutely possible, but Daedalic​​​​​​​ has given players another option. Depending on which path players take​​​​​​​, the other inhabitants of the sectors will have shifting opinions of the Voyager and act accordingly. The base game is required, but those who own the Expansion Pass will automatically receive Year of Hell when it is released. #3422. Why Mags Flanagan From The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Looks So Familiar

"The Hunger Games" franchise is back with a story fans have been waiting a very long time for. "Sunrise on the Reaping" is the darkest movie in "The Hunger Games" series, flashing back to the famed games in which Haymitch Abernathy won. Originally played by Woody Harrelson, that character is a fan-favorite, but this movie does a lot of work to help fill in crucial elements of his character, played this time by Joseph Zada.

"Sunrise on the Reaping" takes place on the "Hunger Games" timeline 24 years before the events of the first movie. It follows sixteen-year-old Haymitch from District 12, beginning on the morning of the reaping for the 50th Annual Hunger Games, also known as the Second Quarter Quell, the biggest Games yet with twice as many tributes. But Haymitch isn't the only classic character who gets more time to shine in this entry.

Plenty of "Hunger Games" characters return in this prequel in younger form, including Caesar Flickerman (played by Oscar winner Kieran Culkin) and Effie Trinket (played by Emmy nominee Elle Fanning). But they're not the only ones who will be familiar to fans of the series. There's also the matter of Mags Flanagan, a very important character in the history of both the books and the movies. Originally played by Lynn Cohen in "Catching Fire," she won the 11th Hunger Games and volunteered as tribute during the 75th games.

This time around, the younger version of Cohen is played by actress Lili Taylor. The role is crucial, as Mags is the one who mentors Haymitch en route to his time in the games. But for those who feel Taylor looks familiar, there's a good reason for that: She's a great actress with one heck of a resume.

Lili Taylor got her start as an actress in the late '80s/early '90s, starring in movies such as "Mystic Pizza," "Say Anything," and "Born on the Fourth of July." She worked steadily throughout the '90s in movies, in addition to doing some television, including an episode of "The X-Files." Some of her other notable credits from this period include "Ransom" and "The Haunting."

One of her earliest, big breakout roles came in the early 2000s on "Six Feet Under," one of the best HBO shows of all time, as Lisa Kimmel. She also continued to work very steadily in movies during this period, earning credits in "Brooklyn's Finest" and "Public Enemies," among others. Though not often in the spotlight as a lead, Taylor tends to use her talents in memorable supporting roles.

The 2010s were particularly kind to Taylor. 2013's "The Conjuring" kicked off the biggest non-Marvel cinematic universe, and she had a major part to play as Carolyn Perron, one of the heads of the household at the center of that movie's haunting. It's arguably her most notable role to date. She reprised the role in "The Nun" and "The Conjuring: Last Rites." That same year, she also starred in "Hemlock Grove," one of the first original shows produced by Netflix.

Taylor has over 100 credits to her name so we can't possibly go over all of them, but some other titles viewers might recognize her from include "The Maze Runner: The Scorch Trials," "Leatherface," HBO's "Perry Mason," "Outer Range," "Fear Street: Prom Queen," and most recently Marvel's "Daredevil: Born Again," where she played Marge McCaffrey.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is in theaters now.

#3421. New Pokémon TCG Release Is Already The Most Valuable Of All Time

Pokémon Trading Card Game has just unveiled a brand-new release that is likely going to be the most valuable thing ever issued by the game. There’s no downplaying just how much money the Trading Card Game moves, either with the sale of frequent expansions or with the pricey sales of individual cards. There are some pretty expensive cards in Pokémon TCG: Delta Reign, the latest set release for the game, with some cards being sold individually for well over $700 – and there are some older, rarer cards that are worth even more money.

An example of that is the legendary PSA 10 Pikachu Illustrator that was sold for nearly $16.5 million this year. However, that card’s value may have just been surpassed, even if we never really get confirmation of it. According to a new report by PokéBeach, Pokémon China has decided to celebrate the franchise’s 30th anniversary with the release of pure-gold versions of all the Pikachu cards from the Pokémon TCG: 30th Celebration set. As seen in the report, there are a total of 30 Pikachu cards, all of which are made of 99.9% pure gold.

The report mentions that each card, individually, weighs 30 grams. Based on the gold prices this week, 30 grams of gold costs nearly $3,500, meaning that this is the price, in gold, for each card. All 30 Pikachu cards from Pokémon TCG: 30th Celebration made in pure gold amount to approximately $106,000. Of course, that is taking into consideration their value in gold alone. Given the fact that these cards are all unique and one-of-a-kind, their value would be much larger, especially with potential buyers on the market.

That, however, may not be the case. These 30 pure gold Pikachu cards are being displayed at a Pokémon Card Art Illustration Exhibition event set at the Lafayette Culture and Arts Center in Shanghai. The exhibition takes place from November 28 through December 27. After their time on exhibition, it’s unclear what will happen to the cards. There are no openly-discussed plans of selling the cards to the public, meaning that they may not become the most expensive Pokémon TCG cards of all time.

According to the report, the cards seem to be made from sheets of gold with a print layer over them. As such, the very foundation of the cards is made of gold. A beautiful detail is on the back side, where the illustrative swirls around the Poké Ball are not printed over, letting the gold shine through. These are beautiful new card designs that will make collectors with a huge budget weep because it will be impossible to purchase them. Although they won’t have market value, they will likely be labeled as some of the rarest Pokémon TCG cards ever.

Exactly what will happen to these cards after the exhibition remains to be seen, but this is a huge way of saying goodbye to a year full of celebratory efforts, in honor of the franchise’s 30th anniversary. Pokémon China really went all-out with these new pure gold Pokémon Trading Card Game prints.

#3420. South Park's Season 29 Finale Features The Scariest TV Scene Of 2026

"South Park" has been on a roll recently. When the show finally left behind its Mr.-Garrison-as-Trump allegory and stopped doing endless specials (even if most of those were fantastic), it found its stride again in Season 28, which took on AI and deepfakes in the funniest way possible. Then, Season 29 took on everything from the data centers, to "looksmaxxing" and "aura farming" in a hilarious "Backrooms" parody, to club sports in a great "Heated Rivalry" parody, to the US beef shortage, and more.

It's been a funny season, and it's been a heartfelt season at times, particularly when the show killed Kenny (again) and decided to replace him with none other than a kid version of Randy (complete with mustache). It has even been a romantic season, with the Tweek and Craig romance-focused episode. What "South Park" usually isn't, however, is scary. That changed with the Season 29 finale, which delivered the scariest TV scene of 2026 — twice.

In the finale, "City Endings," the town of South Park (renamed this season as South America) is hit with major power outages that disrupt the town's "GTA VI" gametime. It is part of a conspiracy involving secret deals the government made with billionaire weenies. At the same time, there's paranoia involving supposed Chinese spies and possible cyberattacks from that country.

In the middle of all this, Cartman, Stan, and Kyle are also haunted by visions of the late Kenny, who died after being blown up by an e-bike in the season's premiere. Except this is not just Kenny, but a zombified version that haunts the boys in the form of horrific ghouls that even infiltrate "GTA VI," like a spectre out of "The Ring."

"South Park" has toyed with the horror genre before, usually body horror. There was the Michael Jackson parody with Mr. Jefferson slowly rotting away, for example, or the HumanCentipad. The Season 29 finale, however, features one of the wildest and most gruesome eldritch abominations in the nearly 30-year history of the show. It starts with several scenes of Kenny simply standing creepily in the background, stalking the boys as if to try and send a message.

"City Endings" is a legit horror episode, which is rare from the show that spent nearly a decade on a silly weed farm storyline. The image of Kenny just standing in the background, his face obscured by his hoodie but with bright eyes just shining like Pennywise in "It," is already quite disturbing and terrifying. Then, when the boys finally catch up to Kenny, who leads them to the cemetery and to his own grave, he shows off his gruesome zombie face and starts dissolving like that guy in "Poltergeist," in excruciatingly disturbing detail, before exploding in a pool of blood.

It's enough to make your skin crawl, but it's not even the scariest scene of the episode. That climax comes in later, while the boys are playing "GTA VI" at Butters' house. We see the zombie Kenny monster with long spiky teeth, deranged eyes and elongated limbs with claws crawling out of the TV like Samara Morgan from "The Ring." It is the stuff of pure nightmares, and by far the scariest scene in 2026 television.

#3418. 8 Funniest ‘Far Side’ Comics About Fruits and Vegetables

Decades after Gary Larson concluded his comic strip The Far Side back in 1995, fans of the series continue to read it regularly, and new fans are discovering it all the time. Some of Larson’s most beloved comic strips feature animals drawn in his signature style, including dogs, chickens, and especially cows. He often gave these animals human-like intelligence and other anthropomorphic traits and depicted them in very human-like scenarios.

Larson didn’t just do this with animals, however. The man had a strong surrealist streak​​​​​​​, and sometimes he’d make all sorts of things the subjects of his comic strips​​​​​​​. This includes fruits and vegetables, which he often paired with a bit of wordplay or some common association with the given food group.

Here are the eight funniest Far Side comics featuring fruits and vegetables. You’re also welcome to snack while enjoying them.

Larson began publishing The Far Side on Jan. 1, 1980, making this one of his earliest comics, when it appeared only in The San Francisco Chronicle​​​​​​​. It depicts a frustrated carrot threatening his kids with a terrifying story of how actual carrots are treated.

One of Larson’s signature moves in The Far Side was to take a well-known idiom and interpret it in the most literal way possible. Here, the biblical phrase “forbidden fruit” gets twisted into a comic where a lime is trying to enter a fruit-themed nightclub which doesn’t allow anyone who’s green.

On second thought, I’m not quite sure if that’s a lime, as it only vaguely resembles one. I don’t recall ever seeing a lime with a stem like that. Perhaps it’s a guava? Or a green plum? I’d say maybe a pear, but it isn’t at all pear-shaped. Perhaps the fruit is some other kind of fruit that isn’t yet ripe​​​​​​​, which means it could be a whole bunch of things. And maybe that’s part of the joke, as he’s not yet ripe enough for the adult nightclub? I’m really not sure.

I’m also unsure whether the fruits in this comic are​​​​​​​ anthropomorphic fruit or if they are people dressed like fruit. Just look at the human-like arms of the banana. That, to me, suggests that the banana is a man in a banana suit, yet his face is more fruit-like.

Mr. Larson, I have a lot of questions about this comic. Please write me at your earliest convenience.

Carrots seem to be a particular favorite of Larson’s as they show up more often than any other vegetable​​​​​​​ (except maybe potatoes). Here, two “Carrots of the evening” try to pick up a passing celery​​​​​​​ as a customer. While we don’t know whether he accepts the offer​​​​​​​, I’m thinking he does and there’s nothing wrong with that. Prostitution should be legal and I don’t see a ring on that celery’s finger.

Mr. Potato Head appeared in a handful of Gary Larson comics​​​​​​​, but this darkly funny one is easily the best. It depicts Mrs. Potato Head on a witness stand, testifying against her husband who had chased her around with a “Veg-o-matic.” I especially love how furious Mr. Potato Head looks here. Even Don Rickles’ Mr. Potato Head from the Toy Story films never had eyes quite this angry.

Nowadays, for the most part, vegetarians are fairly common, but in the 1980s and 1990s, when Gary Larson was still doing The Far Side, it was far less “normal.” As a result, vegetarians became punchlines​​​​​​​ in a number of Larson's comic strips. This one is a great example, in which​​​​​​​ a bunch of “Early vegetarian” cave people triumphantly carry back a carrot. I especially love the detail of them carrying shovels as their weapons.

And here’s a pretty similar comic, but it's worthy of greatness for its depiction of a hairy “Wooly Watermelon.”

Vegetarians are once again the punchline in Gary Larson’s funniest-ever comic starring fruits and vegetables, as a meat truck is about to crash into Noreen’s Vegetarian Cafe. The horrified faces of Noreen’s patrons make​​​​​​​ this laugh-out-loud funny​​​​​​​.

#3417. Anya Taylor-Joy’s 93-Minute Crime Thriller 'Thoroughbreds' Is the Perfect Watch Before It’s Cut From Streaming

One of the most unsung releases of the last decade was 2017’s Thoroughbreds, a thriller deep in the film noir mode with three great actors going toe to toe. With Anya Taylor-Joy, Olivia Cooke, and Anton Yelchin as the architects and participants of a murder plot, it’s less a crime movie and more of a character study, with director Cory Finley mining both pathos and extremely dark comedy from the premise. In an era where minimal-location movies about the sociopathy of the rich were frequently successful discourse machines (including Taylor-Joy’s 2022 vehicle The Menu), Thoroughbreds was a classically amoral story of kids whose wealth insulates them from consequences, yet you still root for them. The movie was unfortunately ahead of the curve with its note-perfect plotting and criminal ideation, as well as its cast.

While the late Anton Yelchin had found major success in movies like Green Room or even the modern Star Trek films, Cooke and Taylor-Joy were just getting started, some years away from the blockbuster extravaganzas of Dune and House of the Dragon. Coming some years before that, Thoroughbreds suggested great depth from all three actors, playing them against each other as they all fight for their own agendas, while also giving viewers the chance to identify with potentially evil teens. The movie is leaving Starz on November 30, but its study of youthful sociopathy and the tenuous nature of female friendship means it should remain a cult classic for years to come.

Thoroughbreds is a movie of interiors, specializing in the rich, old money homes of its protagonists Amanda (Olivia Cooke) and Lily (Anya Taylor-Joy), who live in suburban Connecticut. From the very beginning, when Amanda mercy-kills her crippled horse (leading to the title) in an unnerving moment, the movie keeps its distance from the characters, with director Cory Finley’s camera holding on scenes and moments for long stretches. Rather than the aspirational gleeful immorality of the classic teenage murderer movie Heathers, Thoroughbreds is methodical and ironic. The fancy decor, the emotional repression, and the basement tanning beds all go hand in hand with Amanda’s claims of an inability to feel anything. You might wonder if she’s just being an edgy teenager, especially after the horse euthanizing moment. But the movie’s visual language backs her up.

In a twist directly out of Alfred Hitchcock’s Strangers on a Train, the movie’s narrative begins to hinge on a murderous favor. Lily, effectively tasked by Amanda’s mom to befriend her troubled daughter, has an abusive stepfather named Mark (Paul Sparks), and Amanda, in her emotionless wisdom, presents a solution: kill him. The girls have a means of laundering the murder in the form of drug dealer Tim (Yelchin). Olivia Cooke’s portrayal of Amanda veers beyond creating an empathetic version of somebody suffering from an undisclosed mental illness, but it never goes into villain territory either. The movie’s cold and heavily adorned visual sensibility might have Yorgos Lanthimos-esque ironic distance from what you see, but it means that the relationship between the two girls becomes increasingly complex, in a way that it wouldn’t be if viewers were directly keyed into how the girls see each other.

Cory Finley had reportedly envisioned the movie as a play originally, and that feeling lingers in the film. The minimal cast and locations, as well as the long takes and reliance on dialogue, have the potential to feel theatrical, but the movie is sophisticated on the level of cinematic storytelling, commenting on its cast with its staging and using its widescreen compositions for both comedy and terror as chickens come home to roost. As he told IndieWire, the story began with the idea of a character who couldn’t feel anything. As the friend seeking to take advantage of that to help her own family situation, Anya Taylor-Joy’s Lily is effectively not much different.

The movie’s cinematic lineage is rich, drawing from Alfred Hitchcock (besides Strangers on a Train, his highly theatrical one-take experiment Rope, with its homoerotic murder conspiracy, has a clear line to Thoroughbreds) as well as ‘90s evil rich kid movies like Cruel Intentions, but with a much less moral stance. Peter Jackson’s true-crime classic Heavenly Creatures also feels like an influence, with the fantastical sequences substituted for cold stylization. When Amanda and Lily’s plans go awry, we see the truth of what the girls are willing to go through with, how calculating they can be with the other’s emotional headspace. A different movie about teenage murder conspirators might let them off the hook, but Amanda’s dreams of wild thoroughbred horses suggest that a cruel end is coming to everybody.

#3416. Avengers: Doomsday TV Spot Confirms RDJ's Doctor Doom Has A Scarred Face

Marvel Comics fans know Doctor Victor von Doom is scarcely ever seen without his iron mask — a mask that hides his supposedly horribly scarred face. But with Marvel Studios choosing former Tony Stark actor Robert Downey Jr. to play Doom in the upcoming "Avengers" movies "Doomsday" and "Secret Wars," there's been an expectation that Doom's mask coming off will be a jaw dropping moment.

Now, Chris Evans has claimed that Doom wears his mask for the entirety of "Doomsday." But that could only mean he'll keep the mask on until "Secret Wars." Even then, there's the chance that Doom is so disfigured that his face isn't even recognizable as RDJ. A new TV spot for "Doomsday" does suggest Doom has his scarred face, while also teasing we're eventually going to see exactly what's under his mask ... but not yet.

In this TV spot, Magneto (Ian McKellen) tries to telekinetically rip off Doom's mask — it is made of metal, after all. But Doom does not restrict himself to the laws of science. There's evidently a magical seal on the mask (note there appear to be runic designs across Doom's costume), because glowing green tendrils extend out from Doom's hood and grab the mask, slamming it back onto Doom's face. A brief glimpse of Doom's face, visible through the mask's eyeholes, shows hints of pale macerated skin and scar tissue.

In the "Fantastic Four" comics, it was originally said that Doom suffered his scars during an experiment in college. A machine he built to contact the "nether world" (later revealed to be an attempt to reach his mother's damned soul) exploded in his face, leaving him scarred.

Now, Doom's co-creator Jack Kirby intended that Doom actually only had a thin facial scar — but Doom's ego can't stand even that small imperfection. Later "Fantastic Four" writer/artist John Byrne melded the two ideas. The machine explosion only slightly damaged Doom's face, but then Victor — convinced his face was already ruined — put his freshly forged mask on before it cooled, and that is why he has a horribly scarred face.

The greatest source of Doom's torment is completely self-inflicted. The exemplary 1989 "Doctor Strange and Doctor Doom: Triumph and Torment" goes with Byrne's interpretation. When Doom seeks out the wisdom of the wizard named the Aged Genghis, the sorcerer alludes to Doom's "minor disfigurement." We then see Doom's (barely scarred) face as Victor lashes out at the insult.

It's unclear what origin "Doomsday" will go with, if any of them. Marketing suggests the Marvel Cinematic Universe's Doom will be driven by a lost wife and child, not his mother. What is clear from this TV spot is that Marvel fans can expect to see Doom and Magneto — the two greatest villains of Marvel Comics — clash onscreen. Doom's wizardry here refutes the obvious conclusion that Magneto wins easily because he controls metal and Doom is concealed inside metal armor.

"He is pain, he is extinction," Magneto declares, setting up Doom's famous third person double entendre: "I am Doom!" Ian McKellen's Magneto was the first villain of the Marvel movie boom that kicked off with 2000's "X-Men." Bringing him back to face (and presumably fall to) Doom is some classic carnival barker marketing that would make Stan Lee proud.

"Avengers: Doomsday" is set for theatrical release on December 18, 2026.

#3413. Tor Books Pulls Book Cover Due to AI Artwork Controversy

A major name in the fantasy publishing world is apologizing to readers this week after fans learned one of its upcoming book covers contained AI-generated artwork.

Tor Books—an imprint of Macmillan known for publishing top names in fantasy, sci-fi, and speculative fiction, including Brandon Sanderson, Jeff VanderMeer, and TJ Klune—is set to release the second book in Ilona Andrews’ epic fantasy series in September 2027. However, the release is already mired in controversy after Tor revealed the book’s cover art, only to pull it within days over concerns that it was created using generative AI.

The book at the center of Tor’s AI controversy is This Crown Will Not Rule Me, its next release from Ilona Andrews (the pen name of married writing duo Ilona and Andrew Gordon). It will be the second in Andrews' Maggie the Undying series, a planned trilogy pitched as “the page-turning politics of Game of Thrones meets the worlds-spanning romance of Outlander.”

Tor initially shared the cover art for This Crown Will Not Rule Me in a November 17 Instagram post promoting the upcoming book. However, the publisher deleted the post just three days later and issued an official apology, stating it had “Learned that generative AI was used in the creation of the cover.” The apology post claimed that both Tor and Ilona Andrews were unaware the cover artist had used AI to create the design until after sharing the design.

Tor's statement also said that the cover art would no longer appear on any completed books, as using AI-generated art violates its standard contract with cover artists. The publisher then said it would be “bolstering [its] internal review process to mitigate the possibility of this happening again.”

Notably, the cover of This Crown Will Not Rule Me was initially credited to Andrew Davis, the same artist who designed the cover of This Kingdom Will Not Kill Me, the first book in the Maggie the Undying series. It's unclear whether Tor plans to change that book cover for future editions.

In a separate statement on their website, Andrews revealed that fans of the series initially alerted them to the possible generative AI use on the cover shortly after it was posted.

Providing some context for how an AI-generated cover design slipped through undetected, Andrews wrote, “In this case, the cover was commissioned by our publisher, and a sketch was provided to the art department. It looked like a typical cover sketch. We didn’t know enough to see cause for concern.” However, they also said they were “painfully aware that we lack expertise in this area.”

Despite the scandal, the authors encouraged fans not to attack the cover designer on social media. “We don’t know what was going on [in] that person’s life or what led to this unfortunate incident,” wrote Andrews. “This situation is miserable enough already.”

This is far from the first time a major publisher has found itself at the center of a generative AI controversy. In March, Hachette canceled publication of the upcoming horror novel Shy Girl after discovering that its author, Mia Ballard, had used generative AI to write some, if not all, of the book.

Much like the Tor controversy, the Shy Girl scandal also came to light thanks to readers on social media. Rumors that Ballard had used AI to write Shy Girl first grew widespread in January, after book influencer Frankie’s Shelf posted a video essay on YouTube, titled “i’m pretty sure this book is ai slop." In that video, the influencer analyzed an earlier, self-published version of the book, claiming that while Ballard's prose did not seem "100% AI-generated," it bore several hallmarks of AI-assisted writing, including repetitive phrasing, misused adjectives, and awkward metaphors.

The New York Times then ran Shy Girl through AI detection software, finding evidence the book had been written with AI, and approached Hachette with the results. Hachette ultimately discontinued printing Shy Girl in the UK, where it had already been released, and canceled its US release altogether. Ballard later told the Times that the AI-generated passages had been inserted without her knowledge by an unnamed friend whom she had trusted to edit her draft.

Six months later, in August, Minotaur—another Macmillan imprint—killed its $2.4 million two-book deal with author Jerry Falade over suspicions that Falade had used generative AI when writing his crime novel Call Me, I’ll Hide the Body.

Minotaur, which won the rights to Falade’s manuscripts in a 14-way bidding war, ultimately canceled publication of Call Me, I’ll Hide the Body and Falade's planned second novel, killing negotiations for a possible big-screen adaptation. Falade later denied using AI to write the manuscript and claimed he had documentation to prove the book was entirely human-written.

Beyond major publishers, Andrews is also navigating more than one AI-related controversy. In the same blog post that they apologized to fans for the AI cover of This Crown Will Not Rule Me, the duo said they had signed a contract with a production company known for using AI-generated visuals earlier this year to adapt their work as a vertical drama series. Andrews claimed they had "specified no AI and asked that only human actors and writers would be used," and said that the unnamed company had agreed to their terms.

However, Andrews says they have since terminated that contract after realizing “that the generative AI involved in the company’s other productions did not align with our preferences.” In a blog post, Andrews said both incidents “illustrate how new and confusing the creative landscape has become” in the era of generative AI.

#3411. Steve Martin And John Candy's Classic Thanksgiving Movie Is A Paramount+ Streaming Hit

John Hughes made some of the most beloved movies of all time in his eight directorial efforts, to the point where it's nearly impossible to rank the films he wrote and directed. Still, there are few movies that reach the specific balance of comedy with such an emotional punch as Hughes does in 1987's "Planes, Trains and Automobiles." This is a goofball movie that borders on the surreal, with some of the most bizarre imagery in a comedy movie, while also delivering some of the most heartbreaking and heartwarming moments that came out of the 1980s.

The film stars Steve Martin as Neal Page, an uptight marketing executive forced to be paired with Del Griffith (John Candy), a goofball salesman with a heart of gold, when their journey from New York City to Chicago is disrupted. What was meant to be just a short cab and plane ride home just in time for Thanksgiving ends up being a three-day odyssey full of shenanigans, attempted murder, and much more.

It's no wonder, then, that "Planes, Trains and Automobiles" is the No. 1 movie streaming on Paramount+ on Thanksgiving Day 2026. After all, there are plenty of movies about Christmas, to the point where it's easy to overlook Thanksgiving, and with good reason. For one, it's not really a holiday outside the U.S. and Canada (and even then, celebrated on different days), and the imagery is not dissimilar to Christmas anyway. Still, the best Thanksgiving movies deliver a very specific tone that's less about holiday magic and more about celebrating what we have despite the horrors of daily life. From the opening minutes of "Planes, Trains and Automobiles," it's clear this movie could not be set at any other time of year except during the chaos and anxiety of Thanksgiving.

The travel chaos that is quite unique to Thanksgiving is the crux of "Planes, Trains and Automobiles." The arrival of snowstorms that plague the East Coast of the continental United States, the huge flux of travelers, and the general anxiety and irritability of travelers around the country add to, well, a very stressful time of year. It's why Steve Martin's uptight businessman Neal is so relatable. The film simply nails the feeling of needing to interact with others and ask for their help while being utterly frustrated with having to deal with anyone at such a bad time. It's also why John Candy's performance is such a tightrope, because his character has to be annoying in addition to being charming. Del's not really someone you'd want as a travel companion, yet he is absolutely the best person you want as a friend.

That tricky balance is what makes the movie so memorable, and why John Candy's best line remains the best Thanksgiving movie quote ever. Neal and Del are forced to not only set aside their differences, but actually recognize the humanity in each other while acknowledging that they themselves are flawed. This is a highly empathetic film that's all about how we should find love and camaraderie even in unlikely companions. That is why the film so perfectly captures the spirit of Thanksgiving, because it's not about estranged family members, but rather complete strangers who must come to learn they need one another and that they should be grateful for what they bring into each other's lives. Togetherness is not just for family members, or even people you like, but also for strangers you come to appreciate despite the ways they annoy you.

#3409. 8 Essential Thriller Books Everyone Should Read at Least Once

The safest way to chase an adrenaline rush is to read a captivating thriller book. These stories rely on one or more mysteries to ramp up tension, provoke intellectual curiosity, and deliver a sense of catharsis. Fiction is often a safe space to explore uncomfortable emotions, and thrillers deliver on this front by allowing readers to escape into worlds brimming with danger.

Take genre staples like Gone Girl or The Silent Patient. While the two couldn’t be more different in tone and subject matter, both thrillers heavily rely on misdirection and the recontextualization of events to deliver twists. These picks are a staple in every “must-read” list for good reason, just like the ones Polygon has highlighted below as genre essentials. Without further ado, here are eight thriller books you should read at least once in your life.

The Oscar-winning Conclave was a surprising front-runner in a year dominated by flashier films like Anora and The Brutalist, and its source material is just as disarmingly good. The premise of a papal conclave held right after the pope’s death might feel a bit too somber, but Conclave unfolds like a tense political thriller that balances breakneck pacing with intricate detail. Jacopo Lomeli is tasked with the responsibility of overseeing the papal conclave in the event of the tragedy, and four cardinals are promptly chosen as leading candidates. But there’s more to the conspiracy than one would expect, turning the novel into a thrilling clash of ideologies that is also a deft exploration of inner conflict.

The Talented Mr. Ripley introduces us to Tom Ripley, famously played by Matt Damon in Anthony Minghella’s 1999 film adaptation and Andrew Scott in Netflix’s Ripley. Tom is struggling to make ends meet in New York, prompting him to carry out petty cons. When shipping magnate Herbert Greenleaf approaches Ripley to persuade his son, Dickie, to join the family business, the opportunistic young man readily agrees. Patricia Highsmith presents an unforgettable anti-hero, whose actions follow irrefutable internal logic despite being morally wrong. The novel is a fascinating character study about sociable forms of evil and how they manifest when you least expect it.

A “whodunnit” framework propels most mystery thrillers, but The Secret History operates with a tense, slow-burn “why-done-it” narrative. The novel’s unreliable narrator, Richard Papen, immediately tells us about a murder, a crime for which he is “partly responsible.” This curiosity to understand the why and how makes this dark academia campus novel especially riveting. The novel’s secluded setting in Vermont adds to the isolation of the six tight-knit students at its center, whose obsession with all things Ancient Greece comes with a heavy price. Tartt’s characters are flawed, obnoxious, and compelling, successfully retaining our avid interest despite being deliberately disengaged from the world at large.

Blake Crouch has written engaging sci-fi books like Recursion and Upgrade, and Dark Matter leans heavily into sci-fi thriller territory with its propulsive pacing. The story follows physicist Jason Dessen, who is kidnapped and sent to a parallel universe, where his life plays out differently due to a drastically different choice he made in this timeline. In fact, this version of Jason has built a cube that enables travel between countless alternate worlds, which changes his understanding of quantum mechanics. Dark Matter is easily accessible for anyone, as its convoluted premise unfolds in a way that’s fun and easily digestible. This is undoubtedly popcorn entertainment, meant to be read while you’re waiting at the airport.

David Cronenberg’s adaptation of The Dead Zone is both a taut thriller and a quietly melancholic movie about a man with a strange gift. A child named Johnny Smith issues a prophetic warning after an ice-skating accident, and grows up to become a small-town high school teacher. Things take a turn after an accident-induced coma makes Johnny gain frighteningly accurate psychic abilities, along with a vision of the end of the world. Stephen King’s source material excels in conveying the eerie, lived-in horror of weighing extreme choices to determine the fate of those around us. Johnny’s predicament, although fantastical, feels deeply human in the way the personal and the political seamlessly blend together.

A bona fide bestseller that has been adapted countless times on the screen, Rebecca is the definition of a Gothic novel with exceptional thriller elements. The book opens with an unnamed narrator lamenting that she cannot return to her husband’s estate, as it has been destroyed. Looking back, she recounts how she married the older, wealthy Maximilian de Winter, whose first wife, Rebecca, drowned in a sailing accident. Although the narrator does her best to acclimatize to her new life, every person at the estate seems haunted by Rebecca’s memory, to the point of undermining the new bride’s sense of self. Rebecca is a timeless classic about memory and identity, one that is also an exemplary entry in 20th-century Gothic fiction.

Stieg Larsson’s “Millennium Trilogy” is spectacular as a whole, but The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo stands out for several reasons. The book introduces us to journalist Mikael Blomkvist, who is facing jail time after losing a libel case. Although Blomkvist retreats from the public eye, he takes an interest in a curious disappearance case after meeting Henrik Vanger, the CEO of Vanger Enterprises. Blomkvist, however, isn’t the only person involved, as the exceptionally gifted investigator Lisbeth Salander has been hired to evaluate his history and skill set. The novel is a labyrinth of clues, red herrings, and twists, along with a gritty exploration of abuse and institutional failure.

If you like the Oscar-winning neo-noir mystery, Mystic River, chances are that you’ll also like the book it is based on. Three boys — Dave, Sean, and Jimmy — grow up together in Boston. Tragedy strikes when Dave is abducted, and he returns after managing to escape, deeply traumatized. Fast-forward 25 years; the three men have been shaped by their respective circumstances, brought together by a grisly murder and the unsavory realization that one of them might be involved. Mystic River is a book that delves beneath the surface, compelling us to understand how grief carries on into adulthood. There’s immense thematic weight to this book about the tussle between choice and fatalism in the face of injustice.

#3408. 'The Last of Us' Meets 'Silo' in Hulu’s 4-Part Sci-Fi Thriller

Post-apocalyptic sci-fi thrillers have become some of TV's best shows. With examples like The Last of Us or Silo, these stories have grown incredibly popular for their spectacle and epic tales. The genre is more than gruesome stories about the world ending, as it offers a deep exploration of universal human struggles. While these recent examples have earned considerable attention, and rightfully so, they are not the first. In fact, Snowpiercer took a similar approach in 2020. The series creates an immersive world full of danger and division that all fans of the genre should watch.

Snowpiercer delivers a unique premise and incredible worldbuilding that sets it apart. Inspired by the 2013 film of the same name, the story isn't totally original, but the series builds on the concept that always deserved more than two hours. And Snowpiercer certainly expands the idea with four unforgettable seasons. Though it may not have gained the popularity that other comparable series have, it still deserves attention. Six years later, Snowpiercer is the perfect binge watch for anyone who loves sci-fi thrillers, dystopian worlds, or complex moral questions.

Snowpiercer features a world like no other, where a massive luxury train is the only place people can live. Eerily set in 2026, the story takes place seven years after an environmental disaster created a new ice age, killing much of human civilization. However, some survive on a constantly moving train designed by eccentric billionaire Mr. Joseph Wilford (Sean Bean). While the movement keeps them alive, the survivors continue to struggle. The system is strictly divided into distinct social classes. The elite live in the front, third-class laborers keep the machine running, and the stowaways, known as the Tailies, are just trying to survive. However, the dynamic alters when a series of murders threatens the train. Head Engineer Melanie Cavill (Jennifer Connelly) pulls Chicago police officer Andre Layton (Daveed Diggs) up from the Tail to uncover the truth.

Layton has his own motivations. He dreams of revolution and believes this investigation can take him one step closer, allowing him to map out the train. However, the fallout spirals as the train is full of secrets. Most prominently, the passengers begin to realize that inventor Joseph Wilford isn't running the train because Melanie abandoned him during boarding, leaving him for dead. Although this society is confined to a train, Snowpiercer covers a lot of ground as it explores the brutal realities of civilization, oppression, and unavoidable moral questions of survival. This is the crux of the series, giving it a dark and fascinating tone.

What stands out most about Snowpiercer is its worldbuilding. A train is an uncharacteristic setting, but it comes with plenty to explore as the series delves into how different biomes separate the classes, how food is grown, and even how the passengers deal with their dead. These may seem like small details, but they reveal a lot about the world and the desperate characters who inhabit it. Through these elements, the series brings this society to life and creates something new. As the story goes on, Snowpiercer even explores beyond the train, showing the devastation of the icy world and further immersing the audience in the dystopian setting.

Idris Elba has fans on the edges of their train seats.

Though this concept is rare, the story is inspired by the movie, but the two are far from the same. Of course, there are similarities, but Snowpiercer isn't even strictly a remake. The series takes the concept, but uses different characters and circumstances to tell its own story. With significantly more time, the series sets a slower pace, building tension and introducing the world a little at a time, which is a luxury the film doesn't have. Ultimately, that dedication to the story is what makes Snowpiercer work. The series stands out, even as the dystopian genre grows, and though it's a few years old now, Snowpiercer is an unmatched sci-fi watch that deserves more attention.

Snowpiercer is streaming on Hulu in the U.S.

#3407. Resident Evil 1 Remake Leaves Gamers Seriously Split

The future slate of Resident Evil games will only continue to become more fascinating with each new release and announcement. For instance, Resident Evil 10 will be an enormous milestone for the franchise and could possibly feature the return of S.T.A.R.S. Alpha Team’s Jill Valentine, and which mainline entry is chosen to be remade after Resident Evil Veronica may be quite telling.

There are Resident Evil remake rumors floating about with regard to virtually every game that hasn’t yet been remade, to be fair, but one could be more intriguing than the rest. Indeed, anyone who is a massive fan of Resident Evil 5 may not want to hold their breath. It could be a long but satisfying road to Capcom finally succumbing and exploring co-op gameplay again, and it may take a highly anticipated detour to a duology that fans are itching to revisit.

According to Dusk Golem, as per Twitter/X, “the possibility of doing a Rev 1 Remake has been tossed around.” Again, there are few Resident Evil games that haven’t had their names thrown around with the rumor or potential for them to one day receive a remake of their own, and it was only a matter of time until a sliver of credence was leant toward the belief that Resident Evil Revelations would be treated to one. Plus, if Resident Evil Revelations gets a remake, it’s almost guaranteed that its sequel will, too.

Fans seem to be generally excited about Resident Evil Revelations possibly receiving a remake, though user AKA_Sparda is skeptical about how bloated Capcom’s release schedule might be thereafter. Moreover, user Vagabond85 argues that they’d be pleased to see a Resident Evil Revelations remake make some tonal changes, writing, “The hypersexualization of characters like Jessica really kill the tone of an otherwise pretty strong entry.” However, remakes of Resident Evil Revelations and Resident Evil Revelations 2 would be thrilling due to where they land canonically and chronologically in the series.

Before Resident Evil Veronica was officially announced as a remake of Resident Evil Code: Veronica, it seemed unlikely that we’d ever get one. Resident Evil Code: Veronica is set between Resident Evil 3: Nemesis and Resident Evil 4, for instance, and thus, Resident Evil Veronica is launching out of order. This essentially means that any random Resident Evil game could get a remake and simply be sewn into the fabric of the remake timeline that’s been woven, but a Resident Evil Revelations remake would give much-needed context for the franchise’s most epic rivalry.

Ironically, Resident Evil Revelations is set before Resident Evil 5, after the events of Resident Evil Code: Veronica. And, because Resident Evil’s Chris Redfield appears in Code: Veronica, Revelations, and Resident Evil 5, a remake trilogy dedicated to Chris may be in store. Resident Evil Revelations and Revelations 2 are fairly distinct gameplay-wise, and their stories are incredibly unique with pieces of narrative and lore that are barely even remarked on in other mainline Resident Evil installments, so having them remade and repackaged for a new generation of players would be terrific.

#3406. Apple's AirPods Pro 3 Are $100 Off During Black Friday

Apple AirPods Pro 3 are not only my favorite earbuds I've ever owned, they might also be my favorite headphones of all time. The Pros sound great, come with excellent noise cancellation and transparency modes, and are packed with modern features that go beyond listening to music. I'd recommend these to any Apple user looking for the best overall audio experience at full price, but when they're $100 off, I actively encourage you to buy these now.

On the surface, Apple's third-generation AirPods Pro are among the best ways to listen to audio on your Apple devices. The earbuds sound great: I'm not an audiophile or a headphone reviewer, but to my ears, the Pros deliver excellent sound quality, with plenty of bass and great sound separation. I frequently turn to mine when I want to pay close attention to a new album, or watch a show or movie with intricate sound design. Plus, like other AirPods, the Pros are great for jumping between your various Apple devices. I'm constantly switching between my iPhone, Mac, and Apple TV with mine, and they seamlessly move between each—at least, most of the time.

The noise cancellation on these AirPods is also stellar. I used to take my AirPods Max with me on planes, but lately, I've been fine with just my Pros, since the noise cancellation seemingly blocks just about as much background sound as my over-the-ear headphones. Equally great are both the transparency modes, which pump in outside sounds while you're wearing your AirPods, and Adaptive Transparency, which automatically adjusts the level of transparency based on how loud or soft your surroundings are. This is a great mode for wearing your AirPods in loud environments, so you can still hear everything without the noise becoming overwhelming. To that point, these AirPods are actually FDA-certified hearing aids.

There are plenty of other features available here as well, especially if you have a compatible iPhone. AirPods Pro 3 have a built-in heart rate sensor, so you can track workouts without an Apple Watch; you can translate conversations in real time with Live Translate; "Conversation Awareness" lowers the volume of your audio and turns on transparency mode when you start speaking; and they run for eight hours on one charge with noise cancellation enabled.

This isn't an in-depth list of the AirPods Pro 3's set of features. But suffice it to say, these earbuds are worth their full MSRP of $249. So not only can I wholeheartedly recommend them at $149, but I'd say they're an easy buy if you've been thinking about picking up AirPods for yourself.
