#3404. IndieWire Honors Film Celebration to Fête John Turturro, the ‘Artificial’ Cast, Los Javis, and More

IndieWire, the definitive outlet for creative independence in film and TV, announced on Wednesday, November 25 the final additions to the lineup for the Winter 2026 edition of our IndieWire Honors event, featuring our largest lineup yet of film honorees. Curated and selected by IndieWire’s editorial team, IndieWire Honors is a celebration of the filmmakers, actors, and artisans key to crafting some of the most exciting cinematic works this year.

The newly announced honorees include “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” star Yahya Abdul-Mateen II and costume designer Trish Summerville, who will be receiving the Spotlight Award. They join previously announced honorees John Turturro, Monica Barbaro, Andrew Garfield, Ike Barinholtz, Yura Borisov, James Gray, Adam Driver, Beth de Araújo, Mason Reeves, Gemma Chan, Ruth Madeley, David Greaves, Javier Ambrossi, Javier Calvo, Jeon Do-yeon, Anthony Ippolito, James Ortiz, Neal Scanlan, Mag Sarnowska, Paul Lambert, and Travis Knight. Related Stories Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’

Additionally, IndieWire has announced that the incoming awards ceremony will be hosted by writer and comedian Demi Adejuyigbe, whose latest special “Demi Adejuyigbe Is Going to Do 1 (One) Backflip” is now available to stream on Dropout. Previous IndieWire Honors emcees include Emmy winner Alex Edelman, Emmy nominee Robby Hoffman, multi-hyphenate Dewayne Perkins, and lauded comedians Vinny Thomas and Atsuko Okatsuka.

IndieWire Honors will take place on Thursday, December 3 in Los Angeles, starting with an intimate cocktail reception and awards ceremony. IndieWire will also begin rolling out exclusive editorial content, including honoree profiles, on Friday, November 27 through the lead-up to the awards night. Throughout the ceremony, into the next day, IndieWire will publish photos and exclusive social content from the event as well.

“It’s thrilling to be able to recognize the artists behind so many of this year’s most exciting and compelling films,” said Brent Lang, IndieWire’s editor-in-chief. “They dazzled us with their talent, inspired us with their willingness to take risks, and left an indelible mark on cinema. We are excited to celebrate their accomplishments.”

“It’s exciting to celebrate such an eclectic group of film talent for this year’s IndieWire Honors,” said James Israel, IndieWire’s SVP and Publisher. “We are also pleased to continue to celebrate top craft artisans in entertainment.”

The Winter 2026 IndieWire Honors honorees are:

The fact that he is known for being a frequent collaborator of both Spike Lee and the Coen brothers conveys just how expansive an actor Turturro is. The Brooklyn native is quintessentially New York, as most recently proven in Sony Pictures Classics’ acclaimed Sundance premiere “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” written and directed by Noah Segan. Yet, a filmmaker can still drop the performer into the corporate dystopia of sci-fi series “Severance,” or have him go on a Southern odyssey in “O Brother, Where Art Thou?,” and he just as well hits it out of the park.

With nearly five decades of film work under his belt, starting with an uncredited role in “Raging Bull,” Turturro manages to be one of the few veteran actors who continues to best himself year after year.

The pair of Madrid-based directors colloquially known as Los Javis are not shy about cluing the audience in on the shoulders upon which they stand on. They cast Penélope Cruz and Lola Dueñas, two muses of auteur Pedro Almodóvar, as the most important women within their epic adaptation of an unfinished play by Federico García Lorca, another one of Spain’s queer artist forefathers. That reverence is balanced by the confidence in their own eye for new talent, weaving together three different timelines led by three relative unknowns, including most notably, indie musician Guitarricadelafuente, who also contributed the poignant original song “La Nieve” to the project.

Made outside the Hollywood system and chosen to represent Spain in the Best International Feature Oscar race, the Netflix release “La Bola Negra” is a film of immense scale. If viewers knew nothing of the director duo before seeing the film, they come away with a crash course in everything they are about. Considering how they won both the Best Director Award at Cannes, and the coveted People’s Choice Award at TIFF, it seems to be an experience most cinephiles enjoy.

“Tallgrass” is the code word that unlocks what makes the creative collaboration between “Paper Tiger” writer-director James Gray and star Adam Driver such a feat. Though the Neon release, which premiered at Cannes, is their first time ever working together, the filmmaker imbues the two-time Oscar nominee with such a specific vision of what it feels like to realize one’s time has gone by. Though the film is another deeply personal work in the oeuvre of the Queens-born auteur, Driver adds a more broad portrait of a figure wrapped up in crime, slowly feeling the overwhelming situation constrict and constrict.

“Josephine” was not made to be an easy watch, but boasts the rare feat of winning both the Grand Jury Prize and Audience Award at the Sundance Film Festival. Written and directed by Araújo, and starring Gemma Chan and Mason Reeves as mother and daughter, the drama is a bold exploration of how little control parents have over their children being confronted by certain horrors in life that there’s no guarantee of avoiding.

An early release for new distributor Sumerian Pictures, “Josephine” has only felt more necessary as the year has gone on, and news stories like the Cornell rape case have come to the forefront. It is a conversation piece about a subject many wish to evade, that puts forth the effort to reach meaningful discourse.

The most bold artistic choice in “Artificial,” the latest film from prolific director Luca Guadagnino, is to not proffer any romance in becoming one of the Promethean figures. The repeated refrain of “Feel the AGI” rings as a benevolent threat by the time the two hours and 20 minutes of the Neon release are over. Garfield, Borisov, Barbaro, and Barinholtz, all four playing key figures in the genesis of OpenAI, play incredibly off of each other as tech titans forcing a smile as they convince their audience artificial technology is inevitable. Join or die. Their joint efforts to invoke a common sense of humanity would be funny if the reality of the situation weren’t so uncanny.

Re-teaming with her “Secret Sunshine” director Lee Chang-dong almost 20 years later, the “Possible Love” star is unmissable as a woman caught in a class divide between her blue collar, out-of-work husband, and the couple that hosts them as a means to interview them for a documentary. It is a role that she said uses “the whole entirety of her body” to push back against the weight of capitalism. The Netflix film chosen to represent South Korea in the Best International Feature category at the 2027 Oscars offers a feast of ideas, with Jeon’s layered turn as Mi-ok alone being enough fodder for many conversations to come.

All sorts of biopics enter theaters each year, but few task their leads with the difficult job of playing someone still actively in the public eye. In Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky,” from Amazon MGM Studios, newcomer Ippolito deftly captures the distinctive look and sound of a young and hungry Sylvester Stallone. But what is more impressive than that form of transformation is how the 27-year-old actor captures the spirit of the unlikely star and scribe of the 1977 Best Picture winner. How some of his best moments come when he himself plays Rocky is a meta element we are still unpacking, but add it to the overwhelming evidence that Ippolito is one to watch.

There is a standout moment in Oscar winner Siân Heder’s “Being Heumann” in which Madeley, as trailblazing disability rights activist Judy Heumann, asks a well-meaning congressman what he means by calling her “inspiring.” “Inspired to do what?,” she says. It is a moment that clarifies that the film about Heumann leading the successful protest to get the government to sign Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act is not standard fare about a woman in a wheelchair overcoming odds, but a film about her refusing to let those odds overcome her.

Madeley embodies a fight against circumstances that applies to more than just the disability community. May casting directors take notice of the limitless potential she offers as part of any type of ensemble.

As the President and CEO of Laika Studios, Knight has spent over 20 years educating audiences on the artform of stop-motion animation. And still, in his latest film “Wildwood,” a fantasy epic taking place in the forests outside Portland, Oregon, Knight directs scenes that seem inexplicable. It is hard enough to animate one bird flying, using that technique, yet the Fathom Entertainment release sees whole flocks fly off toward a war between species. The film’s commentary on parents and children is as heartrending as the craft behind how the film was made is genuinely inspiring to filmmakers of all types.

Talk about legacy. Decades after his father, noted documentarian William Greaves, hosted a party for the surviving members of the Harlem Renaissance, “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” co-directed finished the film, one of the gems of Sundance 2026. To listen to Black luminaries from the ‘20s speak about how their work has endured into the ‘70s, with the dramatic irony of watching the film through a modern lens, is a singular cinematic experience. In a year where there is so much conversation around what pushes the documentary artform forward, the Neon release delivers both necessary context and innovation.

There is humor in having puppetry, one of the world’s oldest artforms, at the center of a conversation around innovation, but come on. Ortiz’s performance as Rocky in “Project Hail Mary,” supported by the work of visual effects team leaders Scanlan, Lambert, and Sarnowska, made us fall in love with a spidery alien rock that has no mouth or face. Puppetry’s forebearers would have still found that to be an insurmountable challenge. Hence, why the artist behind the fan favorite character opposite Ryan Gosling in the Amazon MGM Studios blockbuster deserves their flowers for helping viewers go beyond their earthly imaginations.

Though the latest film from director David Fincher and screenwriter Quentin Tarantino furthers the mis-adventures of Cliff Booth, the role that earned star Brad Pitt an Oscar, the Netflix film has an identity all its own. The work of costume designer Trish Summerville and actor Yahya Abdul-Mateen II are two elements that put that into focus, really easing the audience into the jump forward to 1977, where the silks flowed, and fur dripped off new screen icons akin to the latter’s Rodrick “Hot Rod” Harrison. This go-round allows viewers to have an appreciation for more than just Hollywood, but the greater Los Angeles area, and all the distinct styles it brought in that pivotal ‘70s moment.

#3403. Stephen King's Psychological Thriller Officially Says Goodbye to Streaming

Glide, not walk, or miss out on King’s best film adaptation on HBO Max

Stephen King’s books have inspired countless adaptations over the years. Several have even been adapted for the screen more than once, including Firestarter (1984 and 2022) and The Running Man (1987 and 2025).

However, one film adaptation stands out for its distinctive impact on the horror genre. That film is Brian De Palma’s 1976 supernatural horror classic, Carrie, featuring Sissy Spacek as our titular protagonist. And while its story has been adapted multiple times in both film and TV, the original remains unbeatable.

With Carrie leaving HBO Max on Nov. 30, there's never been a better time to hide from your family this Thanksgiving and spend the afternoon watching a young woman pushed to the brink and unleashing supernatural violence.

King's story follows awkward 16-year-old Carrie White as she faces torment at home and at school. At home, her abusive mother’s religious fanaticism creates an oppressive environment. At school, a group of popular girls targets her. When Carrie gets her first period, her main bully, Chris (Nancy Allen), cruelly humiliates her and encourages the girls to pelt her with tampons. Carrie’s teacher, Miss Collins (Betty Buckley), punishes Chris and bars her from attending prom. Furious, Chris begins plotting revenge against Carrie.

However, Carrie’s discovery comes with a frightening catch: Whenever she becomes upset, she can move objects with her mind. As she struggles to understand and control this mysterious ability, Chris carries out her plan to humiliate Carrie in front of everyone at prom. The two events collide, turning the night into a bloodbath as Carrie unleashes an unprecedented wave of vengeance against her tormentors, including her mother.

Over the years, Stephen King has never hesitated to speak out about adaptations of his books that, in his view, stray from the original meaning. One well-known example is Stanley Kubrick’s The Shining, which King fans know he has criticized so harshly that he once described the film as “a big, beautiful Cadillac with no engine inside it.”

King feels quite differently about De Palma’s Carrie. In an interview with Cinefantastique, he praised De Palma’s take on his book, even though the film is far more satirical than the novel.

“Sissy Spacek was excellent, but right behind her — in a smaller part than it should have been — was John Travolta,” King said. “He played the part of Billy Nolan the way I wish I’d written it, half-funny and half-crazy.”

Over the years, King’s Carrie has been adapted in many ways, though not all for film. The latest adaptation is by Mike Flanagan, known for Midnight Mass, and has generally been well received, with an 85% Tomatometer score on Rotten Tomatoes.

Yet, as beloved as Flanagan’s adaptation is, horror fans owe it to themselves to watch the classic that launched the Carrie franchise. For one thing, King was absolutely right to praise Spacek, who captures Carrie’s vulnerability with heartbreaking precision while also conveying her rage through subtle yet striking physical gestures. Even a single twitch of her eye makes you stand up straight, waiting for her to snap.

More importantly, as the first screen adaptation of King’s work to achieve both critical and commercial success (it earned $33.8 million at the box office on a modest $1.8 million budget), Carrie undoubtedly helped make King a household name in horror. It showed that his work could translate well to the big screen and paved the way for later cinematic classics like The Shining, Cujo, and Christine.

With such monumental success behind it, the only question we’ve got is this: Why aren’t you watching Carrie right now? Go on, git.

Carrie is available to watch now exclusively on HBO Max. But don’t wait too long; it leaves the streamer on Nov. 30.

#3402. 8 Elite HBO Miniseries to Binge Right Now

HBO has long had a reputation for prestige, cinematic shows and miniseries. But the network has come a long way since The Far Pavilions and has become synonymous with top-tier, critically acclaimed miniseries. Several of the miniseries that HBO has produced over the last couple of decades are not just another feather in their hat but icons of their genre, TV classics of their time, and standouts among their contemporaries.

While 2001’s Band of Brothers has become the gold standard for war-drama television, 2019’s Chernobyl excels in translating a traumatic human event into an intricate character study. Between adaptations of bestselling novels and intriguing original stories, here are our picks for elite HBO miniseries that you can binge right now.

Scottish comedian and actor Richard Gadd of Baby Reindeer fame returns with another chilling miniseries, Half Man, which he also writes and stars in. The six-part psychological thriller unspools the complicated, violent, lifelong friendship between Gadd’s Ruben and Jamie Bell’s Niall, after an unexpected incident at Niall’s wedding forces them to reconnect with their past. Stuart Campbell and Mitchell Robertson portray the younger versions of Ruben and Niall.

Half Man is a story about toxic male friendships, but it is the show’s treatment that makes it more intense and raw than most. While Niall is an intricately written character, Ruben is a drastic departure from Gadd’s fragile, sensitive role in Baby Reindeer, and the actor-comedian thrives as the aggressive, tormented character. Deeply disturbing yet delicate in its own way, Half Man is an exceptionally intense show that easily ranks among the best TV dramas made in the 2020s.

Created by Steven Spielberg and Tom Hanks in their second collaboration following Saving Private Ryan, Band of Brothers is a 21st-century television classic adapted from the non-fiction book by Stephen E. Ambrose. Set during WWII, the war drama recounts the story of the “Easy” Company, 2nd Battalion, 506th Parachute Infantry Regiment of the 101st Airborne Division of the US Army on the Western Front between D-Day and their occupation of Berchtesgaden. Kirk Acevedo, Eion Bailey, Damian Lewis, Ron Livingston, and Neal McDonough portray various real-life characters.

Band of Brothers became an instant classic when it premiered 25 years ago and has since been an HBO landmark and often cited as a benchmark of the genre. The 10-episode miniseries combines a dramatized narrative with documentary-style, candid interviews with real veterans, reconstructing one of the grimmest times of human history in the most thoughtful way. A remarkable tribute to the sacrifices of a whole generation of American soldiers, Band of Brothers is surely a must-watch for genre fans.

Created by David Simon, Ed Burns, and Evan Wright, Generation Kill is an often-forgotten war miniseries that adapts Wright’s non-fiction book of the same name, chronicling his experiences as an embedded reporter in the US Marine Corps during the 2003 Invasion of Iraq. Set during the first phase of the war, the series follows Wright, played by Lee Tergesen, as he rides along with the U.S. Marine Corps' 1st Reconnaissance Battalion on their way to Baghdad. Other real-life people are portrayed by Alexander Skarsgård, Billy Rush, James Ransone, and Stark Sands.

Generation Kill is often considered one of the most visceral and grounded portrayals of war on television. At the time of its broadcast, it was among the most prestigious shows of the genre and is undeniably one of the best war shows of the 2000s. However, despite its critical acclaim and several accolades, Generation Kill has mostly faded from mainstream attention and has been overshadowed by bigger productions.

Britain makes more detective television than any country has any business making, and somehow almost all of it is good. Here is the one you belong in, what it says about you, and the case for it being the best of the four.

You want the tea, the gossip and the vicar behaving oddly. Midsomer is a county where the scenery is beautiful, the fete is on Saturday and the murder rate is roughly that of a small war, and absolutely nobody involved thinks this is strange.

You feel other people's grief as if it were handed to you personally. Broadchurch is less a whodunnit than a study of what a small town does to itself when it finds out that the answer was always going to be somebody everybody already knew.

You go through things rather than around them. John Luther is the best detective in London and a liability to everybody who works with him, and the show is completely honest that those two facts are the same fact.

You say the thing and you do not dress it up. Vera Stanhope turns up in a hat and a mac, is rude to almost everybody, and is the only person in the room prepared to ask the question that the family has been waiting years for somebody to ask.

Created by David E. Kelley, The Undoing is loosely based on Jean Hanff Korelitz’s novel You Should Have Known and follows Grace (Nicole Kidman), a wealthy therapist in New York City, whose perfect life begins to unravel when her renowned oncologist husband, Dr. Jonathan Fraser (Hugh Grant), is accused of murder. As the investigation proceeds, Grace and her family learn shocking truths about Jonathan, making her question her marriage, profession, and the truth of her life. Other key cast members include Noma Dumezweni, Édgar Ramírez, Donald Sutherland, and Noah Jupe.

Elevated by the star power of its cast and refined production design, The Undoing is truly an elite miniseries and one of the finest HBO has produced in the 2020s. Nicole Kidman and Hugh Grant steal every scene with their commanding presence, even if the plot loses momentum occasionally, making this six-episode psychological crime thriller a highly engaging watch. The show has earned praise for its acting, cinematography, and strong plot twists, but has also been criticized for its writing and pacing.

Now considered one of the most immersive screen portrayals of the disaster of 1986, Chernobyl is a dramatized retelling of the titular nuclear plant explosion in Ukraine that resulted in the devastation of all life in the region for decades. The series takes a closer look at the accident from the perspectives of all the key people involved, exploring the events leading up to it and its aftermath. The show boasts a strong ensemble cast, with Jared Harris, Stellan Skarsgård, Emily Watson, Paul Ritter, Jessie Buckley, and more in notable roles.

Created by Craig Mazin, Chernobyl is a masterfully made miniseries that cleverly unpacks the horrific history within its limited runtime. While the show takes some dramatic liberties, trading fact for fiction, it does so engagingly, with powerful performances and an atmospheric setting. The series has since remained a critical darling and a fan favorite, distinctly capturing the emotional and physical intensity of the real tragedy.

Starring Kate Winslet as protagonist Marianne “Mare” Sheehan, Mare of Easttown follows the titular police detective in a small Philadelphia town, where she attempts to solve the murder of a local teenager while being tormented by a similar case from a year ago. Mare continues to search for truth while grappling with past guilt, the loss of a child, divorce, and her declining reputation. Julianne Nicholson, Jean Smart, Angourie Rice, and Guy Pearce also star in key roles.

When Mare of Easttown first premiered, it was a class of its own as a crime drama thriller miniseries. Its gritty story, grounded characters, and deeply emotional plotlines all come together to make this an intense show that is sure to leave an impact on the audience long after the credits roll. Created by Brad Ingelsby, Mare of Easttown has become a modern classic for HBO that thrives on Kate Winslet’s exceptional, award-winning performance, which is often considered her TV best.

Based on Criminal Justice by Peter Moffat and created by Richard Price and Steven Zaillian, The Night Of centers on a Pakistani-American college student named Nasir “Naz” Khan (Riz Ahmed), who wakes up after a nightlong party fueled by drugs and alcohol next to the dead body of a woman he met the night before. With missing memories of the night and evidence pointing to him as the killer, Naz leaves his fate in the hands of a resolute lawyer named John Stone (John Turturro). Bill Camp, Michael Kenneth Williams, and Poorna Jagannathan appear in key roles.

The Night Of is an excellently made crime drama that grips the audience with its tightly-knit plot and deep, character-driven storytelling. The show’s creators elevate the original material by putting an intelligent spin on classic tropes and making it a timely story. When it premiered, the crime thriller was critically praised for its masterful production, layered characterizations, and riveting performances by Turturro and Ahmed.

A Southern Gothic psychological thriller miniseries created by Marti Noxon, Sharp Objects is a series adaptation of Gillian Flynn’s debut novel of the same name and follows Camille Preaker (Amy Adams), a reporter suffering from alcoholism and psychological troubles, who returns to her hometown in Missouri. Recently discharged from a psychiatric hospital and returning to her controlling mother, Adora (Patricia Clarkson), Camille is forced to confront her personal demons while investigating the murder of two young girls. Chris Messina and Eliza Scanlen also have main roles.

The HBO adaptation of Sharp Objects stays true to Flynn’s original crime novel in tone and themes but varies in format and pacing. In fact, the slow-burn storytelling balances the show’s atmospheric setting and dark themes to better explore the characters’ fractured psyches and meditate on their emotional states. Headlined by intense performances from Adams and Clarkson, Sharp Objects is one of HBO's best crime thriller miniseries of the 2010s.

#3400. 16-Episode Existential Sci-Fi Masterpiece On Netflix Is A God-Tier Adaptation

Some sci-fi stories are so profoundly human, introspective, and existential on the page that adapting them on the screen should be impossible. More often than not, even some of the most ambitious filmmakers leave such stories alone. However, every once in a while, someone dares to translate such stories to the screen and the result turns out to be beyond impressive.

Perhaps Denis Villeneuve’s Arrival is an incredible example of this. The sci-fi movie turns Ted Chiang's stories into a masterful exploration of time, destiny, free will, and the stories we tell ourselves to find meaning. Similar to Arrival, the sci-fi series, Pantheon, goes to extreme lengths to capture the essence of Ken Liu's award-winning sci-fi stories.

Like Denis Villeneuve’s Arrival, Pantheon seems fairly simple in its early moments. The sci-fi show on Netflix unfolds in a world where mind-uploading technology is becoming accessible for the masses. However, what starts as a tale about a global conspiracy evolves to an existential scale that questions everything from humanity's place in the universe to the nature of consciousness.

Ted Chiang's novella, Story of Your Life, was seemingly never meant to be adapted for the screen. It heavily relies on teleological physics and linguistic relativity to explore time travel. Yet, screenwriter Eric Heisserer and director Denis Villeneuve turned it into a 2-hour cinematic masterpiece by tricking viewers into reading flash-forwards as flashbacks.

In Pantheon, creator Craig Silverstein picks up many of Ken Liu's short stories that present fragmented explorations of post-humanity. He then binds them into a singular narrative that starts a relatable family drama but grows into an existential war story. Pantheon does not shy away from being incredibly ambitious with its storytelling. But, like Denis Villeneuve's Arrival, it never forgets it is about its human characters.

On the screen, science fiction can risk feeling too sterile and hollow if its ambition outgrows its human stakes. There are cosmic elements in both Arrival and Pantheon that give a glimpse of how insignificant human lives can seem in the vastness of the universe. Yet, in both, the high-concept sci-fi is always anchored in human grief.

Pantheon originally premiered on AMC+, but it is now available for streaming on Netflix in the U.S.

Arrival introduces an alien language through ink-ring logograms to make sense out of an abstract concept like non-linear time. It never dumbs this down and respects viewers' intelligence by allowing them to do a lot of intellectual heavy lifting. Pantheon achieves something similar by using animating as a visual language as it walks through complex ideas surrounding

In the best existential sci-fi books, post-humanity is the threshold. They question whether a machine can think or whether achieving singularity would be a boon or bane for humanity. Pantheon, in contrast, blows right past this. Boom! The series keeps pushing the boundaries of existential sci-fi until it is far beyond base realities, linear time, and biological life.

It begins with a familiar exploration of how digital cloning and consciousness uploading can pave the way for many moral and ethical challenges. Once uploading becomes safe, it shifts to a civilizational schism, showing how those who refuse to "upload" themselves are biological relics while the ones who conformed are almost godlike.

Before its credits start rolling, Pantheon also ambitiously leaps millions of years ahead in time. With this, it attempts to highlight how, despite becoming almost godly omnipresent beings with the ability to simulate infinity, meaning only exists in human vulnerability and the inability to know what lies ahead. Here lies the beauty of Pantheon's unforgettable exploration of existential sci-fi.

#3399. ‘Filipiñana’ Could Be the Philippines’ First-Ever Oscar-Shortlisted Feature — Even as the Film Was Dealt an Unexpected Tragedy

A posh, Philippine country club’s colonial secrets are exposed in Rafael Manuel’s evocatively creepy, grimly funny, and austerely constructed social satire, “Filipiñana,” set outside Manila.

Writer/director Rafael Manuel’s film, which won a World Cinema special jury award at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival, also stands a chance at being his country’s first representative on a Best International Feature Film Oscar shortlist. While the Philippines was among the eight countries that submitted during the category’s inaugural year in 1956 (with Lamberto V. Avellana’s “Child of Sorrow”) along with France, Italy, and others, it’s never been nominated or shortlisted. Related Stories Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’

Executive-produced by Manuel’s former mentor Jia Zhangke, “Filipiñana” follows a tee girl who discovers something is off (and downright sinister) about the club’s administration, specifically president Dr. Palanca (Teroy Guzman). She’s played by Jorrybell Agoto, who, at just 32 years old, died earlier in November after a short battle with lymphoma.

IndieWire’s interview with filmmaker Rafael Manuel took place a week before the news, though he shared in a later statement, “The tragedy of this loss cannot be put into words. The world has just lost one of its brightest stars. We have just lost a great friend. But our thoughts and prayers go out especially to Jorybell’s family, who have just lost a loving ate [the Filipino word for older sister] and a devoted daughter.”

An elegaic air, too, hangs over the film in retrospect and even before Agoto’s passing, as “Filipiñana” dwells in ghosts of the Philippines’ imperial past and Spanish occupation.

“No one explains it to you beforehand,” director Manuel told IndieWire of touring with his first feature for nearly a year. (We spoke over Zoom while he smoked a cigarette in his Amsterdam apartment.) “What I’m starting to realize is the biggest difference between short and feature is that with short festival, it’s kind of the end goal. When you premiere at your festival, you’re so happy, and it’s done; it’s like people get to see it finally. But with a feature film, it’s just the beginning, and no one explained this to me.”

Manuel joins the ranks of Lav Diaz, Brillante Mendoza, the late Lino Brocka, and many others to represent the Philippines at the Academy Awards — a concept, he said, that was never really on his radar.

“When we were coming up with this film and the genesis of the film, you don’t really think about an Oscars race,” said Manuel. “You just think about making the best film you can. And especially coming from Southeast Asia, access to the American market, even getting a U.S. theatrical release, it’s not something that’s very common. Usually, your usual route is via the European arthouse market. So it’s been really surprising and in the best way possible, seeing how well received the film is in the States, in North America, and in the Anglo world in general.”

The process was a “very challenging one,” he said, as the Philippines is taking the Oscar push very seriously from a governmental perspective. “And to be the first film that’s seriously backed by the government means a lot to us,” he said, especially for a film that’s critical of government and social hierarchy.

And there are hat tips not only to Jacques Tati, but also to Wes Anderson and Michael Haneke, at least in reviews, in terms of the movie’s flattened remove from violence and its dryly observational approach where everything in the frame is meticulously arranged.

“I get why people are saying Michael Haneke and Wes Anderson,” he said. “I mean, Jacques Tati, obviously, he’s a really big influence for me, but for example, with Haneke, I feel like we tackle violence very differently from how Haneke tackles violence. And I think with Wes Anderson, I see it because of the colors, because of the symmetrical framing and all of that, but I think this is very much a satire of that. And so, yes, we use a lot of Western codes and Western aesthetics in the film, but because it’s a film that deals with Western influence in the Orient, it was a film that deals with colonization. So the form and the aesthetic of the film is very much part of the satire. It’s the form.”

He added, “It’s a polarizing film. I think it’s either you love it or you hate it, and I think that’s the same whether you’re in the West or in the Philippines.”

The distribution of world cinema in the Philippines also helps to explain the divided palate for “Filipiñana,” as audiences have very little exposure to arthouse cinema from the outside world.

“In the Philippines, distribution of world cinema, it’s almost nonexistent. In Metro Manila, we have basically one or two arthouse cinemas, independent cinemas. The rest of the cinemas are all in shopping malls, and all they play are local rom-coms or Marvel movies,” he said. But issues in the West of audience fatigue over shopworn, recycled I.P. and familiar material also apply in the Philippines.

“It’s been a hot topic lately in the Philippines and consumers and audiences complaining about formulaic Filipino filmmaking. They’re tired of the formulaic rom-coms. But then the thing is that in the Philippines, I would say 90 percent of people have never seen a Lav Diaz film, even maybe 99 percent of people haven’t seen a Lav Diaz film,” Manuel said of the slow cinema master behind last year’s submission, the Gael García Bernal-starring “Magellan,” which also dealt in the Philippines’ colonized history. (Diaz and Manuel share producers, including Bianca Balbuena and Bradley Liew, though they’ve never actually met.)

“Filipiñana” marks a break from tradition in terms of its Westernized style — and chatter has been flying on Letterboxd over the film since the Sundance premiere. (“I look through Letterboxd sometimes. Well, I used to, I stopped. And then the unhealthy thing with Letterboxd, for me especially, is that I’ll skip all the good comments and I’ll just read all the bad comments,” he said.)

“When you’re faced with something different with arthouse cinema, like Filipino arthouse cinema, when Filipino audiences are faced with Filipino arthouse cinema, and you get some violent reactions, then it begs the question, ‘When you’re complaining about being tired of formulaic Filipino filmmaking, what exactly do you mean, and what exactly is it that you want?’ Do you just want Hollywood films but with brown faces in them? Because I don’t think that’s the answer either.”

“Filipiñana” is now streaming on Kino Film Collection.

#3397. Watch ‘The Sheep Detectives’ VFX Supervisor Break Down the ‘Sheep-Isms’ That Made His Characters Stand Out

It’s not every day you see a movie where talking sheep get to be the stars. But Kyle Balda’s “The Sheep Detectives” does exactly that. The Amazon MGM film flips the whodunnit formula on its head with a barnyard murder mystery in which a group of sheep have to solve the murder of their beloved shepherd. Much of the film’s success can be attributed to the juxtaposition between a whimsical plot and the realism with which it’s executed. The sheep might talk and solve crimes, but they look like real animals you’d find on any farm.

During the VFX section of IndieWire’s recent Craft Roundtables, “The Sheep Detectives” Visual Effects Supervisor Graham Page broke down the meticulous research process that made the sheep look so lifelike. Related Stories How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’? Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It

“To make them look real, talking about practical and how important that is, I from Day One felt like you had to base these characters on real sheep,” Page said. “We filmed [real sheep] with multiple cameras and getting on boxes. We had a script, almost, like ‘These are the things the sheep need to do in the film.’ Even before an animator can touch it, another artist modeled the skeleton and the muscle and fat. And then you have a rigger and a facial artist, all of these artists.”

He went on to explain how that research process produced character-defining details that they would not have discovered any other way.

“We started to come up with what we would call ‘Sheep-isms’ that help kind of bring some of that natural movement,” he said. “There’s a little ear twitch. And a human can’t twitch their ear, but it felt so right. We were like ‘This is really nice,’ and it emphasized the character and the story and the emotion. But it was brought out of a sheep.”

#3395. ‘All of a Sudden’: Why Does an 11-Minute Scene Centered on a Whiteboard Lecture Work So Well Onscreen?

It is an unorthodox sequence. In the middle of “All of a Sudden,” Mari (Tao Okamoto) pulls out a whiteboard and markers to diagram the principles of nature vs. capitalism for her new friend Marie-Lou (Virginie Efira). The scene lasts 11 minutes and digs into material you would expect in a university seminar, not the latest cinematic achievement from the Oscar-winning director of “Drive My Car,” Ryūsuke Hamaguchi.

While a guest on this week’s Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Hamaguchi acknowledged the whiteboard is not what we generally consider to be cinematic, but then again neither is the three-hour-and-17-minute film about two women who form a powerful bond by talking about life, their life’s work, and the ever so sexy topic of eldercare for dementia patients. Related Stories How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’? Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It

And yet “All of a Sudden” blew away the world’s toughest critics at Cannes. Now, its distributor, Neon, heads into this weekend’s holiday theatrical release believing it has a legit shot at winning over the more commercially oriented Oscar voters — and becoming one of the (increasingly common) foreign-language Best Picture nominations. Neon similarly released “Sentimental Value” and “The Secret Agent” to Best Picture nominations the year before.

The whiteboard scene is not an extraneous aside, but a critical turning point in the women’s relationship. We asked the film’s writer/director why it not only works, but was deemed vital to the film.

“In trying to answer why this somehow works, I think there’s a few layers to it,” said Hamaguchi while on IndieWire’s Filmmaker Toolkit podcast. “And one maybe is because it really is something that is far removed from what is generally considered as cinematic. Perhaps because of that, it brings about a certain suspense, where you wonder, ‘OK, what is this for? What is this actually going to do?’ And there’s a certain sense of wondering that happens.”

The scene comes a little over an hour into the film. Neither woman wants their magical evening to end. Mari follows Marie-Lou to her job as director of a nursing home, where she struggles to implement her passion project, “Huminitude,” a patient-centered care method based on touch and eye contact, which Mari sees in action. What prompts Mari’s whiteboard seminar is an attempt to help her new companion put into perspective the resistance she faces in implementing Huminitude and open the door to problem-solving.

“I think the second part [of why the scene works] really comes down to the efforts of the actors that are performing this scene,” said Hamaguchi of Okamoto and Efira, who shared the Best Actress Prize at Cannes. “For Tao, I think it was an incredibly difficult scene to perform because first of all she really needed to understand all of the concepts that she was describing here and to really understand everything intellectually. And so in her preparation she did read a lot of the relevant books to really understand what she is talking about.”

Hamaguchi believes the key to his dialogue-driven film is not necessarily how the words are spoken, but the performance of the listening and how the words are received. In Efira’s whiteboard scene, we see a shift from determined frustration to open enthusiasm that changes the direction of the film itself.

“The attitude of listening that Virginie portrays in this moment, I think, is very important and really supports this scene,” said Hamaguchi. “She’s not uninterested in what is going on, but in fact she feels that this is something that she should really be exploring together and she’s there and very much present. And I think this attitude of interest and curiosity really starts to work on the audience as well. And so in that sense I think ultimately this scene really works because of the actors’ performances.”

One topic that comes up in most post-screening Q&As is that both actresses were not working in the native language. Hamaguchi himself had to work with an interpreter to direct his leads. This is not the first time Hamaguchi has worked this way. On the podcast, he said that, in his experience directing the play inside “Drive My Car,” the language barrier was less of a hindrance and could even aid actors in listening to one another, as shown in the whiteboard scene.

“I felt that, in fact, this kind of difficulty that exists can in fact provide an environment for even more heightened concentration than you might have if you were speaking the same language,” said Hamaguchi. “ I think that actually when you can actually hear a lot and get a lot of information from somebody’s voice, you can, in fact, precisely feel just how concentrated the person is when they’re saying something by listening to their voice.”

Asked if any of his collaborators or producers ever questioned the whiteboard scene after reading the script, Hamaguchi said no, and speculated why: “Because it’s so unusual, I think people understood that this is something that I really wanted to do.”

“There were some questions around, ‘This section feels a little long. Is there anything we can do about that?’” recalled Hamaguchi, adding that he made a concerted effort to cut his four-hour script to a three-hour, 16-minute running time.

“For me, I was ultimately trying to bring in the shortest version that I felt was accurate for this moment. But ultimately, there is this understanding that this moment is a very important turning point within the film, and so I believe that the producers also understood this.”

“All of a Sudden” is now playing in select theaters.

#3394. Star Trek: Duty And Honor Officially Brings Back Worf

Star Trek fans will almost certainly be familiar with the legendary character Worf. The Klingon, first introduced in Star Trek: The Next Generation, has appeared in more episodes throughout the entire show's history than any other character, making him both a fan-favorite staple and a constant fixture. It is for this very reason that his reappearance on multiple shows and subsequent new Star Trek content no longer feels terribly surprising, although it is always appreciated.

Fortunately, for those who cannot get enough of Worf and want a brand-new Star Trek release to tide them over, the iconic character is returning once more in a new release that is targeted at dedicated fans. Titled Duty and Honor, this new Star Trek project offers a different type of experience than the one most fans will be used to, all while putting Worf front and center. Suffice it to say, it could end up being the definitive Worf Star Trek release should its creators play their cards right.

Duty and Honor is the upcoming expansion for the critically acclaimed deck-building game, Star Trek: Captain's Chair. The base game, for those who've missed out thus far, is an in-depth, strategic experience in which players take on the role of one of six captains (either Picard, Sisko, Burnham, Shran, Koloth, and Sela) and must attempt to complete various objectives and obtain the highest score by playing cards from each character's corresponding starter deck and any they obtain throughout.

Widely praised as being a compelling and highly detailed Star Trek experience with strong theming and phenomenal representation of the characters included, Captain's Chair (developed by WizKids) has gone on to get multiple expansions. The latest, the aforementioned Duty and Honor, adds four new captains to the experience, as well as their corresponding decks, thus greatly increasing the level of replayability and variety within the game.

Duty and Honor is adding Captain Worf as well as the fan-favorite Deep Space Nine Cardassian, Gul Dukat. Two additional captains will also be added, although WizKids has not yet confirmed who they will be. Of course, included in their decks will be iconic ships, characters, and locations associated with them, so dedicated fans are in for a treat. While it isn't quite a new series, it should hopefully make up for the canceled Worf series that fans never got the chance to see.

The base Star Trek: Captain's Chair game that is required to play the Duty and Honor expansion costs $59.99. It is currently available for back-order on the official WizKids website and is expected to be shipped in Q4 2026.

The Duty and Honor expansion for Star Trek: Captain's Chair costs $39.99. It is currently available for pre-order via the official WizKids website, as well as other assorted retailers. It is estimated to have a release date of Q3 2027, according to the official store listing, which means it'll release any time between July 1 and September 30. Considering how well-received the other Star Trek: Captain's Chair expansions have been, fans can likely rest assured that Duty and Honor will do Worf proud.

#3393. Anya Taylor-Joy’s 2-Hour Thriller Is Still Her Greatest Movie 10 Years Later

Anya Taylor-Joy’s film debut in Robert Eggers’ The Witch may have given the actor a cult following, but it was her role in M. Night Shyamalan’s Split in 2016 that made her a household name. A year after she shocked horror fans as Thomasin, she took on an incredibly different role in the thriller. A return to form for Shyamalan, Split takes on the complex issue of DID. Dissociative Identity Disorder is at the crux of the movie as James McAvoy takes on 24 separate identities in his role of Kevin.

Viewers only get to see some of them, but his immense talent in showing just a few is one of the best examples of character work. Even more impressive is Taylor-Joy, who stands toe to toe with the performer in her role as Casey Cooke. One day when Casey is out at a birthday party, she and acquaintances Marcia (Jessica Sula) and Claire (Haley Lu Richardson) are abducted by some of Kevin’s most insidious personalities. In the locked room drama, Casey weaponizes her wits and her own experience with trauma to escape her captivity and save her life.

M. Night Shyamalan features have typically been divisive in recent years, and Split is no different. In the movie, the director posits that DID can present itself not just in personality changes, but with physical characteristics as well. One of the most notorious of these personalities, the Beast, has more muscle definition and becomes literally bigger than the other personalities. This may be controversial with the mental health community, but there is no denying that this offers a fascinating new perspective on the subject of trauma.

Kevin materialized these personalities as a response to his overbearing and abusive mother. His foil in the film is Casey, played by Anya Taylor-Joy. Immediately, it is clear that Casey has a superpower that the other abductees do not. Slowly throughout the film, Casey’s own abuse and trauma are revealed, which allows her to empathize with Kevin. While Marcia and Claire want to break their way out by force, Casey understands that the best way to escape is through intelligence and subtlety.

This is a difficult balance to maintain, but Taylor-Joy does it almost effortlessly. She establishes this in the abduction scene as it slowly dawns on Casey that there is no escape. When Kevin’s personality, Dennis, enters the girls’ car, he subdues the other two easily in the backseat. Casey, who is in the front, immediately understands the danger in this encounter. As a single tear rolls down her face, she knows that there is no point in fighting and is taken as well.

What could be considered weakness or a fault in her character is exactly the opposite. Casey knows that she is a survivor. She has endured one monster before and will find a way to survive this one as well. Casey is characterized by her creativity in finding a way out of horrifying situations, which aids her until the very end of the movie. Just like in The Witch, Taylor-Joy accepts the task of a difficult character that could be misunderstood and instead makes it iconic. In the decade since Split first premiered, no other character has quite reached the heights of this one.

#3392. This Apple Watch Is a Lifehacker 'Gift of the Year' Award Winner, and It's $50 Off During Black Friday

Apple has three main Apple Watch "lines." There's the flagship, currently the Series 12, which represents Apple's mainstream wearable. For athletes and users who think they'll put their watches through some extreme scenarios, there's the Ultra line, currently the Apple Watch Ultra 4. And while both the Series 12 and Ultra 4 are excellent devices in their own right, they can be pretty pricey (particularly the Ultra). That's why the third category, the SE, is actually best for most people, and Lifehacker's choice for best smartwatch gift of the year. Better yet, the third-generation SE is currently $50 off ahead of Black Friday, perfect for most people asking for an Apple Watch this year.

The SE 3 does just about everything you'd expect an Apple Watch to do. It, of course, has a heart rate sensor to keep tabs on your pulse, including high and low heart rate alerts; the ability to track dozens of different workouts and exercise types (including swimming, thanks to the device's water resistance); a sleep tracker with daily analyses available in the Health app; notification forwarding to check in on your alerts without opening your iPhone; and the ability to send and receive text messages.

It comes in two sizes (40mm and 44mm) depending on how large or small you prefer your watch. No matter which model you get, the watch comes with the S10 chip, Apple's last-generation watch processor. While it isn't as fast as the current S11 chip, the S10 is more than capable of running watchOS 27. Apple says the SE 3 can run for up to 18 hours on a single charge, and up to 32 hours in Low Power Mode, with fast charging from 0% to 80% in 45 minutes.

The majority of the features missing from the SE 3 aren't essential. Apple's other watches have things like bigger, brighter displays, additional health tracking tools like hypertension alerts and an ECG sensor, longer battery life, and Audio Intelligence—the latter of which might be a benefit to miss, depending on who you are.

If your giftee wants or needs any of those additional features, Series 12 or Ultra 4 might be a better choice. But for anyone who wants the essential Apple Watch experience, the SE 3 is simply the best-value watch Apple sells right now—especially at this discount. Right now, the watch starts at $199 for the 40mm watch, or $229 for the 44mm. You can also save on the cellular versions of these watches: $249 for the cellular 40mm watch, and $279 for the cellular 44mm model.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

#3391. Will Ferrell Golf Comedy ‘The Hawk’ Canceled at Netflix After Just One Season

“The Hawk,” a Will Ferrell golf comedy that debuted just this summer, has been canceled by Netflix and will not return for a second season, an individual with knowledge told IndieWire.

Ferrell co-created the series in which he plays a former top golfer who is now trying to return to the tour. And while it figured to be a tentpole series for Netflix, one that carried possibly the most expensive budget for a comedy series on Netflix and reunited Ferrell with his “SNL” co-star Molly Shannon and co-creator Harper Steele, it didn’t connect with critics or audiences.

“The Hawk” spent just three weeks on Netflix’s Top 10 when it debuted back in July, topping out at #2 in its second week on Netflix with just 6.2 million views. Ferrell’s vulgar, loudly-dressed golfer with a personalized visor and big mess of bleached blonde hair played a lot like some of Ferrell’s other string of sports comedies throughout the years. But even our critic was perplexed by the series’ tone that makes it sometimes play like a “bizarre addiction drama.” Related Stories ‘The Hunting Wives’ Review: Season 2 Reloads Without Slowing Down in Netflix’s Delirious Soap ‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Finale Hinges on Two Monologues — Let Ethan Hawke and Sterlin Harjo Break Them Down

Steele, in a recent appearance on “Late Night with Seth Meyers,” tipped her hand a little that the show was likely ending when she let slip that, “I was working on a short-lived but probably the best show ever, ‘The Hawk.’”

The cancellation comes in the wake of a changing of the guard at Netflix, with Peter Rice taking over for veteran creative chief Bela Bajaria. Our critic also recently wrote about the challenges Netflix is facing right now in getting audiences to discover new series in the ways they used to.

But at the same time, Netflix has already renewed a couple of other comedy series that even premiered after “The Hawk” later this year, including “Nobody Wants This,” “A Different World,” “Tires,” “Big Mistakes,” and “The Four Seasons.” Netflix is also still working with Ferrell’s Gloria Sanchez Productions on three new series, “All the Rage,” “Prep,” and another scripted series from Nikki Glaser.

#3389. What Are Local Movie Theaters Showing for Thanksgiving 2026?

One of the great things about going to the movies by yourself is that, technically speaking, you’re not alone. Even if you’re the only person in the auditorium, somebody thought about what you might like to watch, put it on the calendar, and made sure there was a place for you to sit.

That’s something worth being grateful for this Thanksgiving.

Earlier this month, IndieWire surveyed the programming at independent movie theaters across the United States on Election Night. Continuing that exercise over Thanksgiving weekend reveals another delightful cross-section of American film culture — albeit with considerably more cannibalism. Related Stories How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

At the Music Box Theatre in Chicago, where audiences have spent more than two decades celebrating Thanksgiving by singing along to “The Sound of Music,” moviegoers can also catch Ruggero Deodato’s “Cannibal Holocaust” late Friday night. It’s hard to imagine the Von Trapps sticking around for that one, but there’s something lovely about a neighborhood institution accommodating both crowds.

In Seattle, the Beacon is observing its own Thanksgiving tradition with “Blood Rage,” the gloriously ridiculous slasher that made cranberry sauce an enduring point of reference for a certain subset of horror fans. For a somewhat more realistic depiction of the horrors of going home for Thanksgiving, SALA Event Center in Los Alamos, New Mexico, is showing Jodie Foster’s “Home for the Holidays.”

In Cambridge, Massachusetts, the Brattle Theatre is celebrating Black Friday with a double feature of “Chopping Mall” and “Night of the Comet.” If you’d rather watch people die in a shopping mall than go to one yourself, that’s certainly an economical alternative. Meanwhile, Minneapolis’ Trylon Cinema is spending the biggest shopping weekend of the year celebrating the work of documentary filmmaker Barbara Kopple, screening her Oscar-winning “Harlan County, U.S.A.” and “American Dream” as part of a series dedicated to class struggle.

Thanksgiving also marks the 50th anniversary of the Band’s legendary farewell concert, held at San Francisco’s Winterland Ballroom in 1976. At Film Streams in Omaha, Nebraska, audiences can spend Friday morning watching Martin Scorsese’s “The Last Waltz.” That half a century later, people are still getting together to experience a concert most of them weren’t alive to attend speaks to one of the more miraculous things movies can do.

And in Portland, Oregon, stop-motion animation studio LAIKA is expressing its gratitude to its hometown audience by offering free screenings of “Wildwood“ on Sunday at theaters across the area, including the historic Hollywood Theatre. Considering how many thousands of hours of human labor go into making a stop-motion animated feature, there’s something especially sweet about giving people whose real home served as the setting a chance to enjoy the outcome together.

Of course, what Americans celebrate on Thanksgiving — and whether they celebrate it at all — varies considerably. On Wednesday, California Indian Nations College is presenting a free screening of “People of the West,” a documentary series examining the history of California’s Indigenous peoples from Indigenous perspectives, in Palm Desert. At the historic Raymond Theatre in Raymond, Washington, a free Saturday screening of a documentary about the Qwayat Canoe Society’s journey to Nisqually offers an opportunity to learn more about a living Indigenous tradition.

And for anyone navigating a particularly painful holiday season, a film festival in Magnolia, Texas, is making a different kind of space. Presented by the nonprofit My Grief Angels, Grief Fest is hosting an in-person community screening on Black Friday, with films also available to watch virtually throughout Thanksgiving weekend. Dedicated to exploring loss and healing through cinema, the festival recognizes just how complicated an invitation to celebrate can be.

There are innumerable ways to spend a long weekend like this, and movies aren’t a substitute for the people we wish we could spend it with. But the wonderful thing about indie exhibition is just how much of it depends on random people thinking about other random people. Someone has to remember that a certain movie exists. Then someone else has to think it might mean something to you. And finally a different person has to care enough to bring it all together.

Whether you’re somebody who spends every Thanksgiving with the same people or a cinephile whose traditions are still taking shape, consider making a little time for your local movie theater this weekend. Thank the person who takes your ticket, and tell the programmer when you love something they booked. Maybe even invite that friend you’ve been meaning to catch up with.

There are so many extraordinary works of art to see in this lifetime and never quite enough time to see them all. How lucky we are to get to watch some of them together.

#3388. Reality Is Even Darker Than Jonathan Nolan & J.J. Abrams' 103-Episode Sci-Fi Masterpiece Predicted

Even though Jonathan Nolan and JJ Abrams’ underrated sci-fi series from the 2010s explored a dystopian vision of a surveillance state, reality ended up outdoing this CBS hit. When Firefly was canceled after only 14 episodes in 2002, there is no way that the show’s creators could have known just how influential the short-lived series would be. Without Firefly, viewers might never have gotten SyFy’s Dark Matter, Killjoys, or Bass X Machina, not to mention the show’s influence on the Guardians of the Galaxy movies.

Similarly, author Phillip K. Dick's contributions to the world of sci-fi literature had an almost immeasurable influence on the genre in the years after their original publication. His short story “We Can Remember It For You Wholesale” was loosely adapted into director Paul Verhoeven’s satirical sci-fi action thriller Total Recall, while his sci-fi noir novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? spawned the entire Blade Runner franchise.

Arriving on CBS in 2011, when Fringe’s success and the arrival of 2008’s theatrical spinoff The X-Files: I Want to Believe had reignited interest in sci-fi police procedurals, Person of Interest also benefitted from a killer premise. Person of Interest followed Jim Caviezel’s CIA officer John Reese as he began working with an eccentric inventor and billionaire tech mogul, Harold Finch.

Finch’s invention, simply called “The Machine,” was designed to use an algorithm to predict when terrorist attacks would happen. What made the mogul’s innovation so noteworthy was his claim that “The Machine” could predict terrorist attacks before the offenders themselves had even planned them. Reese is the first CIA operative to use this technology to track down individuals, and Person of Interest doesn’t shy away from the moral and ethical implications of this plan.

In fact, throughout its five-season run, Person of Interest never makes it entirely clear whether “The Machine” is a good idea at all, and modern real-life policing has only made the show’s predictions seem tame in comparison. Where The Machine was designed to avoid prejudiced policing, real-life predictive algorithms used by the police rely on racially biased data from existing police reports.

While Person of Interest had a villainous AI that tracked civilians without their consent, real-life private companies have created this infrastructure and currently license these technologies out to law enforcement agencies, from police departments to ICE, to monitor civilians with no criminal record. Where The Machine almost never makes any mistakes, real-life facial recognition software is notorious for often falsely identifying innocent civilians, especially people of color.

Although Prime Video’s superhero satire The Boys became infamous for accidentally predicting real-life events in its comedic storytelling, Person of Interest was alarmingly prescient in the show’s depictions of policing developments that ran roughshod over the rights of civilians. However, where Finch was transparent about how The Machine works, the private companies that run real-life surveillance tech offer no transparency over oversight.

While The Machine was used to save ordinary civilians from terrorism, real-life policing technologies are used for immigration enforcement, avoiding low-level work, and tracking civilians without their consent. Thus, if Person of Interest’s story got anything wrong, it was assuming these technologies would come from caring, troubled geniuses, and not from for-profit private companies who aren’t answerable to anyone.

#3386. 33 Years Later, the Coldest Quote in Action Thriller History Still Hits Hard

The Fugitive took the world by storm when it was released in 1993. Not only was this action-thriller film, based on the television series from the 1960s, a massive box-office success, but it was also a critical darling and, miraculously, a major Oscar contender, receiving nominations for Best Picture and a win for Tommy Lee Jones for Best Supporting Actor. Starring Harrison Ford as Dr. Richard Kimble, a man wrongfully convicted of the murder of his wife who goes on the run from U.S. Marshals, The Fugitive, directed by Andrew Davis, shares little resemblance to other movies recognized by the Academy Awards, even the other blockbusters. And that especially applies to Jones' surprising Oscar win for playing U.S. Marshal Samuel Gerard, who leads the charge in pursuit of Kimble. When voters heard Gerard's legendary line, "I don't care," one of the coldest lines in thriller movie history, they had no choice but to hand Jones the Oscar.

Harrison Ford was at the peak of his powers in the early '90s, with two iconic characters in Han Solo and Indiana Jones already under his belt. To upend his heroic status on the big screen, The Fugitive had Ford on the defensive, running away from federal prosecution for a crime he didn't commit, but who can really be sure that he didn't slay his wife? Operating on the opposite side of the law and serving out justice is Tommy Lee Jones as the unflappable Samuel Gerard, who unconventionally has his big showdown with Kimble during the film's first act inside a storm drain. Obtaining a lost gun, Richard Kimble has Gerard in his crosshairs, but rather than shooting, he, once again, insists that he didn't kill his wife, to which Gerard, holding his hands in the air in compliance, responds, "I don't care!" These three words immediately entered the Hollywood canon.

Jones, the consummate professional who has consistently carried a no-nonsense, unfussy attitude to the screen, perfectly distills his persona with The Fugitive's most biting line of dialogue. It may not be a quippy retort or badass affirmation, but Gerard laid down the law and outlined the harsh reality of Kimble's predicament while being confronted at gunpoint by a potentially violent fugitive. Most movies provide their law enforcement officers with an altruistic motive, complemented by a flowery speech about the moral importance of the law, but The Fugitive underlines that being a sworn officer is just a job. It is not in Gerard's job description to be the judge and jury of Kimble's murder case, and his opinion is irrelevant, even if he believed his innocence. The line is a sobering punch in the face for Kimble, whose profession as a doctor relies on giving opinions and persuading clients.

It's the rare callback line that doesn't deserve an eye roll.

The Fugitive is a truly timeless film. Its rich simplicity, tight narrative and genre construction felt like a throwback to Golden Age Hollywood, which likely appealed to members of the Academy Awards. With two towering stars, a compelling premise, and a balanced confection of spectacle and character, The Fugitive, which later received an unnecessary sequel, U.S. Marshals, makes the art of filmmaking look easy, as it nails the fundamentals of narrative storytelling with ease. The moment that even the stuffiest Oscar voters had to put their hands up and give Tommy Lee Jones the statuette had to have been the "I don't care" scene in the storm drain, as the Men in Black actor delivered the fury of a Shakespeare monologue in just three one-syllable words. There's something so undeniable about Jones' conviction as his character faces a crossroads. A desperate Kimble could feasibly pull the trigger, and Gerard shows fear, but he never lets it interfere with his devout commitment to his job.

Speaking to the movie's timeless nature, "I don't care" is a moment that could have emerged in a Warner Bros. thriller from the 1940s. The brevity of the line is not its only admirable feat, as Tommy Lee Jones' signature moment in The Fugitive crystallizes the dramatic weight of the film. Andrew Davis' enduring thriller is devoid of themes and subtext in the traditional sense because it's a film about characters defined by their actions. Samuel Gerard has nothing of deep substance to say to Kimble during this pivotal moment. He just wants to bring this man into custody. When you're stuck in a grave misunderstanding, arguing with someone defined by their profession is an impossible mountain to climb.

#3384. Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’

“I’m not one of those people that try to act like I don’t want the thing. I want the thing. I’m excited about the thing,” said recent Academy Award nominee Danielle Brooks. “I know how much it has impacted little Dani when I’ve watched Oprah Winfrey or Whoopi Goldberg or Viola Davis or Halle Berry receive [Oscars], and listened even to the speeches now, [from Emmy winners] Niecy Nash-Betts and Sheryl Lee Ralph. They push you to continue to work hard.”

Though her 2023 role in “The Color Purple” cemented the Grammy winner’s status as a performer who has at the very least been nominated for each letter of EGOT, the real reward the recognition among her peers has brought is the opportunity to executive produce and star in projects like the Walter Thompson-Hernandez film “If I Go Will They Miss Me,” which premiered at Sundance 2026 to rave reviews. “Yes, I have the desire to be receiving awards one day,” said Brooks, “but at the end of the day, I get to do that with my work. I get to do that with stories like ‘If I Go,’ where my goal is for people to feel seen.” Related Stories How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

The coming-of-age drama set in Watts, California sees the actress play a mother named Lozita doing her best to hold her family together while there’s inscrutable tension between her partner, recently released from prison, and their imaginative 12-year-old son. “I started out in theater, so to me, it’s never been about a paycheck,” joked Brooks. “It’s always been about the story and what you’re putting out into the world. And so, when I watched [Thompson-Hernandez’s] short, I was like, ‘Yo, this is different. I ain’t never seen nothing like this.’ And it was captivating just the way he was shooting it.”

Expanding on what drew her to the project, which came to her during her time bouncing between Los Angeles awards press for “The Color Purple,” and the New Zealand set of “A Minecraft Movie,” Brooks said “They handed me the script and it was really the conversation, sitting down with Walter, his passion for his community, hearing about the real Lozita who had unfortunately passed away from cancer two years prior, hearing about the Compton Cowboys, just getting to talk to him about relationships between kids and their parents and the complications that it can bring.”

She said, “I like the balance. I got to have a little comedy, but I got to do some drama and it does my heart well.” While “Minecraft” brought her “laughs all day with Jack Black and Jason Momoa,” “If I Go” brought Brooks “purpose.” “I’m excited that we get to share stories like this where people are really dealing with their personal issues and healing and all of that stuff,” she said.

Having screened the film in Los Angeles the night before, Brooks said “You can feel the energy of everyone feeling super represented and feeling a sense of ownership. It’s cool hearing the audience be like, ‘Yeah, yeah,’ When you talk about the planes passing by, or the story about the fuel engines falling on elementary schools. People remember and know that to be a part of what has happened in LA, and the fabric of LA.”

One job that was foundational to how she approaches projects like “If I Go” happens to be Brooks’ breakout role as Taystee on “Orange Is the New Black.” Coming out of the prestigious Julliard School, her mind was more so on “how am I going to make my money for the subway and pay for my college tuition and how am I going to pay for this PB&J sandwich?,” when she booked the role on the series for the then-nascent streaming service Netflix. “I didn’t know what I was stepping into at the time. ‘Orange’ was looked at as a webseries, so nobody knew what this was about to be. But once we got into the work, I was like, ‘Oh, this is deeper than that.’ I remember talking to people who’ve been incarcerated, and I remember even doing a clothing drive for women who have just come out of prison so that they could have clothes for job interviews and stuff like that. We were really invested in the community and giving back,” said Brooks.

“We had that as a group, as storytellers, but then individually, I was watching my co-stars have a point of view, have something to say. And so, I [was] just learning that being an artist is also a form of activism,” she said. “That was one of the beginning seeds planted in my head once I was in the industry, because I’ve always known that what we do is about service, that’s number one. But I hadn’t experienced that on this level.”

Since then, Brooks’ goal has been to tell at least one story a year that incorporates a bit of activism, and with “If I Go,” the actress and producer has been more active than ever. “I’ve deemed us the little engine that could, because I really believe that we can take this far. My goal is that we just get as many eyeballs on it as we can. But the truth of the matter is nothing moves like money does. And that’s what I’ve learned is you’ve got to get really creative and strategic about how you can push a movie into the face of the people when you don’t have the money.”

“If I Go Will They Miss Me,” distributed by Rich Spirit, has truly been an indie success story, making over $1 million at the box office from the humblest of beginnings. As Brooks noted, that haul has been hard fought, with her, Thompson-Hernandez, and her co-star J. Alphonse Nicholson touring as much of the country as they can to screen the film, and even abroad. “I’m going to Africa this week, I got invited, but then I learned there’s a film festival in Africa. So, I’m like, ‘Can we take the film to Africa?’ And they said, ‘Yes.’ So now, the film’s going to be in the festival there,” said the actress.

She continued, “It’s even in the form of fashion. People pay attention to what you’re wearing and then they’re like, ‘Why you got that on? Oh! She had a premiere.’ Boom. It’s insane how many tricks I have been working to get people to pay attention to this film that is worth paying attention to.”

One of the more beautiful aspects of this “If I Go” experience has been the way in which her community has shown up for her and the film. Snoop Dogg and Ava DuVernay have Instagrammed about it, while Helen Hunt and André Holland have even hosted talk backs for the film. But in terms of creativity, one marketing strategy takes the cake. “Issa Rae, even at her restaurant, she did a menu dedicated to ‘If I Go’ where it was a discount, 15 percent off or something if you bought a ticket,” she said. “People understand the importance of this,” said Brooks. “If the film wasn’t good, I wouldn’t be doing all this.”

On the awards front, the challenge is still getting the film in front of the steak eaters who still make up a good chunk of the awards body, and maybe do not immediately think they identify with the material. “The Academy is working really hard to change that narrative by who is allowed to vote. The voting party is shifting, but that’s what I’m experiencing right now,” said Brooks.

But regular filmgoers have a role in getting smaller, truly independent films awards recognition too. “The general audience plays a huge part because the culture tells the voters where to look, what is important,” said the actress. “The people, we have a voice in this too. I think we make it very clear what we want to see, but it’s a weird cycle.” Studio films have a budget for billboards, commercials, advertisements, and more. “When you are a small independent film, you have to be that big machine on your own to get it out there. And that’s a lot of work, and that’s a lot of time, and that’s a lot of smarts,” said Brooks. “You’ve got to have a lot of faith and hope too. You’ve just got to believe that what you’ve created is strong. And I do know that we all do, myself, J. Alphonse, Walter, MACRO, Rich Spirit, we believe in this film wholeheartedly.”

“Movies like these are worth telling, and I think they do reach who they need to reach, and they do lock in with the world on a larger scale when they’re supposed to,” said Brooks, reflecting on the fruitful journey “If I Go” has already had so far. “This is the thing I’m most proud of in my whole career because just the fact that people are having conversations, hard conversations with their loved ones, and they’re finding ways to heal.”

“If I Go Will They Miss Me” is now available to rent on all platforms.

#3383. Alaska Woman Killed After Walking Into Spinning Plane Propeller at Airport

A horrific scene unfolded at an Alaska airport just 2 days before Thanksgiving ... a woman was killed after walking straight into a plane's spinning propeller.

According to Alaska State Troopers, Christina Blake was driving on a taxiway at Big Lake Airport Tuesday afternoon when a small plane landed. The pilot stopped to give Blake room to move her car ... but instead, she got out, approached the aircraft and walked directly into its spinning propeller.

Police, firefighters and paramedics rushed to the airport shortly before 5 PM ... but Blake was pronounced dead at the scene. The pilot was uninjured.

Here's where things get particularly puzzling ... authorities say Blake had no apparent connection to the pilot, the plane or the airport, and investigators don't believe she intentionally walked into the propeller.
