Upgrading your TV's sound doesn't necessarily mean spending a fortune on a full home theater setup, especially with early Black Friday deals bringing substantial discounts on soundbars and audio systems from Sony, Bose, Samsung, and LG. Sony has some of the biggest price cuts, with savings of up to 32% across select Bravia Theater models, including more than $700 off its premium Theater Trio system.

Samsung's Dolby Atmos soundbars are also discounted by as much as $400, while Bose and LG have more affordable options for anyone looking to improve dialogue clarity, add some bass, or enjoy surround sound without a complicated setup. Whether you're shopping for a compact speaker for a bedroom TV or a more immersive system for movie nights, here are the deals worth considering.

For anyone building a premium home theater around a large TV, the Sony Bravia Theater Trio is down to $1,498 from $2,199.99, saving you $701.99, or roughly 32%. Unlike a conventional soundbar, the Trio uses three separate front speakers for the left, center, and right channels, helping spread dialogue and effects across a wider soundstage. You can read PCMag’s “excellent” review for more details.

The Sony Bravia Theater Bar 7 is down to $718 from $869 for anyone who wants a single soundbar under the TV. Its nine speakers include upward- and side-firing drivers that widen the soundstage and give Dolby Atmos some height, but there’s no subwoofer, so the now $898 Bar 7 with a wireless sub bundle (down from $1,099.99) might be the better pick for deeper bass.

Moving down Sony's lineup, the Bravia Theater Bar 6 is $548, down from $699.99, and pairs a 3.1.2-channel soundbar with a wireless subwoofer and upward-firing speakers for Dolby Atmos height effects. Spending $100 more gets you the Bravia Theater System 6, now $648 from $799.99, which adds rear speakers in a 5.1-channel setup for movies and games where sound moves behind you.

For a more affordable upgrade, the Sony Bravia Theater Bar 5 is down to $278 from $349.99, saving you nearly $72. It's a 3.1-channel system with a dedicated center speaker and wireless subwoofer, so dialogue should come through more clearly while music and movie effects get some additional low-end presence.

Sony’s older systems are discounted too, including the HT-S400 at $258, down from $299, which pairs a 2.1-channel soundbar and wireless subwoofer with S-Force Pro Front Surround to widen the sound for everyday TV, sports, and casual movies. The HT-S40R is arguably the better deal at the same $258, down from $329.99, since it adds two rear speakers for a full 5.1-channel setup, though neither model supports Dolby Atmos.

For smaller rooms or for anyone who mainly wants dialogue to come across more clearly, Bose has two compact soundbars on sale: The newer Bose TV Speaker (2nd Gen) is down to $239 from $299, with an updated acoustic design that Bose says improves clarity and overall sound performance. Meanwhile, the original Bose TV Speaker is $199, down from $279, and offers a similarly compact design with a dedicated dialogue mode and adjustable bass.

Samsung’s HW-Q800H is down to $697.99 from $1,097.99, a $400 cut on a 5.1.2-channel Dolby Atmos soundbar with a wireless subwoofer. Its side- and upward-firing speakers help place effects around and above you, while a dedicated center channel keeps dialogue clear during busy action scenes.

For something that takes up less space, the Samsung HW-S60D is $277.99, down from $399.99, and fits seven speakers, including side-firing drivers, into a compact 5.0-channel soundbar. It also supports Dolby Atmos, Adaptive Sound, and a voice enhancement mode, along with Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, AirPlay, and Chromecast for music streaming. That said, it has no upward-firing speakers or subwoofer, so its height effects and bass won’t match that of the Q800H.

If you're looking for a complete surround sound system without spending several hundred dollars, the LG S6FTR is down to $249.99 from $399.99, saving you $150, or roughly 38%. It's a 5.1-channel home theater package with a soundbar, subwoofer, and dedicated rear speakers. That makes it particularly appealing for action movies and games, where directional sound adds to the experience.

The LG S40TR is another affordable option for anyone who wants rear speakers included in the box. It's currently $199.99, down from $279.99, and offers a 4.1-channel arrangement with a wireless subwoofer and two rear speakers. This should give movie soundtracks a greater sense of direction than a basic soundbar, while the subwoofer handles the lower frequencies that smaller TV speakers often struggle to reproduce.

At just under $187, the S60T is the least expensive system in this roundup, pairing a 3.1-channel soundbar with a wireless subwoofer for clearer dialogue and fuller sound than your TV’s speakers. That said, it lacks rear speakers and Dolby Atmos height channels, so it’s better suited to someone who wants a simple, affordable upgrade without filling the room with additional hardware.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

#3379. ‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Finale Hinges on Two Monologues — Let Ethan Hawke and Sterlin Harjo Break Them Down

[Editor’s Note: The following review contains spoilers for “The Lowdown” Season 2 Episode 8, “The Tower” — including the finale’s ending.]

“I saw the structure of the episode as these kind of waves that crash upon Lee,” Ethan Hawke said in an interview about “The Lowdown‘s” Season 2 finale. “The way life works, it’s not like, ‘Oh, this one thing happens and then you change.’ It’s usually a series of things that happen, and the walls of your defenses come down.”

Lee’s walls were certainly up when “The Lowdown” Season 2 began. Untethered by the acclaim for his Season 1 exposé on Dale Washberg (Tim Blake Nelson), Lee reacts with vehement defensiveness. He mocks the journalists who named him Tulsa’s Journalist of the Year during his acceptance speech. He alienates his friends and embarrasses his daughter. Related Stories Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’ Will Ferrell Golf Comedy ‘The Hawk’ Canceled at Netflix After Just One Season

He’s a mess, and when Ginger (Betty Gilpin) walks into his life with a tantalizing new story, he’s lucky — not because she’s the woman of his dreams carrying his drug of choice (a “truthstorian’s” next crusade), but because grounding forces are on the way in the form of his estranged father, Lee Raybon Sr. (Tommy Lee Jones), as well as a few clear-eyed, full-throated friends. Over the course of a riveting, revelatory Season 2, they all help to bring Lee back to himself, one wave at a time.

The finale’s first swell comes as quite a surprise — two surprises, really. When Lee pulls up to the funeral home, prepared to pay a terse goodbye to his departed dad, so, too, does his former business partner and best friend, Wendell (played by Peter Dinklage). Wendell tells Lee he’ll “always be grateful” for Senior’s guidance when they were younger, and it’s immediately clear he’s not about to take the man’s final tribute as lightly as his son may have hoped.

“When Tommy’s character dies and there’s a funeral, we’re all like, ‘Well, wouldn’t Wendell be there?’ I mean, they’re really great friends,'” Hawke said. “I called Peter up and I was like, ‘Is there any way you’d come down for one day to be just at this funeral?’ And Peter was shooting in London and flew in and flew right back. He came in and made it happen for us.”

But Dinklage’s return was no mere cameo. Creator Sterlin Harjo knew better than to let the opportunity go to waste.

“I think there was a Shakespeare monologue in it first, and it was beautiful,” Harjo said. “Then Peter suggested the Dylan Thomas. […] I can’t imagine a more exciting way to have Peter be in your show than doing this Dylan Thomas poem that’s a gentle poem, but he does it with this rage — how it’s supposed to be read. It’s amazing.”

Volunteering to speak when Ray (Michael Hitchcock) gets overwhelmed, Wendell spends a few seconds scrolling to find the right poem (“Do not go gentle into that good night”) and then tears into it with vigor. Dinklage’s recitation is more of a resuscitation — powerful enough to wake the dead, it wakes Lee up, snapping him into the present and bringing him back to life.

“When he’s doing the poem, he came in at a 10,” Harjo said. “The only direction I gave him was, ‘What if you build to that?’ And that’s what he did, and it was just unbelievably great.”

“That one is violent and abrupt,” Hawke said. “It’s a friend shaking you up.”

In Hawke’s case, Lee’s friend was his real friend. He knew Dinklage “loved poetry,” and he even knew a little bit about what his fellow actor would bring to this poem.

“This is where collaboration is really mysterious about how it works and when it works really well,” Hawke said. “I’ve been friends with Peter Dinklage since, I don’t know, 1990. […] We both arrived in New York around the same time, and we used to sit around and tie one on and try to flirt with girls and read poems. We used to geek out about how much we loved the ways people would read poems in the old days. If you hear Dylan Thomas read a poem or you hear Orson Wells read a poem, they weren’t afraid of feeling or emotion or a theatricality. They weren’t afraid of passion — actual passion — and caring and looking foolish.”

“We’re living in an age of irony and cynicism and detachment, and this definition of cool being that you don’t care. Whereas the definition when I was growing up was Bob Marley and John Lennon and Miles Davis and those guys cared a tremendous amount. They weren’t detached. They were completely attached. So for me to watch Peter bring that to his performance was like, ‘Let me show you kids how to do a poem!’ [laughs] ‘You got to do it like your life depends on it.'”

“The key to that scene is the interaction between him and Lee,” Harjo said. “I love that he’s watching Lee the whole time. It’s like there’s no one else in the room and he’s doing it for Lee. I love that.”

“The camera does pick up subconscious,” Hawke said. “A lot of times I’ll see work that might be good, but it has no subconscious to it. I can tell there’s no secret sewn into the filmmaking. And Sterlin loves — you can call it poetry, you can call it whatever you want — but [he loves] when there’s multiple layers happening. […] And so for me, I’m not just sitting there with an actor doing this scene. I’ve known this guy for 30 years and I know what this poem means to him, and he knows me.”

“If there was an Academy Award for Best Single Scene, I would give it to Peter Dinklage in our show.”

While Dinklage may have to settle for an Emmy, Harjo had to write the other big finale monologue for an actual Oscar winner. At the reception, Lee’s daughter Francis (Ryan Kiera Armstrong) reads a passage from her grandfather’s journal, written shortly after Lee Jr. was born, as a way to honor her ancestor. Then, as Francis speaks Senior’s words, Senior appears seated behind her, and Tommy Lee Jones takes over the scene.

“The bigger thing about that monologue is I knew it was coming,” Harjo said. “I was like, ‘Oh shit, I got to write this thing for Tommy Lee Jones.’ I kind of had Tommy Lee Jones dialed in through the whole season. I felt like I could really write his voice. But when it came to that monologue, I’m like, ‘God, he’s already known for one of the best monologues in the world at the end of ‘No Country for Old Men,’ and I can either try to do a fancy monologue that isn’t like that at all, or I could lean into the fact that Cormac McCarthy and the Coen brothers did this really well already, and there’s no way that I don’t know that as a filmmaker. So I’m going to lean into it and almost give homage to that speech.'”

“Not to toot my own horn, but I feel like I nailed it,” he said, laughing. “Of course, it filters through Tommy Lee Jones and all of a sudden it’s like this fucking amazing thing that he does. It was wonderful being on set. Just watching him give that, it was unbelievable. I could have used any take and it would’ve been amazing in a different way.”

Throughout the monologue, Lee sits in thoughtful silence. He’s not only absorbing what his father wrote and remembering who he was; he’s also recognizing his shifting role as a son who’s now a father. There’s a connection across generations. Yes, his responsibility to his daughter means avoiding repeating his dad’s mistakes, which Lee is well-aware of, but it also means honoring his father’s better intentions, like the ones he voiced in that journal and Francis is voicing again now.

“Lee’s adamant that he’s nothing like his father,” Hawke said. “The first thought I had is, ‘All right, this is why Lee Raybon is obsessed with the truth: It’s that his father was a chronic liar.’ If you grew up in a house where your parent was really comfortable lying to you, you would get obsessed with people in power misleading you, and that would really drive you.”

“But then as we played the scenes deeper, I realized that Lee was lying to himself; that he was just as manipulative as his father is. He just does it in the name of truth. All this bad behavior that he was in denial of, he’d actually internalized it, and he was so much like his dad that he was completely blind to it, which is behavior I’ve seen in so many friends. It’s amazing. But I had to live through it. I didn’t get it when I was reading it. I got it when I was playing it, and that was very powerful for me.”

One way Harjo & co. illustrate Lee’s development over the course of Season 2 is simple: He listens. Instead of shouting, pontificating, or generally causing chaos, Lee spends much of the finale hearing what everyone around him has to say. Even when he’s up his own ass or annoying the hell out of folks, he has a community who cares about him, and their steady presence in his life is what eventually breaks down his defenses.

“The first [wave] is Peter reading that poem, and then the second one is gentle and persuasive where my daughter is revealing to me that my father did love me,” Hawke said. “Part of the thing you learn watching this show is that Lee feels like he has to conquer the world to be worthy of self-respect. His daughter is saying, ‘It’s right here for you, and it always has been.'”

While another monologue played a significant role in how the episode plays out — Ginger’s speech to Francis, outside the bookstore — that moment wasn’t about Lee. (“The whole idea was Ginger and Francis don’t really get to hang out, but they are alike,” Harjo said. “Ginger immediately recognizes it and probably also knows that she had a father that was a lot like Lee.”) So his final wave comes from a curious source.

“The third one is just this final little moment that happens with Vickey (Abbie Cobb) when she tells him his fortune is bad and he sees it as a good thing. He understands that everything is point of view, and for him, towers coming down would be good.”

“Those are the three steps that I think are designed to get Lee back on his feet again,” Hawke said. “That push him to be like, ‘All right, you know what? I’m not quitting. I’m going to keep being me, and I’m going to be a better version of me.'”

How he’s feeling when Season 3 starts is anyone’s guess, and that assumes a renewal that’s yet to be announced is still in the offing from FX. But one thing’s for sure: If Lee comes back, he’ll be a changed man — and he won’t be alone.

“The Lowdown” is available on FX and Hulu.

#3378. 7 Masterpiece Christmas Books Better Than ‘A Christmas Carol’

Beatriz (Bea) Valero de Urquia is a Books & Literature author at Collider, where she focuses on Lists surrounding recent bestsellers, classical novels, and everything in between. She is a historian by training and a bilingual reader, moving between English and Spanish literature.   Beatriz began her career as a technology writer at a startup in the UK. Almost a decade later, journalism has taken her to five cities across three continents and into business reporting, cultural criticism, and live TV commentary. She joined Collider in 2026.  Beatriz has a passion for travelling and loves keeping an eye on the books headed to the screen. One of her favorite pastimes is critiquing the historical accuracy of period movies. She also once volunteered for the Charles Dickens Museum. Beatriz also has a core belief that a book is always better than the movie, but she has been happy to have been proven wrong in a couple of occasions.

When she isn’t reading, Beatriz is watching musicals, stage managing Shakespeare plays with a local theater group or doing historical research. She enjoys tracing family trees for her history and genealogy TikTok, creating databases for historical analysis and sifting through 17th-century stories for the novel she is currently in the process of writing.

Every Christmas, we turn to the same stories. The same movies the grandparents like, and the song that plays every single Christmas Eve so that everyone in the family can sing along. It is comforting to have stories to return to. Many of the traditions we return to were actually cemented by none other than Charles Dickens. A Christmas Carol is the most popular, having been adapted hundreds of times. Dickens cemented Christmas as we know it today, but that doesn't mean there aren't other Christmas stories worth knowing.

A Christmas story can be a Christmas story for many reasons. The setting, for instance, sets the mood, but the values are what stay. During this time of year, it is normal to gravitate toward stories with deeper meaning that reflect on what one is grateful for. Some books have achieved this with incredible mastery. Here are the best.

"'Christmas won't be Christmas without any presents,' grumbled Jo, lying on the rug." Louisa May Alcott's Little Women might not be everyone's go-to Christmas story, but it should be. The word "Christmas" appears twice in the first sentence of the book and, within the first couple chapters, the March sisters have already given away their Christmas breakfast to a hungry family. It is something out of a Dickens story.

The original Little Women volume, not including its continuations, takes place over a year, bookended by two very different Christmases. During this time, Alcott subtly shows the importance of maintaining the values we so cherish during the festive season year-round. Marmee often encourages her daughters to be selfless, humble, studious, and caring. By the end of this volume, Beth is recovering from scarlet fever and the sisters receive the best present they could have wished for: their father's return. The book is perfect for the holiday season.

Claire Keegan's novella Small Things like These is quietly heartbreaking. Set in Ireland in 1985, it follows Bill Furlong, a coal and fuel merchant. The week before Christmas, he goes about his routine while thinking about what presents to get his wife and daughters. One day, he visits a local convent and is surprised to find a young woman named Sarah locked in a nearby shed and asking about a baby. He frees her and leaves her with the Mother Superior, who says she was playing a game. The girl reminds Bill of his mother, who was an unmarried teenager when she got pregnant with him. Over the following days, Bill cannot shake the suspicion that something terrible is going on in the convent.

This story shows that Christmas stories do not need to be wrapped in a pretty bow. It is also possible to read something themed to the season that deals with ethical questions. In the case of Small Things like These, Keegan discusses the difficult topic of Ireland's Magdalene laundries, where young women were imprisoned and forced to do labor. The subject is treated with the dignity and care it deserves, showing how a single person can choose to do what is right in the face of larger injustices, even when the cost is high.

Hogfather is missing. The Auditors of Reality, a group of celestial bureaucrats, have hired the assassin Mr. Teatime to murder Discworld’s Santa Claus equivalent, who gives children presents on the night of Hogswatch, on December 32nd. Without children's belief in Hogfather, the sun won't rise. The only one who understands the importance of Hogfather's role is Death, and so he must step in. Aided by Albert, his reluctant pixie servant, Death puts on a red suit and starts delivering presents. His granddaughter, Susan, is tasked with traveling to the Tooth Fairy's realm to bring Hogfather back.

As funny and magical as all of Terry Pratchett's stories, Hogfather is a wonderful seasonal read. In addition to an incredible display of whimsy, the book includes one of the most thoughtful discussions of the importance of faith and why we go to such great lengths to keep the magic of the holidays alive. "Humans need fantasy to be human," Death tells Susan. "To be the place where the falling angel meets the rising ape."

After Dickens, Russian composer Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky has a monopoly on Christmas. However, not many people know that the Nutcracker ballet, often performed during the holiday season, is based on Alexandre Dumas' story, which is itself an adaptation of an older (and much darker) short story: The Nutcracker and the Mouse King by E. T. A. Hoffmann.

One Christmas Eve (of course), Marie notices a nutcracker under the tree. That evening, while playing with the nutcracker, she sees mice start to come out from beneath the floor. Their leader seems to be a seven-headed Mouse King, taller than all the others. Suddenly, all of Marie's toys come to life and, led by the nutcracker, begin to fight the mouse army. They are at a disadvantage, so Marie throws her slipper at the Mouse King to stop him from capturing the nutcracker. The morning after, Marie wakes up with a bandaged arm and no idea if the events she witnessed were real. The only person who believes her is her godfather, who then tells her the tragic story of Princess Pirlipat and Madam Mouserinks, the Queen of the Mice, which explains the origins of nutcrackers.

Yes, this story was written by the same author who wrote both Breakfast at Tiffany's and In Cold Blood. And yes, it is a perfect Christmas classic. Truman Capote's "A Christmas Memory" is set in rural Alabama in the 1930s. It was inspired by Capote's own life and his experience of the holiday season in a family with financial difficulties. The short story is beautiful, warm, funny, and deep. It will also absolutely break your heart.

“It's fruitcake weather!” Buddy's elderly cousin announces, declaring the start of winter. The relationship between the seven-year-old boy and his cousin is the heart of Capote's story. They are two childlike, wide-eyed people in a stern and strict family. During the story, they gather the ingredients to make fruitcakes and share them with friends. Years later, Buddy looks back at the simple magic of those shared Christmases. The prose is as beautiful as the story, and it is worth reading, if only for the last few lines. The cousin character is said to have been inspired by Sook, a relative the author lived with as a boy, who may have had intellectual disabilities. Capote called her "a genius."

The plot of this story is as simple as most people's holiday celebrations. Dubliner Gabriel Conroy is a teacher and part-time book reviewer. One winter evening, he attends a party with his wife, Gretta, hosted by family members. There is music, pudding, a goose, and tipsy guests. While greeting friends and old acquaintances, Gabriel thinks of the speech he has to give. At the end of the evening, a guest sings a sorrowful song. Gretta is moved by the song, and later confesses it reminds her of a young man she once loved who has passed away. Gabriel could be anyone. What makes him stand out is the beautifully crafted way he thinks about life and death.

"The Dead" closes James Joyce's Dubliners. At almost 16,000 words, it can also be a short novella. Whatever its definition, the story is timeless and deeply moving. It discusses local topics related to Irishness, while reflecting on universal themes such as love and loss. The ending, "His soul swooned slowly as he heard the snow falling faintly through the universe and faintly falling, like the descent of their last end, upon all the living and the dead," might be one of the most beautiful and poignant lines in the history of literature.

What is a 14th-century Middle English chivalric romance doing in a list of Christmas books? Well, it is a great story, and it is set at Christmastime, so it meets every requirement to be here. A warning: it is written in alliterative verse, so it might be denser than other picks, although J. R. R. Tolkien himself has an accessible translation. Still, it is absolutely worth the effort. And what better way to end the year's reading challenge than with a classic?

Sir Gawain and the Green Knight takes place in King Arthur's court during the celebrations between Christmas and New Year. Suddenly, a giant green knight interrupts the feast. He offers his axe to any man who dares to strike him. However, in return, that person will agree to take a blow in a year and a day. Sir Gawain, one of King Arthur's knights, accepts and beheads him. A year later, on the way to that appointment, Gawain is taken in by a generous lord and his wife. What follows is a game of temptation and a test of honor that Gawain must pass.

Luckily, the Series 11 is one of them, at least for many of them. Some other upgrades in the new OS include a dedicated Siri app, a new app grid, a new single-tap gesture, among other features. The Garmin vivoactive 5 was $299.99 when it first came out in 2023 as their midrange lifestyle-focused fitness smartwatch. It features a 1.2-inch AMOLED touchscreen and an 11-day battery life (four to five days with the always-on display setting). You can get it for $169.99 right now. It's a great option for anyone looking to get into Garmin for the first time or upgrading from anything below it.

Bone conduction headphones are ideal for activities where it is vital to be able to hear your surroundings. They use a technology that sends audio vibrations to your inner ear while leaving your ear canals open. Shokz is one of, if not the best, brands making bone conduction headphones right now. At the high end of Shokz's offerings sit the OpenRun Pro 2, which impressed me when I tested them out for review. Walmart currently has a restored pair for $93 (originally $179.99 new).

The latest AirPods Pro are a big step up. The third iteration of Apple's iconic earbuds comes with a number of quality-of-life and software improvements that make them worth the typical premium over the AirPods Pro 2—and right now, the AirPods Pro 3 are even cheaper than the previous generation. They're $149 on Walmart as an Black Friday deal, down from $249 and matching their lowest price ever.

Most, if not all, TV speakers aren't great. While you have plenty of options, the quickest and least expensive way to improve your TV's audio capabilities is to buy a soundbar. Compare a soundbar's size to the thin, small speakers jammed into modern TVs. The Vizio 5.1 Pro Soundbar with a subwoofer and rear speakers supports Dolby Atmos and costs just $99 (originally $198). They won't win any audio awards, but it's better than any built-in TV speakers, and for $99, it'll improve your experience without breaking the bank.

If you want to take things up a notch, consider this 5.1 channel sound system. While it's a 5.1 system as well, it reaches a 312W peak power, which will make explosions and thuds feel more realistic. There's also a dedicated dialogue feature for people who don't like using subtitles. For $149.99 (originally $249.99), you can get the ULTIMEA 5.1 surround sound system.

I love projectors and Roku. To me, a Roku projector just makes sense, especially at $119.99 (originally $389.99). This projector is portable and has the Roku OS already installed, so it's easy to project it against a wall, ceiling, or screen, whether it's indoors or outdoors. It's easy to set up; you just need an outlet nearby and to dim or turn off the lights. If you have Bluetooth speakers, you can hook them up to create a more immersive sound.

The TCL Q51GB is a QLED Google TV that is a great value for anyone looking for size, color, and features. The 98-inch class is heavily discounted at its $898 price (originally $1,499.99). TCL makes one of the best QLEDs for the money, and their technology keeps getting better. This TV supports Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos, and if you're a gamer, you get a refresh rate of 240Hz that is automatically triggered with its Auto Game Mode feature.

If you've been holding off on buying a Nintendo Switch 2 until it went on sale and better games were available, now might be the time to pull the trigger. Right now, Walmart is offering the Mario World bundle for $499 (originally $549). The timing of this deal is even more noteworthy, given that Nintendo recently released the Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

Gaming monitors can get pricey fast. At $159.99 (originally $299.99 at launch), this 27-inch Samsung Odyssey G55C curved gaming monitor offers a 1440p resolution, a 1000R curve, a 165Hz refresh rate with FreeSync and G-SYNC compatibility to keep screen tearing to a minimum, and features like Samsung’s Virtual Aim Point and Contrast Enhancer. It's a solid choice for gaming, especially at this price point.

Alienware makes great gaming laptops, and the Aurora is a great option for anyone who wants to get all the essentials without spending too much. At its current $1,099 price (originally $1,999), the Alienware Aurora 16 becomes a mid-tier gaming laptop at a "budget" price. We reviewed the higher-tier Aurora 16X and were impressed with it. The Aurora 16 has a slightly slower processor, a dimmer display with half the refresh rate, a smaller battery, and a weaker graphics card, but given its price, it's great for a gamer looking for a solid gaming laptop in the $1,000 range.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

Amazon has a much larger inventory of tech products on sale, but the ones they both sell are mostly priced the same. While Amazon may have more deals, Walmart usually has a couple of surprise flagship tech products on sale that Amazon will later price match. So taking all of that into consideration, the best one will be whichever has whatever you're looking to buy at the lower price.

Yes. I own these headphones and can vouch they are worth every penny. The headphones are high quality and bring a hybrid style of open earbuds and bone conduction that I haven't seen in other headphones.

No. Walmart+ members did get early access to the sale, though. For future reference, you can sign up for a free 30-day Walmart+ subscription and cancel it afterwards, or get the annual plan for $98 ($8.17/month).

#3375. Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It

[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published on April 24, 2026, when “I Swear” was released in American theaters. Aramayo recently won Best Actor in a Film at the BAFTA Scotland Awards. The film and his performance are eligible for this year’s Oscars, and “I Swear” is now streaming on Netflix.]

When Robert Aramayo signed on to play Scottish Tourette’s activist John Davidson in filmmaker Kirk Jones’ biopic “I Swear,” he could scarcely imagine where the film would take him.

A hit in the UK, the film netted Aramayo a pair of BAFTA wins earlier in the year, as the British actor won both the vaunted Rising Star Award (previous winners include James McAvoy, John Boyega, Tom Holland, Tom Hardy, and those are just some of its biggest names) and the Best Actor trophy (beating out Timothée Chalamet, Leonardo DiCaprio, Ethan Hawke, Jesse Plemons, and eventual Oscar winner Michael B. Jordan). Related Stories ‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Finale Hinges on Two Monologues — Let Ethan Hawke and Sterlin Harjo Break Them Down Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’

But that’s hardly all that happened at the February awards show, which was instantly and forever marred by a number of loud, racist outbursts from Davidson himself that were directed at “Sinners” stars Jordan, Delroy Lindo, Wunmi Mosaku, and more. The fallout from the incident was both swift and prolonged, and will likely impact the domestic release of “I Swear,” which is rolling out in stateside theaters now.

Aramayo’s performance in the film is indeed star-making and awards-worthy, as he brings sensitivity and great courage to his portrayal of Davidson, following him from his earliest symptoms through his current passionate activism. Hopefully, viewers can see and appreciate the work on its own merits, and get to know Aramayo much better, though he has previously appeared in plenty of projects recognizable to American audiences, from “The Empty Man” to “The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power” to a little thing called “Game of Thrones” (young Ned Stark!).

Ahead, Aramayo tells IndieWire about his deep research for the role, everything BAFTAs, and what he hopes will come from more people seeing the film and, hopefully, understanding Tourette’s all the better.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: When I saw the film at TIFF in September, I did my due diligence before I reviewed it, and learned that John is a huge figure in the UK, but relatively unknown in America. How much did you know about him before this film?

Robert Aramayo: John’s made a lot of documentaries, but the big one that probably had the most impact was “John’s Not Mad,” and that was in 1989. So if you speak to people who were around then, they have a lot of very personal stories about watching that documentary and being like, “Wow, is this Tourette’s? What’s Tourette’s?”

So when you get the script, are you someone who then wants to do more research into him, or do you feel like the script is the thing?

The production team and Kirk were so gracious, and they gave me so much time. I think they were like, “Oh, yeah, take a couple of months or something to research and stuff.” I was really thankful for that. The first thing that I did was to meet John; I met him very quickly. And then I went away for a month, and I spent that time gaining as much knowledge as I could about Tourette’s and what it is. That was through watching the documentaries, watching YouTube videos, and reading books.

I based myself in Galashiels and spent weeks with John, just following him around and spending as much time with him as I could. And also traveling through Scotland, meeting people, mainly through [support organization] Tourette Scotland, who lived with Tourette’s as well. I wanted to have, I don’t know, a more expansive view of Tourette’s than just John. Obviously, John was my main focus, though.

When you’re getting ready to meet John, what were you expecting and anticipating? What were you nervous about?

I don’t know what I felt, really. I was so filled with anxiety about, oh my word, am I going to do this? I wanted John to like me. I was already feeling, God, this is going to be a really big challenge. And I met him within days of saying yes.

But then, when I met him, one thing that struck me straight away was his knowledge. He’s got a really amazing knowledge about, obviously, Tourette’s, but also a lot of neurodiversity and how it lives, other conditions that exist with Tourette’s, and stuff like that. He’s got a lot of thoughts about how we can do better and help young people and things like that. He’s very forthcoming with it.

He’s got so much heart. He’s such an amazing, welcoming, supportive man that I was just like, wow, this is a really impressive person that I’m meeting here. Of course, then your anxiety and the responsibility meter have gone through the roof.

Just watching the film, I learned so much about what Tourette’s can entail and the very wide spectrum of symptoms that people can have. What was the most unexpected thing you learned about it during your research?

A couple of things really that had a really big impact on me straight away, and that sort of broke my perception of what I thought Tourette’s was, that anything can be a tic, and that it’s so singular to the person. So if you’ve met one person with Tourette’s, someone said to me, you’ve met one person with Tourette’s. That was a big thing.

And also the fact that there’s a lot of tics that you just don’t see. There’s tics that you don’t see as tics because anything can be a tic, or there’s tics that exist only in somebody’s mind, and things like that, tics linked with OCD. Just the complexity of it was massive.

I learned some statistics recently, which I found really interesting: One in 50 kids in America live with persistent tic disorder, and one in 160 live with Tourette’s, so it’s unbelievably common, it’s everywhere. We have met people with Tourette’s, we meet them all the time. It was part of the experience of the film as well, we met loads of people who were living with Tourette’s undiagnosed. 50 percent of people who live with Tourette’s in the U.S. are undiagnosed, and that was true for us in the UK as well in our experience. Maybe the thing is that we don’t know that that’s what’s happening. That made me think, wow, there’s a real educational piece to this as well.

You are playing someone who is a real person who has been captured on film for many years. People know what he looks like, they know what he sounds like. How do you find the line between impersonation and impression in your performance?

I never wanted to impersonate John. I think I would’ve gone the wrong way if that was what I was thinking. You have to, at a certain point, take ownership of the character and try and make him your own. I was lucky because there was so much that I needed to learn, so for so long, I wasn’t thinking about performance or playing him at all. I was just trying to immerse myself as much as I could in everything, anything that I could get my hands on. Then, at certain point, I moved to thinking about how I was going to try and play my version of John.

In a [narrative] film, you get the opportunity to maybe show a little bit more [than a documentary]. A documentary film crew comes into somebody’s life and they can capture what they can capture, but we could capture way more intimate moments throughout the whole film that John had spoken to.

We could show the moments where he is on his own, whether there’s been an impact or how he’s feeling or his emotional life, how things change over time and stuff like that, and hopefully try and do it with truth and authenticity.

You attended Juilliard, which always seems a little, “Oooohhh, he’s Juilliard-trained.”

But now that you’re a few years out of school, what are the pieces of training that are proving to be most useful to you?

I think that acting teachers and drama school is vocabulary, really. At the time, certain things that teachers would say to me had a massive impact on me and really opened me up to other ways of looking at things, and other things are only impacting me now, as I keep working and as I get older. I think that’s the beauty of drama school, you get flooded with all of this stuff, and then you’re going, “Oh, that’s what they were talking about.” And then there’s things that my teachers would consistently say, “You’ve got to work on this, you’ve got to work on this,” and I’m still working on it. It’s like a toolbox, and every now and again you go, “Oh, yeah, that’s what I need.”

They also made us do liberal arts which — I’m from Yorkshire, I don’t even know what liberal arts meant — but I’d encounter Nietzsche and Plato and all this stuff. I had no time at all to digest anything, but I’d read it and be like, “I don’t really know what’s going on here, but I think this is going to be important one day. I think I’m going to reread this one day!”

What was the morning of the BAFTA nominations like for you?

I knew it was happening that morning. I remember talking to my agent, and we just didn’t speak about it, but we both knew that they were coming out that morning or whatever, so we had a really chill conversation about something else. [Laughs] I put it on in the background, because I thought we had a chance at, I don’t know, something, and then I heard that Peter had been nominated and I was so happy for him. I was elated for him.

So, I was just in that, and I was doing the dishes, and I was like, “Wow, that’s so cool. I can’t wait to go text him.” And then they said my name, and I just absolutely couldn’t believe it. My agent called me back straight away and was like, “Oh, my God.” It was an amazing feeling, but it was really unexpected because I was still really, really sort of overwhelmed by the Rising Star thing.

You genuinely looked so surprised when you won Best Actor at the show. I feel like I would black out in that moment. Do you remember what that moment felt like?

Yeah, because I almost did! I had this weird physical reaction where I sort of went back [pantomimes sitting way back], and I think somebody grabbed me. I think I would’ve just kept going. I would’ve fallen off my chair or something.

I honestly couldn’t believe it. I’m honestly not sure I still can believe that that’s something that happened to me, because for someone like me to be in that group of people blew my mind. I felt like, “Wow, and there I am, that’s my name.” To me, that was the thing that sort of really, really, really, really blew me away. When it happened, yes, it all just becomes a blur, and I’m running down the stairs, and I don’t know what the hell I’m going to say.

Obviously, other things happened at the awards show involving John. As someone who had seen the film, I felt like I had a greater grasp on what was happening; I had that context. Now that the film is coming out in America, what hopes do you have for people seeing the film and how that might impact that conversation?

I think lots of people watch the film, and they feel like their education around Tourette’s has improved and increased, and that would be amazing [if that continued]. I think it’s important to acknowledge that … Tourette’s has an impact on a person who’s ticcing, and the same tic obviously has an impact on the person who’s receiving the tic or impacted by the tic. And it’s important to acknowledge that, because that is what it is. Coprolalia, which is the tic that John has, that tic, it’s not saying what you think, it’s saying the worst thing imaginable. That’s how it was described to me.

I hope people watch the film. And I hope people watch the film and think, “Oh, I’ve learned something about Tourette’s.” I hope that people watch the film from the community, because that’s been an amazing thing as well. People watching it who have lived with Tourette’s or lived with another neurodiverse condition have reached out and said, “I see myself in this.” You want people to go to the movies and enjoy the film, but if people go home and Google “John Davidson” or Google “Tourette’s,” that’d be amazing.

The film is going to introduce you to a much larger audience, but you’ve also been in some massive hits before this one. Which is a fun way to ask: Do you know that “The Empty Man” has a huge cult fandom?

[Laughs] I’ve been told this. What an experience. I loved making that film. It was a long journey with it, and I learned a lot. And it was my first movie that I’d done with James Badge Dale, and I did another one with him as well. And I really, really liked working with him. He’s a really nice guy, and he’s a really talented actor. And the director, David [Prior], was wonderful. I learned a lot on that film. I love that people love that film.

You are also in the “Lord of the Rings” world as well. Are you going to be turning out to see “The Hunt for Gollum”?

I’m so excited. I can’t wait. I’m a massive fan of the Peter Jackson films. I can’t wait to see what they do with it. It’s a really interesting story. I’m glad that they’re doing it and doing it properly.

Now that you’ve had what feels like a big breakthrough, what sort of things are you pursuing next?

What do I want to do next? I don’t know! I feel lucky to just be an actor, to work. I’ve been lucky enough to work with some incredible people on “I Swear,” to work with Kirk and Peter and Shirley and Maxine. People like that, you learn, you grow, you get better. And so if I can just keep doing it, I’ll be happy.

That Rising Star Award feels like a lot of pressure!

I just feel really, really grateful for everyone who voted for me. It’s such a cool award that the public, the British public, vote for you. I feel so grateful for everyone who voted for me. I just feel very, very grateful for the whole thing, for everything, and mainly that people hopefully watch the film and talk about it.

For more information about Tourette Syndrome and access to free resources and support, visit the Tourette Association of America right here.

#3374. Steam Officially Makes 10/10 Single-Player Game 100% Free To Keep Forever

With many of us giving thanks this week, it might be time to extend those thanks to Gabe Newell and the team over at Steam. We see plenty of free games' month to month on the Steam platform, but not all games are made equally. Knowing which free games are worth your time is crucial and luckily, this month, there is an absolute banger 10/10 game available for free on Steam.

Currently sitting with an 'Overwhelmingly Positive' rating on Steam, this narrative-driven story sees you playing as a criminal in a game show competing against other nay do-gooders for your freedom. A combination of mini-games, dialogue choices and adventure game, this darkly humored game show will soon have you questioning if you're really playing for your freedom at all. With 12 unique rival contestants taking part, it's up to you to form alliances, pit others against each other or completely burn your bridges with some to progress through this mystery.

Jackpot Crash Course released earlier this year on May 8. Currently, Chapter 1 is only playable with two more chapters expected to follow shortly. The visuals are gorgeous with quirky expressive characters and a beautiful retro pixel-art-style background making every moment pop on screen. Classing itself as a 'death game show', it certainly feels like a truly unique experience and deserves all the attention it gets from fans. With the narrative hinging on your multiple choices and branching dialogue, there's definitely room for replays too, so players can experience the promised multiple endings.

Fans of Jackpot Crash Course have plenty to say about its first chapter too. One fan wrote:

Can't wait to see how this game continues, it's been a blast so far and I definitely recommend.

Such an amazing game, I need Chapter Two ASAP. This has such great characters, such a great soundtrack, and great overall plot as well. I reply this game a bunch and I would love to play it more and more again!

Jackpot Crash Course is a super fun experience in every way and on top of that it's free! I can't wait for the next parts to come out, and I definitely recommend :)

Jackpot Crash Course is completely free to download from Steam and offers players a unique glimpse into a world where life, death and relationships hang in the balance and your choices can lead to unexpected outcomes. With Grand Theft Auto VI costing anywhere between $80 and $100 to purchase, it's great to get a small fun game for free, like Jackpot Crash Course. With chapter 1 taking roughly three hours to complete, it certainly doesn't waste your time and may leave you yearning for future installments.

There are plenty of great Steam titles that are free to play in their ever-growing library, but Jackpot Crash Course sticks out as something truly unique and quirky. A fun little adventure packed with mini-games and devastating choices that could mean life or death for characters you have gotten to know well over the short runtime. Certainly worth a look for PC players who are waiting for Grand Theft Auto VI to release on the platform. All you've got to lose is some time, so check out Jackpot Crash Course over on Steam today.

#3371. How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

[Editor’s note: The following story contains minor spoilers for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.”]

A few years ago, Quentin Tarantino was set to direct one last movie to fulfill his self-imposed ten film limit before riding off into the sunset. And while he was open about his desire to stay creative in other mediums, not even the most outside-the-box thinkers would have predicted that his next big screen project would be a Netflix movie he wrote for David Fincher. “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is an unlikely miracle that emerged for a few distinct reasons: Tarantino’s hesitance to commit to his final directing effort, Brad Pitt‘s determination to play Cliff Booth again and his longtime friendship with David Fincher, and of course, the collapse of Tarantino’s planned film “The Movie Critic.” Related Stories Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’

Given that “The Movie Critic” was also reportedly set in 1970s Los Angeles, and Pitt had signed on to reprise his “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” role, there was always going to be speculation about that script turning into “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.” Tarantino pours gasoline on that flame in the new film when Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki), the Hollywood manager who serves as both a foil and love interest to Booth, reveals that she used to be a film critic before moving into talent representation. The revelation is not crucial to the plot, though it does provide some clever character development as she explains her view that all movies are the culinary equivalent of hamburgers: enjoyable, but not worthy of serious analysis. Yet the inclusion of those lines kicked off a treasure hunt for fans of a director whose unmade movies are almost as legendary as the ones he actually shot.

A definitive answer to the question of “How much of ‘The Movie Critic’ made it into ‘Cliff Booth?'” is going to be hard to come by. Tarantino scripts are some of the most closely guarded secrets in Hollywood, and even the attached actors are often kept in the dark about scenes that don’t concern them. (In an interview with IndieWire, Debicki denied knowing anything about “The Movie Critic,” and everything we know about Tarantino’s process suggests that she was telling the truth.) Beyond that, reports about “The Movie Critic” suggest that the project was constantly changing, even as it neared the planned start of production. It’s impossible to know about every iteration of the project that may have existed at one point or another, but we can use the history of on-the-record quotes and credible reporting about “The Movie Critic” to make an educated guess about where it ended and “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” began.

Cinephiles spent much of 2023 and 2024 receiving piecemeal updates on what was supposed to be Tarantino’s farewell effort. When the project was first reported in March 2023, all we had was the title and a rumor that it was based on legendary New Yorker film critic Pauline Kael. But two months later, Tarantino began to reveal plot details that suggested it was actually inspired by an unnamed film critic who wrote for a magazine he stocked in the porn theaters that he used to work at.

“All the other stuff was too skanky to read, but then there was this porno rag that had a really interesting movie page,” Tarantino said in a May 2025 interview with Deadline. “He wrote about mainstream movies, and he was the second-string critic. I think he was a very good critic. He was as cynical as hell. His reviews were a cross between early Howard Stern and what Travis Bickle might be if he were a film critic. Think about Travis’ diary entries.”

Tarantino went on to say that the movie would take place in Los Angeles in 1977 (just like “Cliff Booth” eventually does) and would take inspiration from the critic’s real life, though the porno rag he wrote for would be fictionalized as The Popstar Pages. The director explained that he had done research on the largely unknown writer’s life, saying that “He wrote like he was 55 but he was only in his early to mid-30s. He died in his late thirties. It wasn’t clear for a while but now I’ve done some more research and I think it was complications due to alcoholism.” He also added that the role would have gone to an American man in his mid-30s, with rumors that Paul Walter Hauser was up for the part.

Tarantino said that the film, which was set up with his “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” backers at Sony, was set to begin “pre-pre-production” in June 2023, and the film secured a California tax credit to shoot the following year. But by April 2024, Tarantino officially scrapped the project. A blockbuster report in THR detailed the many creative changes that “The Movie Critic” went through during its tumultuous year of pre-production. Pitt’s involvement was never in doubt, but the report says that Tarantino looked at multiple ways of incorporating stars of his previous films like John Travolta and Jamie Foxx. He reportedly considered introducing the concept that his movies like “Pulp Fiction” and “Django Unchained” were real ’70s films that existed in this universe, possibly shooting new sequences from movies-within-movies or having his stars show up as the actors who played those characters. There was also an idea that they would interact with a teenage movie theater usher who would be a Sammy Fabelman-style stand-in for a young Tarantino.

None of which happens in “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.” Debicki’s character says that she wrote movie reviews for a grocery store circular, not a porno rag, and she has far more Pauline Kael than Travis Bickle or Howard Stern in her. And it’s hard to imagine that her and Hauser are ever up for the same parts. The only returning Tarantino characters are Booth and Margot Robbie’s Sharon Tate, who appears in a commercial for his signature fake brand Red Apple Cigarettes. But it’s not hard to see how this film could have emerged from the ashes of that one.

When you put all of the reporting about “The Movie Critic” together, it appears that the only constants were Tarantino’s desire to revisit the vintage L.A. world of “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” bring back Cliff Booth, and illustrate how working in a movie theater and watching ’70s cinema shaped his worldview and his future. The project collapsed because he couldn’t settle on a story that would incorporate all of those elements while containing enough gravity to serve as his directorial mic drop. But regardless of how many specific plot details from “The Movie Critic” survived the transition to “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” all of those elements are present in the movie opening this week.

The film opens with a movie-within-a-movie, a fictional blaxploitation effort starring Yahya Abdul-Mateen II. From there, we see that Cliff is working as a projectionist at the New Beverly Cinema, where he also conducts some of his shadier business after hours. He does tell two of his teenage concession stand workers that their young age means it’s time to clock out — if you squint hard enough, that might be considered an Easter Egg about Tarantino’s youth and his possible inclusion in “The Movie Critic,” but the brief encounter hardly makes them seem like stand-ins for a man who loves to memorialize himself.

In a recent interview with Empire, Fincher said that he and Pitt each played a role in cutting 60 pages from the 230-page script that Tarantino initially turned in, resulting in a movie that took place in his sprawling world but was shaped by the type of movie that his two collaborators wanted to make. Looking through that lens, a plausible story for how one movie turned into another begins to take shape.

If you believe all of the reporting, it seems clear enough that Tarantino scrapped “The Movie Critic” because he had more vibes than plot. And “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” provides those exact vibes in droves. We’ll never be able to truly know how many elements were carried over unless Tarantino ever releases or novelizes his “Movie Critic” script (and even then, we won’t be able to fully trust that he didn’t make changes over the subsequent years.) But the safest guess is that he took the idea of Brad Pitt wandering through a darker, sleazier version of L.A. than the hippie paradise he inhabited a decade earlier and simply replaced the plans to make a grand statement about cinema with a pulpy crime plot that could have been ripped from one of his beloved Elmore Leonard novels. And the film still devotes plenty of time to showing scenes from fictional ’70s movies and TV shows, so Tarantino still had a chance to indulge that impulse.

The only other factor that can’t be dismissed is the possibility of self-referential trolling. Tarantino might love talking about movies more than he loves watching them. His insistence on retiring after ten films has nothing to do with his own enjoyment of the filmmaking process — in his own words, he simply doesn’t want anyone studying his future filmography to declare that he got washed up at the end of his career. Anyone who factors the opinions of future podcasters into his own major life decisions is deeply aware of what people say about him, and it’s possible that he simply included the lines about Karen’s career as a critic to add to the mythology about one of his legendary unmade movies. For all we know, the fact that IndieWire published this essay and you read it could be the exact reaction he wanted. In that case, well played, Mr. Tarantino.

“The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is now playing in IMAX theaters. It will be available to stream on Netflix starting Wednesday, December 23.

#3369. Thanksgiving Earthquake Hits Off Baja California Coast, Magnitude 5.7

A magnitude 5.7 earthquake struck a remote group of islands off Mexico's Baja California peninsula on Thanksgiving ... delivering a holiday shake-up in the Pacific Ocean.

The quake hit Thursday near the Revillagigedo Islands, roughly 216 miles from Cabo San Lucas, at a depth of about 6 miles.

Fortunately, the remote location means the earthquake is unlikely to affect many people ... though it's unclear whether any aftershocks could strike closer to the mainland ... and the region was already rattled by a magnitude 4.2 earthquake just one day earlier.

The Revillagigedo Islands are volcanic and federally protected by Mexico, boasting such a rich marine ecosystem that National Geographic has dubbed them the "Galápagos of Mexico."

The Thanksgiving tremor comes just days after back-to-back earthquakes shook Southern California's beach cities ... including a magnitude 3.2 quake in Orange County early Monday and a magnitude 3.3 quake off Manhattan Beach on Sunday.

Mexico also experienced a magnitude 4.7 earthquake in Baja California earlier this month.

For now, it appears the holiday got off to a shaky start, with no major destruction.

#3368. Ridley Scott’s 116-Minute Sci-Fi Masterpiece 'Alien' Is the Perfect Watch Before It’s Cut From Netflix

If you need any convincing as to why Ridley Scott is held in such high regard by movie fans, you only need to fire up Netflix before November 30 and catch his classic Alien. The pioneering sci-fi horror movie led to a franchise consisting of seven films, two spin-offs, and the TV hit Alien: Earth. However, back in 1979, it was just Scott’s vision that terrified audiences and changed the genre as we know it, with star Sigourney Weaver becoming an icon for the ages. If you’ve never experienced the nail-biting first chapter of the space saga, now is the time.

Set in the year 2122, the film takes place in a future where galactic space travel is not only possible, it’s industrialized. Commercial towing craft Nostromo is diverted to a planetoid, answering a distress signal from an alien spacecraft. Once there, an alien attaches itself to one of the crew without his knowledge, only to burst out of him once he's back on board. Escaping to the dark corridors of the ship, the alien (known as a Xenomorph) grows rapidly and starts hunting down the crew members one by one. Only Ellen Ripley (Weaver), who had reservations about the diversion in the first place, stands a chance of outwitting this terrifying new foe.

Scott conceived of the idea after the success of Star Wars, bringing his own brand of intensity to deep space and making a star of Weaver, who was appearing in her first starring role and just her third movie appearance. Nearly 50 years after its release, it’s still considered a pivotal moment in the sci-fi genre and film in general, thanks to the risks it took with well-known formulas.

The movies you finish at one in the morning.

Prior to Scott’s film, the idea of space travel was mostly aspirational for Hollywood studios. Star Trek invited us to “boldly go where no man has gone before,” Star Wars offered swashbuckling adventures, and a decade on from the Apollo 11 moon landing, space seemed like a frontier. What Alien did was introduce the idea of space as a void, a lonely stretch of isolation where its inhabitants were alone in the truest sense. Scott took that concept and used it as the basis for a classic “haunted house” horror tale, teasing theater patrons with the poster’s tagline: “In space, no one can hear you scream.”

It also broke barriers with its visual presentation. The alien creatures and environments designed by the Swiss artist H. R. Giger looked otherworldly, inspired by surrealistic landscapes and biomechanical concepts. The spaces surrounding Ripley were foreign and unsettling, adding to the sense of being alone against this creature that has no empathy or reason, only the instinct to kill. Its influence is immeasurable – if you’ve seen a sci-fi movie where the crew of a spaceship are picked off by a deadly stowaway, it’s likely Alien’s DNA is in there. In the gaming world, titles like Halo and Doom both share the themes of the movie and its sequels. Its most impactful element, however, was its human star.

Ellen Ripley would have been an outlier in science fiction simply for being a female lead, but her influence goes beyond simple box ticking. She wasn’t like the cavalier heroes we were used to seeing flying through asteroid fields or battling little green men. In Alien, she is pragmatic, resourceful, and tough, doing what she has to do to survive without flourishes or grandstanding. She remained the key component of the first four Alien movies, and inspired a number of female sci-fi lead characters in the years since. The gritty resilience of The Terminator’s Sarah Connor, the relentlessness of Katniss Everdeen, and the strength of Mad Max hero Furiosa all owe something to Ellen Ripley, making her a key component of centering female characters in a historically male-dominated genre.

Given her influence on women in genre filmmaking, it’s surprising that the character was originally written as male, with no dialogue changing when the gender was flipped. Speaking to the American Film Institute in 2009, Weaver pointed out this as what attracted her to the part. “It was a character written as a man, so it was written in a very straightforward way,” she said. “She’s a direct person, who didn’t suddenly have these scenes where she was vulnerable. She didn’t throw up her hands and wait for someone to save her.”

Ridley Scott's Alien still holds up nearly half a century later, providing a benchmark by which all follow-ups, and sci-fi in general, are compared. The simplicity of the storytelling, combined with the complexity of the visual filmmaking, made for an unforgettable deep space nightmare that left everyone wondering what horrors may lie just beyond the stars.Alien is on Netflix, with November 30 as the final day to watch.

#3367. New Lee-Child-Recommended Thriller Series Releases January That Reacher Fans Can’t Miss

When it comes to modern thriller book series, Lee Child is an author readers trust more than many others. His rapid-fire rhythmic storytelling, explosive narrative arcs, and heroes with an unwavering sense of justice have captivated fans for decades. His multi-award-winning Jack Reacher novels have come to define the genre in the present day, with Child’s tale of a wandering former military policeman being a literary thriller staple since Reacher made his debut in 1997’s The Killing Floor.

The only problem with the Reacher books is deciding what to read afterward. They’re almost too good. Plenty of thrillers offer violence and conspiracies, but fewer deliver that same combination of gripping action and a protagonist who makes losing oneself in thousands of pages across an entire series feel like light work. Fortunately, Mark Greaney’s The Gray Man novels offer both, and they have an endorsement from Lee Child himself to prove it. For Reacher fans who’ve devoured everything from The Killing Floor to 2026’s Chain Reaction, Greaney’s The Gray Man saga is the perfect next step, especially with a January release giving readers another reason to discover the series’ lethal yet surprisingly principled leading man.

Rather than a military cop turned drifter, The Gray Man books follow Court Gentry, a former CIA operative turned assassin whose extraordinary abilities repeatedly collide with his stubborn moral code. There are 15 published novels so far, starting with 2009’s The Gray Man, providing plenty of dangerous assignments and double-crosses that are bound to delight any Reacher fan. The latest, The Hard Line, reaches US paperback on January 12, 2027. That makes the newest installment in this Barry Award-winning series easier than ever to dive into for Reacher readers seeking a new literary character to obsess over.

Mark Greaney’s The Gray Man novels have attracted plenty of impressive endorsements, but one particularly persuasive recommendation keeps appearing in press releases, blurbs, and book covers: Lee Child’s declaration, “I love the Gray Man.” It’s a short statement with considerable weight. Few authors understand the appeal of a resourceful, dangerous thriller novel protagonist better than Lee Child, and his approval immediately gives Reacher readers a reason to dive into Greaney’s world.

For any fans of Jack Reacher, the explosive sequence of events that unfold once Court Gentry’s enemies start underestimating him are bound to resonate. Both series understand the satisfaction of watching an exceptionally capable outsider dismantle an opponent’s carefully constructed plan. Money, manpower, and official authority offer little protection against characters like Reacher and Gentry, both of whom can identify a weakness and exploit it before anyone realizes what’s happening. Crucially, the intelligence of both heroes matters as much as their capacity for violence. Just like the best Reacher novels, the thrill and joy of The Gray Man books is in seeing how Gentry assesses a seemingly impossible situation, then discovering just how badly their adversaries have misjudged them.

There’s also a moral stubbornness beneath the brutality that makes The Gray Man’s Gentry a character fans of Lee Child’s Jack Reacher are all-but-guaranteed to fall in love with. Gentry’s profession makes him complicated, but his personal code gives readers something solid to hold onto amid shifting loyalties. Like Reacher, he’s endearing because doing the right thing can make his life considerably harder, but that never leads him to compromise his moral values. That tension keeps the momentum high and the action emotionally grounded. Gentry is, just like Reacher, a character readers want him to survive, and it’s because his commitment to doing the right thing makes him someone worth supporting.

However, nobody should be mistaken into thinking that The Gray Man has nothing to distinguish itself. Mark Greaney gives the familiar appeal of the Jack Reacher novels a distinctive espionage setting that sets his own series and characters apart. Where Reacher frequently uncovers trouble in American communities, Gentry operates amid international intelligence networks, covert missions, and betrayals with consequences across borders. Greaney’s extensive research and training with military and law enforcement personnel help give those encounters a substantial level of detail and authenticity. The result is a book series that offers Reacher fans familiar pleasures while opening up a much larger, more treacherous world.

You can purchase The Gray Man, the first book in the series, here.

The run-up January next year is a great time for Reacher fans to start exploring Court Gentry’s world, especially if paperbacks are their go-to format. The Hard Line, the fifteenth and latest The Gray Man novel, arrived in hardcover and ebook through Berkley on February 17, 2026, alongside its audiobook edition. Its US paperback follows on January 12, 2027, nearly eleven months later. For readers who prefer paperbacks, that wait brings a chance to experience one of the best The Gray Man novels without having to carry around a clunky hardback, but with something more physical than an ebook.

The Hard Line has been celebrated by existing fans of The Gray Man because of how deeply personal the latest conspiracy Gentry gets swept up in becomes. Intelligence personnel are being targeted, while Mark Greaney’s globe-trotting hero faces an assassin whose revenge threatens the people he cares about, including his estranged father. The family dynamic gives the danger an emotional force beyond another hazardous white-knuckle assignment.

Gentry’s extraordinary competence can, of course, keep him alive, but protecting everyone around him is a much less certain proposition. The book has been praised for making an established action hero feel vulnerable again. There aren’t really any bad books in The Gray Man series, but The Hard Line’s combination of superb character development and escalating danger has ensured the series’ most recent installment was instantly celebrated as one of its best.

For Reacher readers who like the sound of a spectacle-heavy thriller that doesn’t skimp on serious consequences for its protagonist, January’s rerelease of The Hard Line is bringing considerably more than another collection of gunfights to paperback for the first time.
