#3364. ‘The Hunting Wives’ Review: Season 2 Reloads Without Slowing Down in Netflix’s Delirious Soap

Amid all the sex and murder in “The Hunting Wives” Season 2 — and there is a lot of sex and murder — the riskiest scene suspends itself between the two. Sophie (Brittany Snow), an East Coast liberal out of place in the conservative Texas town of Maple Brook, and Margo (Malin Åkerman), the mysterious local matriarch who can wrap just about anyone around her finely manicured fingertips, are confronted with a fresh dilemma. For spoilers sake, I won’t get into specifics, but the issue is urgent and impacts them both, without being serious enough to warrant what turns out to be their first-thought fix:

In the moment, their lethal instinct seems reasonable. Margo already shot a pregnant teenager in the woods, and Sophie committed vehicular homicide against Margo’s brother (which invited suspicions about Sophie’s past, considering its eerie similarities to a deadly “accident” back in Massachusetts). Their friends, neighbors, and even a youth pastor met their maker, too — just in the first season! So what’s one more body to bury? Go on! Kill ’em! Get yours! Related Stories ‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Finale Hinges on Two Monologues — Let Ethan Hawke and Sterlin Harjo Break Them Down Will Ferrell Golf Comedy ‘The Hawk’ Canceled at Netflix After Just One Season

But before their bloodlust gets the best of them, their better angels make one last plea. Margo hesitates. Sophie follows suit. The gears start turning as they stare into each other’s wide, worried eyes: Are they really prepared to take another life? Are people that disposable to them? What does their initial response say about how they’ve changed? What does it mean about who they’ve become?

No need to spoil what happens next. The pause makes all the difference. “The Hunting Wives” has always been self-aware, but Margo and Sophie’s recognition of slaughter as their default response to trouble is a critical moment in a second season that reloads without slowing down. Creator Rebecca Cutler knows her Netflix soap is careening past the point where its central couple can reasonably return to lives lived between Margarita Mondays and Sunday church. Killing again, so quickly and carelessly, puts them on the precipice of becoming Bonnie and Clyde Bonnie — known fugitives who are only out for each other. Taking a beat lends the series a critical perspective — a vantage point from the top of the roller coaster, right before the big drop, where you can appreciate for a few brief, fleeting seconds the insanity to come.

Then you’re flying. You (and Margo and Sophie) are convinced it’s better to just move forward. Heck, this crisis isn’t going to fix itself!

Margo and Sophie’s breakneck pace to break necks is mostly a feature in Netflix’s surprise hit. The high-key camp comedy and low-key conservative satire moves quickly, sure, but where its characters are often flustered and panicked, it’s decisive in a way that exudes confidence. Progress is fast but assured. The drama is elevated but mindful. Characters don’t ask for permission or forgiveness; they just go after what they want, what they need, or what they feel they have to have, creating a propulsive viewing experience that zips by in a (muzzle) flash.

It’s a welcome change from prestige dramas that regularly feel like they’re stalling for time. While other shows tout firearms around for so long it’s like they’ve never heard of Chekhov, the hunting wives pull the trigger like they’re expecting money to come out — or lovers. Before you can think, “Wait, are they gay, too?” the person in question is already bending their same-sex partner over a desk. Even Season 2’s in-media-res opening lasts only a few seconds — like it’s flipping the bird to streaming TV’s favorite plot device — giving just the briefest glimpse of cop cars racing up to a giant cabin where Margo is (supposedly) being held hostage and Sophie is (supposedly) with her, holding a gun.

The opening tease only gets funnier as you find out how much unfolds between the start of the season and the flash-forward, especially considering its implication — that Sophie would threaten Margo’s life — makes sense from the start. Sophie begins Season 2 trying to repair her marriage to Graham (Evan Jonigkeit) and distance herself from Margo. The former goal sees her going to counseling sessions (where she comically compares her family to a box she wants to be trapped in), running errands, and playing the dutiful housewife.

The latter goal is harder and, arguably, more important. Margo doesn’t know her brother is dead. He’s not answering her calls or texts, but that’s hardly unprecedented behavior, so Margo ignores it — until the leader of a motorcycle gang (Dale Dickey!) shows up, claiming Kyle owes her, and if he doesn’t pay, she’ll take what she wants from Margo.

There’s never a good time for angry bikers to roar up your driveway demanding money, but it’s a particularly bad time for Margo. She’s in the doghouse with Jed (Dermot Mulroney) over the whole “a high schooler got me pregnant and then I had an abortion” issue, but a) that means she’s living in the pool house, not the poor house, and b) he’s really only mad because it’s a potential threat to his run for governor, which is gaining steam. Margo tries calling and texting Sophie, but she’s not answering. She wants to believe she doesn’t need Margo, love Margo, that she maybe even hates Margo. But a few cleverly laced connections make it clear she can’t.

Outside our core couple, Season 2 introduces plenty of plotlines that could pull them together and/or tear them apart. Callie (Jaime Ray Newman) doesn’t see why welcoming a camera crew to film her friends for a reality show (“Married Justice”) could lead to problems, even when the flirty producer warns participants that they should assume they’re “always on camera.” Her husband and co-star, Sheriff Jonny (Branton Box), is just as foolishly carefree, despite Deputy Wanda (Karen Rodriguez) investigating another dead girl in the woods — aka giving Callie a reason to ask questions about the last dead girl in Maple Brook, aka the aforementioned pregnant high schooler Margo killed.

Speaking of people Margo would prefer to forget, her former boy-toy Brad (George Ferrier), is having a hard time at Baylor. He can’t get over the recent murder of his mother, and his lonely boy coping mechanisms (playing acoustic guitar) soon attract the wrong kind of attention: a predatory music mogul named Chase (John Stamos) who promises to make Brad forget all his worries by turning him into a star (right after he loads him up with booze and drugs).

How Cutler shifts the puzzle pieces around to exert pressure proves just as engaging as before. There are plenty of big, loud laughs to go along with a steady supply of sly jokes and juicy melodrama. Anyone tuning in for the soap should be satisfied, just as anyone eager for some edgy satire should find it.

So long as they’re as open as these characters. “The Hunting Wives” may don MAGA drag to tell its story, but it’s a savage critique of conservative values. There’s Brad’s holier-than-thou father, Reverend Clint (Jason Davis), whose over-reliance on Old Testament discipline masks a hands-off parenting style that feeds his desperate son to the wolves. There’s Jed’s hypocritical right-wing politician, who’s more than OK with a little murder if it helps his campaign (knowing his constituents wouldn’t hold it against him) but can’t abide by his wife’s emotional outbursts in the pursuit of personal independence.

Then there’s the fun fact that everyone is gay (or bi or curious). So much of the show’s tension stems from secret trysts that only need to stay secret because of Maple Brook’s pervasive intolerance. That goes double for Sophie and Margo, whose continued pursuit of their repressed desires manifests in bigger and bigger risks. They get a small taste of what their lives could be like if they could just follow their hearts, sans consequence, forever, and then someone comes along to remind them why they can’t. It so often feels like there’s no real hope for the life they want that they fight like hell for whatever sliver they think they can sustain.

That fight gives the series its heart and its haste, but not everything fares better at a high velocity. By season’s end, Margo and Sophie’s individual interiority is rooted in too many questions and not enough answers, while their relationship feels more symbolic than genuine. Perhaps that’s the point. Perhaps the couple isn’t fated to be together as much as they’re fated to go further alone. Perhaps their relationship is more of a means to an end; a reminder of how far off track they got when they were isolated, and how hard it is to get back on track when the world is working to keep them apart.

Either way, it’s good drama. Either way, they’re going to discover new sides of themselves. Either way, the coaster is already racing ahead. Maybe it jumps the tracks, maybe it doesn’t. Maybe after all that, they really should just keep killing.

“The Hunting Wives” Season 2 premieres Thursday, November 26 on Netflix. All eight episodes will be released at once.

#3361. How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation

Every visual element in animation helps tell the story. That’s especially useful when you’re trying to do something new inside the long, proud tradition of Disney animated movies where magic is afoot. “Hexed” is exactly that: the story of a young girl named Billie (Hailee Steinfeld) who learns there’s more to life than her small-town Ohio hometown and more to her family, particularly her mother Alice (Rashida Jones), than meets the eye.

And by “more,” we mean witches. Lots of witches.

“Hexed” builds on work that writers Jared Bush and Dana Ledoux Miller have done with Disney movies like “Encanto” and “Moana,” and that directors Fawn Veerasunthorn and Josie Trinidad (along with co-director Jason Hand) have done with “Raya and the Last Dragon” and “Frozen 2,” among others. In a way, much of it feels familiar to recent Disney Animation Studios fare: A secret world of wonder and magic awaits just around the riverbend and/or through a magic portal, accessible only by imbuing one’s inner spark with “witchification.” But there is still something fundamentally broken about that magic world that our protagonist is positioned to make happen. Related Stories How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’? Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It

And by “something,” “Hexed” Celeste (Jodie Foster), the queen of the hidden realm of Hexe, who is waiting to complete a moonlit ritual that will change the world forever.

According to Miller, the “Hexed” team differentiates this world from the magic of others in the Disney Vault through character design. “ If you look at Billie, you look at Alice, and you look at Celeste, I think we see their personalities come forward,” Miller told IndieWire. “With Alice in particular, she wears this impractical, tight, fitted skirt suit. For me, that was always indicative of the way she is trying to control everything around her, including herself. Even the way she does her hair, she is trying to make sure that her world is safe and contained.”

But the world isn’t safe or containable, and that’s part of the character design, too. Billie doesn’t just have a sparkle in her eyes — he has a crescent moon, hinting at the importance she may hold in completing Hexe’s magic.

“The crescent moon was something that was done in Vis Dev, and then the lighting department told us, ‘We can track that all the way through,” Veerasunthorn told IndieWire. “[It hints at] something special and witchy about Billie, even though she doesn’t know that about herself yet. The way that you see her hair curled in the same shape of the crescent moon, too, is speaking to someone who is looking to fulfill her potential.”

Billie’s design, from the reflection of the moon in her eyes to the color and shape of her hair to the natural elements woven into her clothes, hints at her tendency toward witchiness — and toward belonging in a world she doesn’t even know she belongs in. “We as the audience, we can be like, ‘Girl, figure yourself out!’” Veerasunthorn joked.

Both Billie and Alice are designed in stark contrast to Celeste, who perhaps has too much figured out in terms of witch magic and her silvery, flowing, regal appearance. “[Celeste’s] magic is elegant and powerful, very controlled,” Veerasunthorn said. “The color of Alice’s magic is in between these two extremes, and we wanted to get the sense that there’s something broken about her magic that we don’t quite understand yet. There’s a lost-and-found quality, and hopefully subconsciously we’re hoping that she can put her magic back together.”

“What was a challenge was that it’s this world of magic, a world of witches, and we’ve seen that a lot in media,” Trinidad told IndieWire. “We were trying to find our unique take on that world and how we could be modern and fresh and also sort of pay homage to our own Disney legacy.”

One key way “Hexed” speaks to that Disney tradition is by having a powerful queen who blurs the line between what’s best for her and what’s best for the world. Celeste is also [SPOILER] Alice’s mother and Billie grandmother; there’s a long and proud Disney tradition of very complicated abuelas to outright villain grandmothers, which Bush himself has contributed to in the past.

“The worst part is that my own mother, who’s absolutely lovely, is a grandmother now to my three boys, and she is deeply offended by my choices,” Bush joked to IndieWire about what he has against grandmothers, anyway. “I think the only grandma I’ve written that’s been undeniably loving nonstop is Grandma Tala [from ‘Moana’] — and she didn’t survive the movie.”

But Celeste is a collection of influences from the writers’ lives, the Disney storytelling tradition, and wider pop culture — and not least the actor who ended up voicing her. “We were trying to figure [Celeste] out, and the second that Jodie said yes to the role, it changed the entire character. Because, to be honest, when you’re writing for Jodie Foster, that’s nerve-wracking,” Bush said. “We better get this right. We better make this character interesting and layered.”

Bush and Miller’s writing intended to create space between Celeste’s polished appearance and the roiling jealousy and insecurity she’s buried underneath. “She’s a real villain in a way that’s icky and, for me, that’s a really fun thing to write. On top of the fact that she’s this person trying to take power and maintain power any way that she can, she’s also weirdly vulnerable and needy at the same time. It’s this really uncomfortable combination of characteristics that was really fun to write and to see what Jodie would do with it.”

Leaving space in the writing for animation and performance, the collaboration between story and animation teams is a core part of the writing for “Hexed” and all other Disney Animation Studios films. “We sit down with our story artists and with our animators, and we say, for instance, ‘the premise is we’re going to a weird place with a bunch of reject familiars. What could happen there?’ And everyone spitballs, and great ideas rise to the surface,” Bush said. “More than anything, what I love doing is trying to find a fun sandbox and then being really willing to go wherever the great ideas go.”

Bush, Miller, Veerasunthorn, Trinidad, and Hand all told IndieWire that this openness to great ideas is what makes Disney animation so special, and can make even familiar storytelling territory feel fresh and exciting.

“Maybe we’re coming for granddads next,” Bush said.

#3360. The Perfect ‘Hunger Games’ Cast if the Movie Were Made in 2026

Pop culture found its favorite love triangle when The Hunger Games was transformed into a blockbuster movie franchise. Based on the young adult novels by Suzanne Collins, the filmis set in a dystopian future in the nation of Panem and follows a teenage girl named Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence), who volunteers to take her younger sister's place in a televised, annual fight to the death. Alongside her fellow district tribute Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson), she must survive the brutal arena while unintentionally sparking a rebellion against the oppressive Capitol.

With the highly anticipated The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping reigniting the obsession with the original, it’s time to ponder what The Hunger Games might look like if it were made in 2026. In our dream iteration, we will fill the ensemble with rising generational stars alongside legends of the craft while reflecting the nature of the characters both in the book and on screen. Though the original cast may be untouchable to some devoted fans, this list is what dreams are made of.

The Hunger Games lives and dies with Katniss Everdeen, the Girl on Fire. Tough and fiercely protective, Katniss sets the action in motion in the first film when she volunteers as tribute after her sister Primrose's (Willow Shields) name is drawn at the reaping for the 74th Hunger Games. Armed with exceptional archery skills, a sharp survival instinct, and a guarded demeanor, she enters the arena alongside fellow District 12 tribute Peeta Mellark. After her breakout Oscar-nominated role in Winter's Bone, The Hunger Games proved that Jennifer Lawrence could play a stoic, self-reliant young woman forced into a gritty, mature environment. Lawrence brought natural athleticism, quiet wariness, and ferocity without over-glamorizing the story's brutal elements.

Lawrence masterfully balanced a relatable authenticity with grounded maturity. She was a reluctant, real-world survivor who was never pretentious, carrying the high-stakes dystopian thriller by projecting real fear and compassion. One young star who masters everything that elevated Lawrence's Katniss is Sadie Sink. Showcasing her knack for portraying complex teenage heroines, Sink excels at playing a guarded young woman who conceals deep trauma and fierce loyalty beneath a tough exterior. Between Max Mayfield in Stranger Things and her recent turn as Jean Grey in Spider-Man: Brand New Day, Sink is no stranger to massive franchises and is never intimidated. While the character would embark on a romantic love triangle, Sink's iteration of Katniss would be fiercely independent and self-reliant. Her ability to play raw, authentic dramatic parts, as seen on Broadway in John Proctor Is the Villain and in the film adaptation of The Whale, would add gravitas, rooting Katniss in weighted reality.

Hailing from District 12, it's Peeta Mellark. The lovelorn baker's son has harbored a long-standing crush on Katniss, so, of course, it added intrigue for viewers watching the 74th Hunger Games, as Peeta and Katniss had a star-crossed lovers' narrative built around them. Unlike other hardened competitors, Peeta used verbal skills, artistic camouflage abilities, and genuine empathy to survive. Joining Katniss in defying the Capitol's orders, Peeta emerged as a co-winner and helped spark the revolution that followed. The green-flag boy of the story, Josh Hutcherson brought authentic emotional depth and warmth to the role, making it easy to champion him. With a gentle spirit and sincerity, Hutcherson instilled a protective love and strategic charm into Peeta that was rightly earned.

Peeta served as the emotional core of The Hunger Games. To take on this part today, an actor who has the will to battle without diminishing his genuine heart and spirit is required. That actor is rising superstar Walker Scobell. Best known for starring in Percy Jackson and the Olympians, Scobell would be a compelling Peeta due to his charm, sarcastic wit, and ability to balance vulnerability with fierce loyalty. Oh, and he's well-versed in action-centric storytelling. Scobell is naturally earnest and charming, which would seamlessly translate to the character. His smile is instantly disarming, though how much smile is there really when you're inside the arena? Though Scobell is a teen action hero, Peeta is defined more by his deep empathy, artistic heart, and emotional resilience. As seen in Percy Jackson and the Olympians, Scobell balances those traits through a pure tenderness. Energetic and expressive, there's a universe in which Scobell would be even more beloved than Hutcherson, and that's quite a high bar to achieve.

Young adult stories need a tinge of a love triangle, and in The Hunger Games, Gale Hawthorne filled that third slot. He is Katniss' best friend and hunting partner, and they share a similar hardscrabble life. Gale fiercely hates the Capitol and the oppressive system of the Games, questioning why anyone would watch them. He serves as the emotional support for Katniss' family while she's in the Games. In the film, Gale was played by a hunk: Liam Hemsworth. He naturally captured Gale's quiet intensity, physical stature, and silent protectiveness. His expressive presence was a means of communication. It also served as a stark contrast in stature to Hutcherson's Peeta.

Hemsworth balanced the range of emotion necessary to bring Gale to life. Playing Gale requires conveying deep loyalty, heartbreak, and quiet resolve against his underlying rage and revolutionary spark. Rather than leaning closer to a Hollywood heartthrob or Gale's physical likeness in the book, the perfect pick would be David Iacono. Tall and muscular with olive skin, dark hair, and gray eyes, Iacono fits the classic look of District 12's "Seam" neighborhood. Audiences are quite familiar with Iacono's ability to play a devoted, caring romantic interest during his time as Cam Cameron in The Summer I Turned Pretty. He excels at portraying the quiet tenderness that Gale would share with Katniss in the woods before the Games tear their lives apart. Iacono has shown he can handle darker, high-stakes crime and thriller material, as seen in Cinnamon, Grand Army, and Fresh Kills. It would give him the edge needed for Gale's eventual transformation. Following his performance in Jurassic World Rebirth, it's clear Iacono can carry heavy physical action and anchor scenes in a massive pop culture franchise.

Four of the largest communities on the planet, and four completely different reasons to belong to one. Here is yours, what it would give you, and the argument you would be having within a week.

You belong to the fandom that is really about comfort. Hogwarts works on people because it is a place rather than a plot, and the pull is not the wizard war so much as the corridors, the food, the weather and the sense that somebody is expecting you.

You belong to the deepest fandom on this list, the one where somebody has always read further than you and is quietly delighted to say so. Middle-earth rewards patience more than any other world in popular culture.

You belong to the loudest and largest tent of the four, the one where three generations are all watching the same thing and none of them agree about any of it. That disagreement is not a flaw in this fandom, it is the main activity.

You belong to the thinking fandom, the one that turns up for the argument rather than the explosion. Trek has always been a series of ethical problems in space, and the people who love it love being asked what they would have done.

With the upcoming film fleshing out the full lore and mythology of Haymitch Abernathy, it will only deepen the allure of this fascinating character. When audiences first met him, it was revealed that he was the only living person from District 12 to have ever won the Hunger Games. Because of his victor status, he is assigned to act as the cynical, hard-drinking mentor to Katniss and Peeta. Despite his vices, he used his sharp wits to help the duo win vital corporate and public sponsors, famously leading them to present themselves as star-crossed lovers. Both a logical and surprising casting choice, Woody Harrelson perfectly blended cynical humor with the genuine emotional depth of a man plagued by decades of trauma. He avoided turning him into a one-note drunken bum, giving him the right amount of preserved dignity beneath the mess.

Though he was known for his over-the-top characterizations in other signature roles, Harrelson's small glances and weary demeanor brought immense fruitfulness to Haymitch. An actor who can do the most while exuding very little, yet serve as an important presence, is crucial. Look no further than Oscar Isaac. A compelling option and a beloved industry icon, Isaac excels at playing sharp, weary, morally complex survivors who carry deep internal trauma as excruciating baggage. Whether it be in Ex Machina, Dune, or Star Wars: Episode VII — The Force Awakens, his previous parts match the haunted resilience of a man eager to move on. He has a knack for playing characters who are cynical, quick-witted, and tired of the system, especially in the second season of Beef. Some fans may fear Isaac would be too put together for the part, but that's the beauty of acting! He can easily transform into the book-accurate Haymitch.

And now we begin our adventure into the colorful world of eccentric individuals! First up, the utterly fabulous Effie Trinket. The colorful, upbeat Capitol escort assigned to District 12 is deeply invested in Capitol etiquette, fashion, and rules, often appearing superficial or overly focused on decorum. Because of her rose-tinted glasses, she remains willfully oblivious to the harsh poverty beneath her in District 12. Though strictly focused on protocol, she slowly grows fond of the District 12 tributes. Elizabeth Banks brought her to life, grounding the over-the-top, satirical character with three-dimensional depth, humor, and heart. Banks crafted Effie's distinct theatricality and cadence by drawing inspiration from classic Hollywood icons.

Effie was infused with a relentless, chipper ebullience that made her feel like a real product of the Capitol's oppressive fascist society. She was a truly engaging character because there was always an alluring mystery tied to her. To capture the same exuberance with genuine heart that eventually seeps through, Alison Brie excels at playing tightly wound, rule-obsessed perfectionists who hide genuine vulnerability beneath a beautifully polished exterior. When it comes to rule-lovers who spiral when plans go off the rails, Brie's comedic precision shone as Annie Edison in Community. From there, she moved into the mix of camp and emotion during her run on GLOW. With a willingness to play modern satire through vocal agility, her voice-acting experience on BoJack Horseman would help her find the right tone for Effie's overtly affected inflection. Now, if you didn't think she could play big, bold, campy characters before, her recent turn as Evil-Lyn in Masters of the Universe is the perfect gateway to Effie Trinket's fabulosity. Put her in a towering wig and avant-garde wardrobe, and a new Effie is born.

No one was nearly as flamboyant, upbeat, and telegenic as the master of ceremonies Caesar Flickerman. Serving as the primary media personality of the Capitol, his job is to put nervous tributes at ease, turn awkward interview moments into crowd-pleasing highlights, and make the brutal Hunger Games feel like an entertaining television spectacle. Caesar is known for his colorful, theatrical attire and annually dyeing his hair, lips, and eyelids in bright, changing themes. Dubbing Katniss as the infamous "Girl on Fire," Caesar was simply a hoot. Stanley Tucci blended smarmy insincerity, theatrical charisma, and subtle cruelty to satirize modern mass media and hypocrisy. Tucci styled Caesar with a glitzy, late-night talk show flair, radiating a fake, plastic warmth and faux sympathy while gleefully sending children off to slaughter.

Going full tilt with unnatural color and taped-back "face work," he exuded a shallow persona obsessed with entertainment as a means to distract from tyranny. Caesar must be played by an actor willing to go all-in in flamboyant theatricality. A phenomenal choice to play the seasoned version of the host is Sam Rockwell. Rockwell is infamous for his physical charisma, rhythmic delivery, and magnetic showmanship. Whether it's the wildly eccentric Zaphod Beeblebrox in The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy or finding the humanity as Bob Fosse in Fosse/Verdon, Rockwell's innate theatricality would give him the range to make Caesar pop on the screen. His high-wattage energy, even in more grounded, realistic roles, is showcased by a smiling mask that covers a dark reality. In projects like Seven Psychopaths, Vice, and Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri, Rockwell has played characters whose charming, fast-talking exteriors hide moral compromise. Rockwell is naturally loose and unpredictable, which is essential for the improv-heavy Caesar. While he would give Caesar a darker edge than Tucci, Rockwell's versatility would translate, no matter what color his hair is.

Evil was personified in the form of President Coriolanus Snow. The tyrannical and ruthless ruler of the nation of Panem, the autocratic Snow maintains strict rule and control over the twelve districts through fear, propaganda, and the brutality of the Hunger Games. He is frequently associated with genetically modified white roses, which he uses to mask the odor of mouth sores caused by his history of poisoning rivals. With a cold, calculating demeanor, Donald Sutherland brought a chilling gravitas, deep political passion, and a quiet menace to a genuine monster in the first film and beyond. As a rationalizing, pragmatic villain, Sutherland portrayed Snow as a brilliant, dangerously calm authoritarian who genuinely believed his cold-blooded control and fear-based suppression was a necessary good. As a long-time activist, Sutherland wanted to ensure Snow was so tyrannical that it inspired political awareness and organization against systemic inequality. He succeeded.

Snow is anchored by chilling physical choices, namely his piercing gaze, soft-spoken smile, and calm acceptance of the physical toll of his past decisions. Sutherland had a natural villainy in his presence. An actor with that same innate evil imagery would be perfect to play President Snow in 2026. Very few actors exude evil with a simple glare quite like Willem Dafoe. His distinct physical features, intensity, and proven track record of playing layered, menacing, eccentric authority figures would let him find a new side of fear in Snow. He excels at playing men who are terrifying at first but deeply psychologically complex, like Norman Osborn in Spider-Man and Thomas Wake in The Lighthouse. His theatrical presence fits the dystopian tyrant archetype. Though Sutherland had a classical image, Dafoe's striking facial structure would convey aristocratic coldness and hidden cruelty without needing to say a word. Dafoe's Snow would be much darker, and isn't that just scary?

Behind every heroine is a personal stylist and costume designer who made them look like an icon. For Katniss, that visionary was Cinna. Assigned to create an image for the District 12 tributes, Cinna designed the dramatic, flame-engulfed opening-ceremony costumes for Katniss and Peeta that secured their vital corporate sponsor. Despite living a life of luxury in the Capitol, Cinna secretly took the assignment with District 12 to quietly align with the growing resistance against President Snow. Flamboyant in image and not in personality, Lenny Kravitz gave Cinna a calm, compassionate essence that was key to the character. As an accomplished musician and fashion-forward artist, Kravitz fit Cinna like a glove. He was naturally smooth with a self-assured poise.

Perhaps using Kravitz as the basis for casting, selecting another musician with fashion in the forefront would be sensational. It's time to feel the rush with Troye Sivan playing Cinna. Cinna is a visionary designer who stands out in the Capitol by rejecting garish excess in favor of sleek, intentional minimalism. Sivan's real-world presence as a fashion icon makes his authority as a couture mastermind completely believable. Cinna is a grounded individual, unlike the loud, theatrically eccentric citizens. Sivan has the gentleness that Cinna exudes, yet can also blend in with high-style charisma if needed. Sivan's artistic evolution, breaking away from commercial pop formulas for raw cultural impact, mirrors Cinna's willingness to risk everything to make a statement. A more contemporary, gender-fluid, and refined aesthetic would reflect how luxury fashion and rebellion look in 2026. Now, if you're wondering about his acting prowess, his resume ranges from X-Men Origins: Wolverine to The Idol.

Some of us dream of creating a brilliant game; Seneca Crane did just that. As the Head Gamemaker, Crane oversees the design and digital control of the survival arena. He orchestrated obstacles, environmental shifts, and hazards for the tributes. When Katniss and Peeta go rogue and threaten to commit suicide, Crane permits them both to survive. Seen as an act of dangerous defiance, Crane is executed. Though a minor, largely unseen background figure in the original novel, expanding him was a brilliant cinematic decision. Wes Bentley collaborated to give Crane his iconic aesthetic. The meticulously sculpted beard became a defining element of Crane. He created Crane in a manner that was an arrogant, out-of-touch showman who cared more about ratings and spectacle than human lives. And yet, when he does flip, it comes from a moment of ill-advised, reluctant sincerity.

Crane must have a quiet, eerie intensity that is defined by a calm, unbothered detachment that makes his sadistic game design feel even more chilling. With a resume filled with dark and twisted Ryan Murphy products, Joey Pollari could find that perfect balance of charm and evil. His ability to take on characters whose polished exteriors slowly crack under immense psychological pressure would translate into an enthralling take on Crane. Like Bentley, Pollari has an editorial, high-fashion edge that makes him a natural fit for the extravagant, image-obsessed elite of the Capitol. With a theater background alongside a resume of nuanced dramas like American Crime and Sugar, Pollari has the control and dramatic gravitas needed to sell the Gamemaker's control-room monologues as if he were directing live theater.

Last, but certainly not least, is Claudius Templesmith, the booming, resonant official announcer and commentator of the 74th Hunger Games. Serving alongside Caesar Flickerman, Claudius broke down and narrated the events for the Capitol audience. He broadcasts major official decrees to the tributes in the arena, including the start of the Games, inviting them to the Feast, changing the rules to allow two victors, and famously concluding his messages with the catchphrase, "May the odds be ever in your favor." Toby Jones brought a distinct, sharp comedic and theatrical energy to the role, capturing the chilling detachment of the Capitol's media machine. He played the part, almost emulating an American football broadcaster. When seen, he presented a physical, smiling, public-facing presence that mirrored how real-world media turns tragedy into spectacle.

While Jones had a specific brand of presentation, finding a performer with a booming presence to be the omniscient "Voice of the Capitol" requires someone who knows a thing or two about putting on a character voice. Look no further than Peter Serafinowicz. As a prolific voice actor, Serafinowicz has lent his talents to Darth Maul in The Phantom Menace and the Fisher King in Doctor Who. Possessing a rich, resonant baritone, he speaks and instantly commands authority. As an actor, whether it be the Sommelier in John Wick: Chapter 2 or Denarian Saal in Guardians of the Galaxy, he can effortlessly pivot from charming commentator to cold, sleek, and intimidating. He's known for mastering satirical news with a broadcast cadence on shows like Look Around You and The Peter Serafinowicz Show. He's perfected the overly polished, slightly detached cadence of a mid-century television presenter. With a blend of cheery professionalism and underlying absurdity, he would thrive as the Capitol's dystopian media machine. Now, if you need further proof that he can commentate on the fly, he's the absolute perfect fit as the humorous host of the reality social strategy series Million Dollar Secret. It's that same energy that would make Claudius astounding.

#3359. Dolly Parton Honored by U2 During Emotional NFL Thanksgiving Eve Halftime Show

Dolly Parton's voice echoed through SoFi Stadium Wednesday night ... as U2 paid tribute to the late country icon during a moving Thanksgiving Eve halftime performance.

The rock band took the stage during the Los Angeles Rams' matchup against the Green Bay Packers ... with frontman Bono singing alongside Dolly's prerecorded vocals on their duet "Torn," as images of the country legend appeared on curtains surrounding the stage.

The tribute was especially emotional because "Torn" is believed to be Dolly's final recorded song before her death in August at age 80, following a private battle with cancer.

Dolly recorded her vocals in June, just two months before she died ... and Bono later told Rolling Stone she actually got out of bed while battling her illness to record the track.

As TMZ previously reported ... Dolly's final recorded song is about a family torn apart by conflict, with lyrics touching on broken relationships and the pain of loved ones turning against each other. Bono has described the track as Dolly's final prayer for America.

U2 also treated fans to classics including "Sunday Bloody Sunday," "Where the Streets Have No Name," and "Pride (In the Name of Love)" during the NFL's first-ever Thanksgiving Eve game.

#3357. 5-Episode Netflix Thriller Series Adapts One Of Harlan Coben's First Novels

While Harlan Coben had penned a handful of Myron Bolitar novels before writing the book that Netflix adapted into a show in 2021, the series was based on one of his first standalone novels. If Prime Video’s Reacher franchise proves one thing, it is that streaming fans love a good page-to-screen adaptation. To be more specific, streaming show adaptations of best-selling crime, thriller, and mystery novels tend to fare extraordinarily well on Prime Video, Netflix, Hulu, and Peacock alike.

Whether it is an adaptation of Andrea Mara’s novel All Her Fault breaking viewing records on Peacock or Netflix’s 30-episode take on Matthew Quick’s book The Night Agent rivaling Reacher in its popularity, the formula has proven a hit over and over again. Recently, Prime Video’s Cross cashed in on this trend, although the streaming service’s 2014 hit Bosch and its many spinoffs pioneered the approach over a decade earlier.

However, the legendary crime writer Harlan Coben is something of an unusual case when it comes to streaming shows. Coben first became a bestselling author back in 1990 with his standalone novel Play Dead, followed, by 1991’s Miracle Cure. However, it was the 12-book Myron Bolitar series that made Coben a star, beginning with 1995’s Deal Breaker. Despite the popularity of this novel series, Netflix has mostly adapted his standalone books, like Gone for Good, to the screen rather than Myron Bolitar novels.

Related in 2002, Gone for Good was a major hit for Coben. The novel follows Will, who is horrified to learn the disturbing truth about his brother Ken’s disappearance eleven years earlier after his girlfriend goes missing in the present day. Released in August 2021, Gone for Good’s Netflix adaptation relocated the story to France and changed some names accordingly, starring Finnegan Oldfield as Guillaume and Nicolas Duvauchelle as his missing brother, Fred.

Unlike Prime Video’s Reacher franchise, Netflix’s Coben adaptations all feature different main characters in stories that have no canon connections. Even though there are plenty of Myron Bolitar books to adapt, and many more YA spinoff novels starring his nephew Mickey, the streaming service has thus far opted to focus instead on Coben’s standalone efforts. These include No Second Chance, The Stranger, The Innocent, The Woods, Gone For Good, Stay Close, Hold Tight, Fool Me Once, Missing You, Run Away, and I Will Always Find You.

If that list seems long, that’s because it is. All told, there are 13 Coben shows on Netflix, with seven being English-language productions, while a further six are foreign-language shows like Gone For Good. Interestingly enough, much like Michael Connelly’s The Lincoln Lawyer was a Matthew McConaughey movie before the novel series became a Netflix show, the first screen adaptation of Coben’s work was a feature length movie, director Guillame Canet’s 2006 thriller Tell No One.

If the fact that Tell No One and Gone For Good are French-language productions didn’t give it away, Coben’s work has a massive worldwide fan base that spans the globe. His twisty thrillers translate well into other languages, which is why The Woods, Just One Look, and Hold Tight were Polish productions, The Innocent is a Spanish series, and 2025’s Caught hailed from Argentina.

Between that Coben series and the same year’s long-awaited comic adaptation The Eternaut, Argentina is emerging as a major hub for Netflix shows. However, it is tough to beat some of the writer’s earliest shows. With its clever twists, inventive plotting, and poignant character work, Netflix’s 2021 hit Gone For Good remains one of the author’s most underrated adaptations to date.

#3354. You Can Get One of These Pocket E-Readers for As Little As $55 During Black Friday

Black Friday is usually a great time to grab a new e-reader, but the ongoing RAM crisis has made that a question mark this year: Amazon recently raised the prices of all its Kindles by around $50 and refreshed the entire lineup, which means your odds of grabbing one at a big discount are low. But you aren't totally out of luck: If you haven't noticed, micro-e-readers—I'm talking credit card-sized, with screens that measure around four inches—are all the rage in 2026, and right now, you can pick up one of them for around $55.

If you too can see the appeal of carrying all of your books with you on a device so small you'll forget it's even in your pocket, it's a great time to jump in: The recently released Xteink X4 Classic is currently 38% off for Black Friday, bringing it down to $54.87, a record-low price. Meanwhile, the smaller X3 is $55.72, or 19% off. Both are available in either "mist grey" or "space black." The discounts should last through the end of Cyber Monday on Nov. 30.

Xteink is a Chinese startup that shook up the e-reading world last year with the launch of the X4, a super bare-bones device that made up for its lack of features and usability with a cheap sub-$70 price point. Since then, a huge online community of fans has formed, sharing tips on Reddit and even coming together to crowdsource an alternate operating system that fixed a lot of early problems. Xteink quickly followed up the X4 with a slate of other devices, including the 3.7-inch X3 and the X4 Pro, which adds a front light and touchscreen (at the cost of screen clarity and two physical buttons).

The X4 Classic and the X3 improve on the original X4 with quality-of-life upgrades like a larger battery, relocated page-turn buttons, a real-time clock, and a tilt-to-turn-page feature. They're also lighter and thinner than the X4, though there is a trade-off involved: They drop the USB-C charging port in favor of magnetic pogo pins that require a separate adapter (included).

These upgrades also increased the cost: The X4 Classic typically retails for $89, $20 more than the discontinued X4 and only $10 less than the X4 Pro, while the X3 launched at $79. But right now, the X4 Classic is just under $55, or around 38% off, and the X3 is about a dollar more. Either is a great option for those who prioritize crisp, readable text above the conveniences of a built-in light or touchscreen, as those add extra layers between the inner screen and outer glass. It's also important to understand what you're getting into: These devices support only e-books without Digital Rights Management (DRM), which means you can't use it to read your existing library of Kindle books. On the plus side, there's no longer a need to worry about flashing new firmware if you don't want to, as the native version has been totally overhauled and is now one of your best options (though the new firmware, called "Licorice," isn't available on the X3 quite yet).

#3347. Venomous Sea Snakes Washing Ashore on Southern California Beaches, Officials Warn

California beachgoers might want to watch where they step ... 'cause venomous sea snakes are washing ashore ... and experts warn more could be on the way.

A yellow-bellied sea snake was discovered Sunday at Bolsa Chica State Beach in Orange County ... marking just the eighth documented sighting of the rare reptile in Southern California.

And here's the kicker ... scientists believe unusually warm waters from El Niño are pushing the tropical snakes farther north, meaning this slithery surprise might not be the last.

Researchers at the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County say high tides through Sunday could bring more snakes onto beaches, with additional sightings possible in early and late December .

Despite their dangerous venom, the snakes aren't typically aggressive toward humans. Still, officials are warning beachgoers to keep their hands off ... advising anyone who spots one to snap a photo from a safe distance and alert lifeguards.

So, if you're hitting the beach this holiday weekend ... keep your eyes on the sand ... you never know what might wash up.

#3341. Atomically Thin Materials Significantly Shrink Qubits

MIT researchers use 2D materials for capacitors in quantum circuits in an effort to scale processors

Superconducting quantum processor and its microwave packaging.

Quantum computing is a devilishly complex technology, with many technical hurdles impacting its development. Of these challenges two critical issues stand out: miniaturization and qubit quality.

IBM has adopted the superconducting qubit road map of reaching a 1,121-qubit processor by 2023, leading to the expectation that 1,000 qubits with today’s qubit form factor is feasible. However, current approaches will require very large chips (50 millimeters on a side, or larger) at the scale of small wafers, or the use of chiplets on multichip modules. While this approach will work, the aim is to attain a better path toward scalability.

Now researchers at MIT have been able to both reduce the size of the qubits and done so in a way that reduces the interference that occurs between neighboring qubits. The MIT researchers have increased the number of superconducting qubits that can be added onto a device by a factor of 100.

“We are addressing both qubit miniaturization and quality,” said William Oliver, the director for the Center for Quantum Engineering at MIT. “Unlike conventional transistor scaling, where only the number really matters, for qubits, large numbers are not sufficient, they must also be high-performance. Sacrificing performance for qubit number is not a useful trade in quantum computing. They must go hand in hand.”

The key to this big increase in qubit density and reduction of interference comes down to the use of two-dimensional materials, in particular the 2D insulator hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). The MIT researchers demonstrated that a few atomic monolayers of hBN can be stacked to form the insulator in the capacitors of a superconducting qubit.

Just like other capacitors, the capacitors in these superconducting circuits take the form of a sandwich in which an insulator material is sandwiched between two metal plates. The big difference for these capacitors is that the superconducting circuits can operate only at extremely low temperatures—less than 0.02 degrees above absolute zero (-273.15 °C).

Superconducting qubits are measured at temperatures as low as 20 millikelvin in a dilution refrigerator.Nathan Fiske/MIT

In that environment, insulating materials that are available for the job, such as PE-CVD silicon oxide or silicon nitride, have quite a few defects that are too lossy for quantum computing applications. To get around these material shortcomings, most superconducting circuits use what are called coplanar capacitors. In these capacitors, the plates are positioned laterally to one another, rather than on top of one another.

As a result, the intrinsic silicon substrate below the plates and to a smaller degree the vacuum above the plates serve as the capacitor dielectric. Intrinsic silicon is chemically pure and therefore has few defects, and the large size dilutes the electric field at the plate interfaces, all of which leads to a low-loss capacitor. The lateral size of each plate in this open-face design ends up being quite large (typically 100 by 100 micrometers) in order to achieve the required capacitance.

In an effort to move away from the large lateral configuration, the MIT researchers embarked on a search for an insulator that has very few defects and is compatible with superconducting capacitor plates.

“We chose to study hBN because it is the most widely used insulator in 2D material research due to its cleanliness and chemical inertness,” said colead author Joel Wang, a research scientist in the Engineering Quantum Systems group of the MIT Research Laboratory for Electronics.

On either side of the hBN, the MIT researchers used the 2D superconducting material, niobium diselenide. One of the trickiest aspects of fabricating the capacitors was working with the niobium diselenide, which oxidizes in seconds when exposed to air, according to Wang. This necessitates that the assembly of the capacitor occur in a glove box filled with argon gas.

While this would seemingly complicate the scaling up of the production of these capacitors, Wang doesn’t regard this as a limiting factor.

“What determines the quality factor of the capacitor are the two interfaces between the two materials,” said Wang. “Once the sandwich is made, the two interfaces are “sealed” and we don’t see any noticeable degradation over time when exposed to the atmosphere.”

This lack of degradation is because around 90 percent of the electric field is contained within the sandwich structure, so the oxidation of the outer surface of the niobium diselenide does not play a significant role anymore. This ultimately makes the capacitor footprint much smaller, and it accounts for the reduction in cross talk between the neighboring qubits.

“The main challenge for scaling up the fabrication will be the wafer-scale growth of hBN and 2D superconductors like [niobium diselenide], and how one can do wafer-scale stacking of these films,” added Wang.

Wang believes that this research has shown 2D hBN to be a good insulator candidate for superconducting qubits. He says that the groundwork the MIT team has done will serve as a road map for using other hybrid 2D materials to build superconducting circuits.

Dexter Johnson is a contributing editor at IEEE Spectrum, with a focus on nanotechnology.

#3339. How AI Will Change Chip Design

Artificial intelligence’s promise and potential for the semiconductor industry

Rina Diane Caballar is a contributing editor covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment.

An array of semiconductor wafers are ready to be made into chips.

The end of Moore’s Law is looming. Engineers and designers can do only so much to miniaturize transistors and pack as many of them as possible into chips. So they’re turning to other approaches to chip design, incorporating technologies like AI into the process.

Samsung, for instance, is adding AI to its memory chips to enable processing in memory, thereby saving energy and speeding up machine learning. Speaking of speed, Google’s TPU V4 AI chip has doubled its processing power compared with that of its previous version.

But AI holds still more promise and potential for the semiconductor industry. To better understand how AI is set to revolutionize chip design, we spoke with Heather Gorr, senior product manager for MathWorks’ MATLAB platform.

How is AI currently being used to design the next generation of chips?

Heather Gorr: AI is such an important technology because it’s involved in most parts of the cycle, including the design and manufacturing process. There’s a lot of important applications here, even in the general process engineering where we want to optimize things. I think defect detection is a big one at all phases of the process, especially in manufacturing. But even thinking ahead in the design process, [AI now plays a significant role] when you’re designing the light and the sensors and all the different components. There’s a lot of anomaly detection and fault mitigation that you really want to consider.

Then, thinking about the logistical modeling that you see in any industry, there is always planned downtime that you want to mitigate; but you also end up having unplanned downtime. So, looking back at that historical data of when you’ve had those moments where maybe it took a bit longer than expected to manufacture something, you can take a look at all of that data and use AI to try to identify the proximate cause or to see something that might jump out even in the processing and design phases. We think of AI oftentimes as a predictive tool, or as a robot doing something, but a lot of times you get a lot of insight from the data through AI.

What are the benefits of using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Historically, we’ve seen a lot of physics-based modeling, which is a very intensive process. We want to do a reduced order model, where instead of solving such a computationally expensive and extensive model, we can do something a little cheaper. You could create a surrogate model, so to speak, of that physics-based model, use the data, and then do your parameter sweeps, your optimizations, your Monte Carlo simulations using the surrogate model. That takes a lot less time computationally than solving the physics-based equations directly. So, we’re seeing that benefit in many ways, including the efficiency and economy that are the results of iterating quickly on the experiments and the simulations that will really help in the design.

So it’s like having a digital twin in a sense?

Gorr: Exactly. That’s pretty much what people are doing, where you have the physical system model and the experimental data. Then, in conjunction, you have this other model that you could tweak and tune and try different parameters and experiments that let sweep through all of those different situations and come up with a better design in the end.

So, it’s going to be more efficient and, as you said, cheaper?

Gorr: Yeah, definitely. Especially in the experimentation and design phases, where you’re trying different things. That’s obviously going to yield dramatic cost savings if you’re actually manufacturing and producing [the chips]. You want to simulate, test, experiment as much as possible without making something using the actual process engineering.

We’ve talked about the benefits. How about the drawbacks?

Gorr: The [AI-based experimental models] tend to not be as accurate as physics-based models. Of course, that’s why you do many simulations and parameter sweeps. But that’s also the benefit of having that digital twin, where you can keep that in mind—it’s not going to be as accurate as that precise model that we’ve developed over the years.

Both chip design and manufacturing are system intensive; you have to consider every little part. And that can be really challenging. It’s a case where you might have models to predict something and different parts of it, but you still need to bring it all together.

One of the other things to think about too is that you need the data to build the models. You have to incorporate data from all sorts of different sensors and different sorts of teams, and so that heightens the challenge.

How can engineers use AI to better prepare and extract insights from hardware or sensor data?

Gorr: We always think about using AI to predict something or do some robot task, but you can use AI to come up with patterns and pick out things you might not have noticed before on your own. People will use AI when they have high-frequency data coming from many different sensors, and a lot of times it’s useful to explore the frequency domain and things like data synchronization or resampling. Those can be really challenging if you’re not sure where to start.

One of the things I would say is, use the tools that are available. There’s a vast community of people working on these things, and you can find lots of examples [of applications and techniques] on GitHub or MATLAB Central, where people have shared nice examples, even little apps they’ve created. I think many of us are buried in data and just not sure what to do with it, so definitely take advantage of what’s already out there in the community. You can explore and see what makes sense to you, and bring in that balance of domain knowledge and the insight you get from the tools and AI.

What should engineers and designers consider when using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Think through what problems you’re trying to solve or what insights you might hope to find, and try to be clear about that. Consider all of the different components, and document and test each of those different parts. Consider all of the people involved, and explain and hand off in a way that is sensible for the whole team.

How do you think AI will affect chip designers’ jobs?

Gorr: It’s going to free up a lot of human capital for more advanced tasks. We can use AI to reduce waste, to optimize the materials, to optimize the design, but then you still have that human involved whenever it comes to decision-making. I think it’s a great example of people and technology working hand in hand. It’s also an industry where all people involved—even on the manufacturing floor—need to have some level of understanding of what’s happening, so this is a great industry for advancing AI because of how we test things and how we think about them before we put them on the chip.

How do you envision the future of AI and chip design?

Gorr: It’s very much dependent on that human element—involving people in the process and having that interpretable model. We can do many things with the mathematical minutiae of modeling, but it comes down to how people are using it, how everybody in the process is understanding and applying it. Communication and involvement of people of all skill levels in the process are going to be really important. We’re going to see less of those superprecise predictions and more transparency of information, sharing, and that digital twin—not only using AI but also using our human knowledge and all of the work that many people have done over the years.

Rina Diane Caballar is a writer covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment. An IEEE Spectrum contributing editor, she's a former software engineer based in New Zealand.

#3336. Florida Thanksgiving Feast Leaves 18 Sick, 15 Hospitalized

A Thanksgiving feast in Florida turned into a holiday nightmare ... with 18 people falling ill from suspected food poisoning and at least 15 landing in the hospital.

The dinner disaster unfolded Wednesday at Leon Medical Centers' headquarters in Doral, near Miami, where employees gathered for an early Thanksgiving celebration.

But the holiday cheer didn't last long ... several staffers began experiencing gastrointestinal symptoms after the catered meal, prompting a massive emergency response.

According to Miami-Dade Fire Rescue, 18 people reported feeling sick, with 15 initially transported to hospitals. The situation was serious enough for officials to declare a Level 3 mass casualty incident.

Leon Medical Centers confirmed an outside catering company provided the food and says it's working to determine what went wrong ... stressing that no patients were affected.

iOS 27 includes a really clever new feature that aims to solve the awkward middle ground between cellular and Wi-Fi connectivity. Here’s how it works and how you can turn it on.

Essentially, the feature detects when your Wi-Fi connection is weak or unusable and intelligently uses cellular data to keep you connected.

One practical example I’ve noticed is when I walk out of my house and get in my car. Oftentimes, my iPhone will cling to my house’s weak Wi-Fi connection, making it hard to start playing Apple Music and queue up directions in Apple Maps.

Connectivity Assist solves that problem. My phone can now intelligently use cellular data to help that transition away from Wi-Fi. It’s one of many really nice quality-of-life improvements in iOS 27.

Another thing to be aware of is that you might use more cellular data with Connectivity Assist turned on. You can monitor your data usage via your carrier’s app or website, as well as in the Settings app on iPhone.

#3334. Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

The AI pioneer says it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big issues

Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.

Andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models in the late 2000s with his students at Stanford University, cofounded Google Brain in 2011, and then served for three years as chief scientist for Baidu, where he helped build the Chinese tech giant’s AI group. So when he says he has identified the next big shift in artificial intelligence, people listen. And that’s what he told IEEE Spectrum in an exclusive Q&A.

Ng’s current efforts are focused on his company Landing AI, which built a platform called LandingLens to help manufacturers improve visual inspection with computer vision. He has also become something of an evangelist for what he calls the data-centric AI movement, which he says can yield “small data” solutions to big issues in AI, including model efficiency, accuracy, and bias.

The great advances in deep learning over the past decade or so have been powered by ever-bigger models crunching ever-bigger amounts of data. Some people argue that that’s an unsustainable trajectory. Do you agree that it can’t go on that way?

Andrew Ng: This is a big question. We’ve seen foundation models in NLP [natural language processing]. I’m excited about NLP models getting even bigger, and also about the potential of building foundation models in computer vision. I think there’s lots of signal to still be exploited in video: We have not been able to build foundation models yet for video because of compute bandwidth and the cost of processing video, as opposed to tokenized text. So I think that this engine of scaling up deep learning algorithms, which has been running for something like 15 years now, still has steam in it. Having said that, it only applies to certain problems, and there’s a set of other problems that need small data solutions.

When you say you want a foundation model for computer vision, what do you mean by that?

Ng: This is a term coined by Percy Liang and some of my friends at Stanford to refer to very large models, trained on very large data sets, that can be tuned for specific applications. For example, GPT-3 is an example of a foundation model [for NLP]. Foundation models offer a lot of promise as a new paradigm in developing machine learning applications, but also challenges in terms of making sure that they’re reasonably fair and free from bias, especially if many of us will be building on top of them.

What needs to happen for someone to build a foundation model for video?

Ng: I think there is a scalability problem. The compute power needed to process the large volume of images for video is significant, and I think that’s why foundation models have arisen first in NLP. Many researchers are working on this, and I think we’re seeing early signs of such models being developed in computer vision. But I’m confident that if a semiconductor maker gave us 10 times more processor power, we could easily find 10 times more video to build such models for vision.

Having said that, a lot of what’s happened over the past decade is that deep learning has happened in consumer-facing companies that have large user bases, sometimes billions of users, and therefore very large data sets. While that paradigm of machine learning has driven a lot of economic value in consumer software, I find that that recipe of scale doesn’t work for other industries.

It’s funny to hear you say that, because your early work was at a consumer-facing company with millions of users.

Ng: Over a decade ago, when I proposed starting the Google Brain project to use Google’s compute infrastructure to build very large neural networks, it was a controversial step. One very senior person pulled me aside and warned me that starting Google Brain would be bad for my career. I think he felt that the action couldn’t just be in scaling up, and that I should instead focus on architecture innovation.

“In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.” —Andrew Ng, CEO & Founder, Landing AI

I remember when my students and I published the first NeurIPS workshop paper advocating using CUDA, a platform for processing on GPUs, for deep learning—a different senior person in AI sat me down and said, “CUDA is really complicated to program. As a programming paradigm, this seems like too much work.” I did manage to convince him; the other person I did not convince.

Over the past year as I’ve been speaking to people about the data-centric AI movement, I’ve been getting flashbacks to when I was speaking to people about deep learning and scalability 10 or 15 years ago. In the past year, I’ve been getting the same mix of “there’s nothing new here” and “this seems like the wrong direction.”

How do you define data-centric AI, and why do you consider it a movement?

Ng: Data-centric AI is the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to successfully build an AI system. For an AI system, you have to implement some algorithm, say a neural network, in code and then train it on your data set. The dominant paradigm over the last decade was to download the data set while you focus on improving the code. Thanks to that paradigm, over the last decade deep learning networks have improved significantly, to the point where for a lot of applications the code—the neural network architecture—is basically a solved problem. So for many practical applications, it’s now more productive to hold the neural network architecture fixed, and instead find ways to improve the data.

When I started speaking about this, there were many practitioners who, completely appropriately, raised their hands and said, “Yes, we’ve been doing this for 20 years.” This is the time to take the things that some individuals have been doing intuitively and make it a systematic engineering discipline.

The data-centric AI movement is much bigger than one company or group of researchers. My collaborators and I organized a data-centric AI workshop at NeurIPS, and I was really delighted at the number of authors and presenters that showed up.

You often talk about companies or institutions that have only a small amount of data to work with. How can data-centric AI help them?

Ng: You hear a lot about vision systems built with millions of images—I once built a face recognition system using 350 million images. Architectures built for hundreds of millions of images don’t work with only 50 images. But it turns out, if you have 50 really good examples, you can build something valuable, like a defect-inspection system. In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.

When you talk about training a model with just 50 images, does that really mean you’re taking an existing model that was trained on a very large data set and fine-tuning it? Or do you mean a brand new model that’s designed to learn only from that small data set?

Ng: Let me describe what Landing AI does. When doing visual inspection for manufacturers, we often use our own flavor of RetinaNet. It is a pretrained model. Having said that, the pretraining is a small piece of the puzzle. What’s a bigger piece of the puzzle is providing tools that enable the manufacturer to pick the right set of images [to use for fine-tuning] and label them in a consistent way. There’s a very practical problem we’ve seen spanning vision, NLP, and speech, where even human annotators don’t agree on the appropriate label. For big data applications, the common response has been: If the data is noisy, let’s just get a lot of data and the algorithm will average over it. But if you can develop tools that flag where the data’s inconsistent and give you a very targeted way to improve the consistency of the data, that turns out to be a more efficient way to get a high-performing system.

“Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.” —Andrew Ng

For example, if you have 10,000 images where 30 images are of one class, and those 30 images are labeled inconsistently, one of the things we do is build tools to draw your attention to the subset of data that’s inconsistent. So you can very quickly relabel those images to be more consistent, and this leads to improvement in performance.

Could this focus on high-quality data help with bias in data sets? If you’re able to curate the data more before training?

Ng: Very much so. Many researchers have pointed out that biased data is one factor among many leading to biased systems. There have been many thoughtful efforts to engineer the data. At the NeurIPS workshop, Olga Russakovsky gave a really nice talk on this. At the main NeurIPS conference, I also really enjoyed Mary Gray’s presentation, which touched on how data-centric AI is one piece of the solution, but not the entire solution. New tools like Datasheets for Datasets also seem like an important piece of the puzzle.

One of the powerful tools that data-centric AI gives us is the ability to engineer a subset of the data. Imagine training a machine-learning system and finding that its performance is okay for most of the data set, but its performance is biased for just a subset of the data. If you try to change the whole neural network architecture to improve the performance on just that subset, it’s quite difficult. But if you can engineer a subset of the data you can address the problem in a much more targeted way.

When you talk about engineering the data, what do you mean exactly?

Ng: In AI, data cleaning is important, but the way the data has been cleaned has often been in very manual ways. In computer vision, someone may visualize images through a Jupyter notebook and maybe spot the problem, and maybe fix it. But I’m excited about tools that allow you to have a very large data set, tools that draw your attention quickly and efficiently to the subset of data where, say, the labels are noisy. Or to quickly bring your attention to the one class among 100 classes where it would benefit you to collect more data. Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.

For example, I once figured out that a speech-recognition system was performing poorly when there was car noise in the background. Knowing that allowed me to collect more data with car noise in the background, rather than trying to collect more data for everything, which would have been expensive and slow.

What about using synthetic data, is that often a good solution?

Ng: I think synthetic data is an important tool in the tool chest of data-centric AI. At the NeurIPS workshop, Anima Anandkumar gave a great talk that touched on synthetic data. I think there are important uses of synthetic data that go beyond just being a preprocessing step for increasing the data set for a learning algorithm. I’d love to see more tools to let developers use synthetic data generation as part of the closed loop of iterative machine learning development.

Do you mean that synthetic data would allow you to try the model on more data sets?

Ng: Not really. Here’s an example. Let’s say you’re trying to detect defects in a smartphone casing. There are many different types of defects on smartphones. It could be a scratch, a dent, pit marks, discoloration of the material, other types of blemishes. If you train the model and then find through error analysis that it’s doing well overall but it’s performing poorly on pit marks, then synthetic data generation allows you to address the problem in a more targeted way. You could generate more data just for the pit-mark category.

“In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models.” —Andrew Ng

Synthetic data generation is a very powerful tool, but there are many simpler tools that I will often try first. Such as data augmentation, improving labeling consistency, or just asking a factory to collect more data.

To make these issues more concrete, can you walk me through an example? When a company approaches Landing AI and says it has a problem with visual inspection, how do you onboard them and work toward deployment?

Ng: When a customer approaches us we usually have a conversation about their inspection problem and look at a few images to verify that the problem is feasible with computer vision. Assuming it is, we ask them to upload the data to the LandingLens platform. We often advise them on the methodology of data-centric AI and help them label the data.

One of the foci of Landing AI is to empower manufacturing companies to do the machine learning work themselves. A lot of our work is making sure the software is fast and easy to use. Through the iterative process of machine learning development, we advise customers on things like how to train models on the platform, when and how to improve the labeling of data so the performance of the model improves. Our training and software supports them all the way through deploying the trained model to an edge device in the factory.

How do you deal with changing needs? If products change or lighting conditions change in the factory, can the model keep up?

Ng: It varies by manufacturer. There is data drift in many contexts. But there are some manufacturers that have been running the same manufacturing line for 20 years now with few changes, so they don’t expect changes in the next five years. Those stable environments make things easier. For other manufacturers, we provide tools to flag when there’s a significant data-drift issue. I find it really important to empower manufacturing customers to correct data, retrain, and update the model. Because if something changes and it’s 3 a.m. in the United States, I want them to be able to adapt their learning algorithm right away to maintain operations.

In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models. The challenge is, how do you do that without Landing AI having to hire 10,000 machine learning specialists?

So you’re saying that to make it scale, you have to empower customers to do a lot of the training and other work.

Ng: Yes, exactly! This is an industry-wide problem in AI, not just in manufacturing. Look at health care. Every hospital has its own slightly different format for electronic health records. How can every hospital train its own custom AI model? Expecting every hospital’s IT personnel to invent new neural-network architectures is unrealistic. The only way out of this dilemma is to build tools that empower the customers to build their own models by giving them tools to engineer the data and express their domain knowledge. That’s what Landing AI is executing in computer vision, and the field of AI needs other teams to execute this in other domains.

Is there anything else you think it’s important for people to understand about the work you’re doing or the data-centric AI movement?

Ng: In the last decade, the biggest shift in AI was a shift to deep learning. I think it’s quite possible that in this decade the biggest shift will be to data-centric AI. With the maturity of today’s neural network architectures, I think for a lot of the practical applications the bottleneck will be whether we can efficiently get the data we need to develop systems that work well. The data-centric AI movement has tremendous energy and momentum across the whole community. I hope more researchers and developers will jump in and work on it.

This article appears in the April 2022 print issue as “Andrew Ng, AI Minimalist.”

Eliza Strickland is IEEE Spectrum's features editor, where she helps develop and shape the magazine’s longform stories. She also oversees Spectrum's coverage of artificial intelligence and biomedical engineering. She holds a master’s degree in journalism from Columbia University.
